ALTA 2013 25 #### DNi-Overview #### A Compelling Business Case **Direct Nickel has developed a game changing process for extracting nickel from laterite deposits. It will position Direct Nickel as one of the lowest cash cost producers in the global nickel industry in the next 5 years. The Process offers unparalleled cost efficiency, capital savings and environmental benefits.** ###### **Why is there an opportunity?** - Nickel is a US$30 billion a year industry. - The demand for nickel is growing and supply is threatened. - Nickel sulphide discoveries are declining yet there is an abundant and alternative supply of laterite resources. - Existing High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) and ferronickel processes are struggling with CAPEX, OPEX, technical risk, delays and commercial failure. **DNi offers a new proprietary processing solution that will position the Company among the lowest cash cost nickel producers in the next 5 years that are able to meet the growing global demand.** ALTA 2013 26 DNi – What Do We Offer?
• CAPITAL SAVINGS
- Cut capital and operating costs by 50% : DNi Process is expected to halve capital and operating costs
compared to other existing laterite processes (HPAL an

d FeNi). Stainless steel vessels rather than exotics.
Smaller plants possible with lower capital intensity.
• OPERATING COST EFFICIENCIES
- Recycling of nitric acid : high recovery and recycling of nitric acid leads to a more environmentally friendly and
sustainable process.
- Additional revenue from by-products : Main product is Ni/Co hydroxides (MHP) in addition marketable products
can be made from the hematite residue and magnesium oxide.
- Lower maintenance costs: maintenance costs are reduced by the low intensity of the process.
• ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS
- Harmful gases and elements are reusable : all NOx gases are captured and converted to reusable nitric acid.
• COMPREHENSIVE IP PROTECTION
- US & Australian patent attorneys manage a comprehensive patent and IP protection strategy for the nitric
acid/nickel laterite space ensuring that the process is for exclusive use by DNi and its licensees

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

A typical lateritic ore body contains several different weathered zones (Figure 1); the limonitic zone closest to the surface and the saprolitic zone towards the bottom. The limonitic zone is predominantly made up of iron oxides, like goethite, while the saprolitic zone is least weathered as it is present in the deepest section of the deposit. It therefore contains mainly silicates such as serpentines. There may be an intermediate zone made up of clays such as nontronite which is usually only present in dry climates. Nickel in these deposits is expected to exist mainly in goethite, clays ( _e.g._ nontronite) and serpentines ( _e.g._ lizardite). 



**Figure 1: Typical laterite profile showing limonitic, nontronitic and saprolitic zones.** 

An understanding of ore mineralogy and elemental deportment is vital for the effective processing of nickel from an ore body. Common ore characterisation techniques, such as Quantitative X-Ray Diffraction (QXRD) and Quantitative Evaluation of Minerals by Scanning Electron Microscopy (QEMSCAN) can be costly, time-consuming or not available at mine sites. QXRD combined with elemental analysis by Energy Dispersive X-Ray Spectroscopy (EDX) is commonly used to estimate nickel deportment. Although QXRD can be used for major miner

al prediction it cannot be used to identify where the nickel is specifically located. Furthermore, techniques such as QEMSCAN may be ineffective for nickel deportment analysis; because the number of counts taken per sample is low, analysis using this technique may be problematic if the nickel concentrations in the target minerals are low. 

A possible alternative to mineralogical analysis for determining nickel deportment is by the selective sequential leaching of nickel-containing minerals followed by the determination of nickel in solution after each leach. This approach, termed diagnostic leaching, could be a simple, accessible, costeffective and more accurate alternative to mineralogical analysis. 

Traditionally, diagnostic leaching employs sequential leach stages to study the elemental speciation in an ore body. The extraction process consists of treating a sample with a series of successive chemical treatments, with each successive stage being more aggressive or differing in nature from the previous step (Hall et al. 1996). The stages often differ by the chemical properties of the extractants, extraction efficiency, experimental parameter effects, the sequence of extractions, matrix effects and the heterogeneity and physical associations in the sample (Kersten and Fцrstner 1989). By studying the metals removed at each stage, the different levels of mineral substitution can be determined within a sample.

Swamy et al. (2003), Sohlenius and Oborn (2004) and Dold (2003) have proposed sequential leach protocols for determining nickel deportment but none have targeted all zones of a lateritic ore body. Using these protocols as a basis, research was undertaken by Chapman et al. (2012) and a new five-step leach process for the diagnostic leaching of nickel laterite ores and determination of nickel deportment in all zones of the ore body was proposed. Each successive step in the proposed diagnostic leach targets specific mineral types. Analysis of nickel in solution after each leaching step allows for the prediction of the location of the nickel i.e. as water soluble, exchangeable, amorphous, adsorbed, structurally bound or “difficult to leach” nickel. A summary of the leach methodology is as follows: 

Step 1: Dissolution of water soluble fraction to determine percentage of water soluble minerals or metals. 

Step 2: Dissolution of exchangeable fraction where exchangeable cations are leached with ammonium acetate (1 M CH3COONH4, buffered to pH 4.5 using 1 M acetic acid): 



Step 3: Dissolution of amorphous fraction where amorphous materials are leached with ammonium oxalate (0.2 M C2O4(NH4)2, buffered to pH 3.0 using 0.2 M oxalic acid): 



Step 4: Dissolution of adsorbed fraction where adsorbed elements on mineral surfaces are leached with dilute sulfuric acid (0.05 M H2SO4): 



Step 5: Dissolution of structurally bound fraction where all oxides and silicates leach using concentrated hydrochloric acid (32 % HCl): 



Using th

ese diagnostic leaching steps, Chapman et al. (2012) have been able to characterise the origin of the nickel in selected ore samples. For example, previous tests on selected nickel laterite ores highlighted spinel minerals that were difficult to leach and quartz minerals present in these ores were found to be nickel-barren. Furthermore, a distinction could be made between nickel in the amorphous phases, namely manganese oxides and low-crystallinity hydrated iron oxides, and crystalline minerals such as goethite, nontronite, lizardite and chlorite-group minerals ( _e.g._ clinochlore). It should be noted that the independent leaching of these main minerals was not possible using the diagnostic leaching technique and if more than one of these minerals is present, the amount of nickel associated with each mineral cannot be determined. However, the leaching methodology is rapid, uses simple solution analysis, and may be an affordable method to determine whether nickel is present in minerals that are difficult to leach ( _e.g._ spinels), amorphous phases and/or leachable crystalline phases. Using these leaches, theoretical nickel leach recoveries can be determined, where the leachable nickel is a sum of all the nickel leached from the five step process and the nickel remaining in the residue after the diagnostic leach has been performed is termed “difficult to leach”. Predicted theoretical nickel recoveries by this method have not yet been compared to those determined from typical atmospheric or ambient leaching processes used in industry. If this diagnostic leach protocol is found to be accurate, the use of diagnostic leaching for the characterisation of an ore body would allow for the determination of recoverable nickel and therefore, smarter mine planning ( _e.g._ introduction of blending, selective processing of ore) to ensure maximum nickel output. 

Typical nickel leaching processes include high pressure acid leaching (HPAL at high temperature and pressure), atmospheric leaching (high temperature, atmospheric pressure) and heap leaching (ambient temperature and pressure). There are a number of processes under development such as the Jaguar process, the sulfation atmospheric leach process and bioleaching (Kyle 2010), the Зaldağ heap leaching process ( _e.g._ Oxley et al. 2006), the ARNi process (Pelser et al. 2009) and the Direct Nickel process (McCarthy and Brock 2011). HPAL is the most common process, and the only one of the above processes commercialised to date. It is said to be the most capital intensive, with high operating costs (Kyle 2010) and is normally used only for limonitic ores as magnesium

41 

silicates (serpentines) are high acid consumers. While high capital costs may be acceptable for large project developments, smaller scale projects are investigating the use of atmospheric or ambient leaching which may be less capital intensive, but with higher acid and limestone consumptions (Kyle 2010). 

According to Whittingt

on and Muir (2000), sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid are the most effective acids for use in atmospheric leaching, with sulfuric acid being the most widely used to date. They suggest using an acid with strength greater than 0.25 M, at temperatures of up to 95°C for 2 h. It is also suggested that pre-roasting and reducing agents are used to enhance the extraction of nickel from limonitic ores (Whittington and Muir 2000). Acid consumptions are relatively high for atmospheric leaching and range from 500–700 kg tonne<sup>-1</sup> of ore (Kyle 2010). Ambient leaches conducted via laboratory bottle roll tests are often used as an approximation to nickel heap leaching. According to literature, acid consumptions for bottle roll tests vary between 400–800 kg tonne<sup>-1</sup> ore (Horizonte Minerals 2012). 

The aim of this project was to determine whether the theoretical nickel recoveries obtained from the diagnostic leaching steps developed by Chapman et al. (2012) are valid. The results from the diagnostic leach are not discussed in detail in this paper but are provided in the paper by Chapman et al. The diagnostic leach validation was done by assessing the correlation between predicted and actual nickel leached from six different samples in ambient (bottle roll) leaches. Bottle roll tests were conducted as an approximation to heap leaching at atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature to obtain nickel recoveries for comparison to the diagnostic leach predictions. Atmospheric leach tests at high temperatures were performed prior to the bottle roll leaches using literature-based experimental parameters to obtain a preliminary indication of the sample reactivity and acid consumption. 

###### **METHODOLOGY** 

###### **Ore Preparation** 

Nickel laterite ores from three deposits (termed Sites 1 to 3) were used in this study. Two samples were used from each of the limonitic and saprolitic zones of the deposits. The ores were dried and milled (P80 < 50 µm) using a ring mill to ensure optimal mineral liberation. Mineralogical ore compositions were determined using a Panalytical Empyrean automated powder diffractometer fitted with cobalt long line focus X-ray tube (6.9 keV) between 2θ angles of 5.01-89.98° (at 45 kV, 40 mA). XRD analyses were performed using TOPAS (Version 3) software. Elemental concentrations in the head ore samples were confirmed by fusing the samples with borate flux and dissolving the resulting glass in weak mineral acid. Concentrations of Al, Ca, Cr, Co, Fe, Mg, Mn, Ni and Si in the resultant solutions were determined by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) using a Varian Vista-Pro instrument. 

###### **Atmospheric Leaching** 

Approximately 150 g of the limonitic and saprolitic ore sample from each deposit were placed into 1 L HDPE plastic bottles, to which 105 g 98 % sulfuric acid and 435 mL de-ionised water were added (261 g L<sup>-1</sup> sulfuric acid, pulp density 25 % w/w). The bottles were pl

aced on a shaker table for 6 h at atmospheric pressure and 70–80 °C (Thermoline Orbital shaker or New Brunswick Innova 4080 benchtop incubator shaker). Slurry samples (10 mL) were taken at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 6 h intervals for all leaches. Each slurry sample was vacuum filtered, solution collected, solid repulped in de-ionised water, filtered, washed and dried at 40°C. Free acidities in the leach solutions were determined by the oxalate method: 0.1 mL of solution (0.2 mL solution for the 4 and 6 h samples) was placed in a 100 mL beaker and an appropriate amount of 50 % oxalate, adjusted to above pH 12, was added to the beaker. The solution was diluted to ~50 mL with de-ionised water and titrated with 0.05 M NaOH to an end point of pH 7.5 using a Metrohm Titrando 904 and sample processor with Tiamo software. Elemental concentrations in the resultant leach solutions were determined for all kinetic samples using ICP-OES on a Varian Vista-Pro instrument for an elemental suite of Al, Fe, Mg, Ni and Si for all solutions, with Ca, Cr, Co and Mn being analysed where present in the ore, based on original mineralogical analysis. Elemental and XRD analyses of the solid residue from the 6 h samples were determined as for the head ore samples.

###### **Ambient (Bottle Roll) Leaching** 

Approximately 100 g of limonitic and saprolitic ore sample from each deposit were placed into 2 L HDPE plastic bottles, to which 170 g of 98 % sulfuric acid and 730 mL de-ionised water were added (pulp density 10 % w/w). The bottles were placed on a bottle roller (Labtechnics) for 80 days at atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature. Solution samples (5 mL) were taken daily for five weeks via filtration using a 0.45 µm acro-disc. Once ICP analysis showed extracted metal concentrations reaching a plateau, sampling was continued every 3 to 4 days for the remaining 6 weeks. Free acidities, elemental concentrations and XRD traces were obtained as for the atmospheric leach tests.

Furthermore, acid consumption is better predicted from mineralogical information than from standard literature recommendations. Sufficient acid was added to the bottle roll leach tests to ensure the ores leached to completion where this was possible thermodynamically within the leach time employed. The nickel recovery from all three saprolite ores was complete within 11 days. Nickel leaching from the limonitic ore samples was complete after 50 days for the Site 2 limonite sample and appeared to be reaching completion for the remain

ing limonite samples after 80 days. XRD results confirmed that lizardite, nontronite and forsterite leached to completion in the bottle roll leach tests as confirmed by the appearance of an “amorphous peak” between 2θ = 20–30° for the saprolite ores. Goethite leached only partially in some cases, as confirmed by the incomplete percentage recovery of iron. Despite the incomplete goethite leaching, the nickel recovery in these samples was higher than expected. This could be because nickel-substituted goethite can leach more readily than unsubstituted goethite in sulfuric acid. 

A comparison of the results for the predicted nickel recoveries from the diagnostic leach tests shows that the diagnostic leach predicts the bottle roll leach outcomes to within 3 % for the saprolite samples. The limonite samples prove harder to predict with an up to 14 % deviation in predictions. This could be because the goethite does not leach as well with sulfuric acid and/or under the conditions employed when compared to the diagnostic leaching step using 32% HCl. From the diagnostic leach, it was predicted that the nickel in the saprolite samples was dispersed across more of the fraction types, while that in the limonite is mainly structurally bound. SEM analysis of the residues from the bottle roll leaches may allow for the confirmation of the location of the nickel in the residues. 

The results from the validation of the diagnostic leach by bottle roll leaching are preliminary in nature and there is scope for improvement and further work. However, we believe that initial results have been shown to be promising. Test work on additional laterite ores including mineralogical residue and possibly kinetic solid sample analysis is recommended to further confirm the diagnostic leach predictions.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Summervale-Westlynn lateritic nickel/cobalt mineralisation, approximately 500 km NW of Sydney (NSW), has relatively high nickel (averaging 0.85% Ni) content and it is amenable to upgrading by physical means. The Summervale-Westlynn deposit, based on drilling data, is largely a saprolitic type formed by alteration of Fe-enriched harzburgites, an ultramafic r o c k of peridotite composition, consisting of olivine and orthopyroxene. The limonitic type mineralisation is less dominant and it has either never been developed or largely eroded. Experimental work showed that the Summervale-Westlynn ores can be upgraded by sizing, wet gravity and magnetic separations. The coarse fraction contained the least amount of nickel and cobalt. Rejection of the coarse fraction by sizing also improved the grade of the remaining ore. Regrinding the coarse fraction and subsequently repeating the gravity and magnetic separation improved the nickel recoveries to some extent. This study showed that a product containing up to 35% more nickel could be made from the Summervale-Westlynn ores. This product is expected to be suitable for ferronickel production. In this paper, the results of the bench-scale tests are discussed.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Summervale – Westlynn (Exploration Licences EL7281 and EL6009, respectively) is a nickel-cobalt prospe

ct of Jervois Mining Ltd located approximately 25 km North West of Nyngan, NSW, straddling the Mitchell Highway (Figure 1). They cover the north east limb of a north south trending arcuate belt of serpentinised ultramafics known as the Westlynn Serpentinite; within the Girilambone-Wagga Anticlinorial Zone. The linear orientation of the belt suggests emplacement along regional deformation or faults of Alpine-type (ophiolite) origin. The EL7281 and EL6009 exploration licence areas of Jervois Mining and the neighbouring licenced areas of others are shown in Figure **1** . 



**Figure 1: EL7281 and EL6009 Ni-Co exploration licence areas for Jervois Mining Ltd. The location of Jervois Mining’s neighbouring scandium and gold tenements are also shown.** 

The Westlynn Serpentinite system is derived from the alteration of a medium grained dunite intruded into the metamorphosed Ordovician Girilambone Group. The Girilambone Group is comprised of phyllites, quartz-mica and chlorite schists, quartzite, laminated siltstone (all with pervasive quartz veins) and conglomerates of Cambrian-Ordovician age; with numerous late Silurian to early Devonian intrusives of ultramafic to intermediate composition. The concession sites are almost completely covered by late Tertiary and Quaternary aged alluvium. 

The two prospects were initially identified from airborne magnetics conducted as part of the Discovery 2000, Exploration NSW and New Frontiers regional airborne geophysical surveys. The tenement was drilled by a team lead by Jervois Mining’s Exploration Manager, Dr. Sanja van Huet. It is interesting to note that despite quite intensive airborne geophysics and ground magnetic surveys across the tenement, no other explorer had drilled a test hole in the anomaly until Jervois was granted the tenement in 2009. 

Preliminary calculations show possible reserves of up to 16.4 Mt at an average grade of 0.85% Ni and 0.064% Co. Further drilling and computer software based proper reserve grade calculations are planned and these activities are in progress. It is expected that the proven reserves of these deposits will improve by further drilling. 

Table **1** shows the present ranking of Summervale-Westlynn deposit among other Australian lateritic nickel deposits. 

The main objective of this paper is to present the results of bench-scale test work performed on Summervale-Westlynn ores.

###### **MINERALOGY** 

###### **Optical Microscopy Determinations** 

Optical mineralogy determinations on saprolite showed the sample was consisted of clay aggregates, patches of bastite - serpent

ine, ex-orthopyroxene, lizardite, antigorite and limonitestained clay. Subordinate scattered Fe-stained and foliated clay is probably serpentine or chlorite ± smectite. Minor opaque oxide grains (3-5%) are disseminated, seen in reflected light to be anhedral magnetite to 2mm long and microcrystalline magnetite ± hematite. Some magnetite and hematite also occur in a fracture with brown clay. The rock chip attracts a suspended magnet. 

The texture and chemistry indicates a former Cr-rich, Ti-poor harzburgite, with Fe-Mn-Ni-enrichment and Mg depletion due to alteration. Most of the anomalous chromium could be in serpentine and magnetite, with nickel possibly in serpentine. Sodium in the assay may reflect saline water as no sodium minerals are visible. 

###### **XRD (X-Ray Diffraction) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) Determinations** 

XRD determinations of five select drill cores samples are summarised in Table **2** . Samples are in general, grab samples. In Table **2** , lizardite is the major serpentine group mineral with a general formula of M3T2O5(OH)4, where M is mainly magnesium (Mg) and ferrous (Fe<sup>2+</sup> ) and ferric iron (Fe<sup>3+</sup> ), but could contain various amounts of aluminum (Al), nickel (Ni), manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), chromium (Cr), zinc (Zn), or lithium (Li); and T is mainly silicon (Si) but could also contain Al, Fe<sup>3+</sup> , or boron (B). Chrysotile and antigorite are rare. 

There is also data, which will be discussed in the next section, indicating that in altered serpentinite, nickel occurs mainly in magnetite and maghemite. The nickel content of lizardite is negligible. Maghemite, a common magnetic mineral at Summervale, is a partially oxidised magnetite. Further alteration (or lateritisation) of magnetite/maghemite produces goethite and hematite. Nickel released from decomposed magnetite is co-precipitated with (or adsorbed on the surfaces of) newly forming alteration products, mainly goethite and clay minerals. 

The presence of low levels of Ni/Co in lizardite is the main factor that makes the physical upgrading possible. 

Colour variations (Figure **2** ) among the Summervale-Westlynn drill core samples indicate various levels of exposure to lateritisation. Green-grey ores are saprolites and altered serpentinites. The green-grey coloured ores contain mainly lizardite and varying amounts of clay minerals and clinochlore whereas brown coloured ores are limonite-hematite and made of mainly goethite, hematite and to a lesser extent maghemite. Dark grey-black colour represents the dominance of maghemite and magnetite. 

The Scanning Electron Microscopy work on one of the drill core samples (SV 49 – limonitic  brown coloured laterite) to identify minerals that host nickel and cobalt showed the presence of up to 5.2% Ni in a mineral phase consisting mainly of Fe-Cr-Mn (Figure **3** ). However, not every Fe-Cr-Mn grain was enriched in Ni to the same extent. The SEM data showed that lower grade Ni was

found often in iron oxides, possibly in goethite. Cobalt, up to 2.5%, was contained largely in a manganese-rich mineral phase (Figure • **4** ), possibly nickel depleted asbolane (Ni0.3Co0.1Ca0.1Mn2+ 1.5O 1.5 (OH)2 0.6(H2O)). Similarly, magnesium-(aluminium)-silicates, iron-aluminium-silicates (iron-stained clay), Cr-spinels and iron-oxides were also largely barren or contained only small amounts of nickel. The SEM study also detected the presence of occasional zircon and rare earth phosphate minerals. It is expected that re-grinding, gravity and magnetic separation on the non-magnetic fraction would recover additional high grade nickel stream. ###### **GRAVITY SEPARATION USING WILFLEY TABLE** A larger scale gravity separation using a lab-size Wilfley shaking table was performed. In this test, a 19.3 kg composite sample comprising thirty-six samples from four different drill holes, each sample representing one metre interval, was used. These samples were varied in colour from brown to greenish grey and in composition from limonitic to saprolitic and altered serpentinite. The test was done at Metallurgical and Minerals Testing Laboratory ( AMML, Gosford, NSW) and involved: (a) drying the individual samples at 110°C and weighing, (b) combining all samples and wet screening at 212 µm (c) grinding oversize and screening at 212 µm repeatedly until 100% passing 212 µm (d) feeding the entire sample onto the table over a 30 min period, giving a nominal feed rate of 0.66 kg /min. (e) collecting seven products from the table, products 1, 2 and 3 gravity concentrates, and products 4 to 7 middlings and tails. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Global demand in base metals has put more pressure on mining low grade disseminated copper and nickel ores. With grades regularly sitting below 1% the removal of unwanted barren material through sensor based ore sorting would significantly upgrade the ore body and remove unwanted contaminants from the downstream processing system. 

X-ray fluorescence is a technology commonly known in the mining industry. It is used in on-site laboratories to assay samples, on core loggers and at the face in the form of a handheld XRF analyser. It works on the principle of secondary x-ray emission to ascertain the elemental composition of the sample. 

Outside the laboratory most XRF systems are only sensitive to elements of atomic number 20 (Calcium) and greater. Their accuracy is directly related to the homogeneity of the sample, the number of readings and the time taken for each reading. 

XRF is most commonly used in the field for base metals and the heavier elements such as uranium and lead. It is thus not surprising that it has been incorporated into ore sorting equipment to sort material based on the elemental composition of each particle. The major problem with using XRF in sorting is the time required for the sensor to produce an accurate elemental composition. Tomra Sorting Solutions has been using XRF in the sorting industry for several years and is now improving the system to g

ear it up for high throughput machines required in the mining industry capable of many thousands of particles per second and hundreds of tonnes per hour on a single sorter. 

This elemental sorting system actually benefits from the disseminated nature of some of the base metal ores. XRF is essentially a surface measurement and disseminated ores produce a more homogenous particle whose surface readings have a strong correlation to the grade of the entire particle. This opens doors for sorting copper and nickel as well as options for more accurately sorting other metals such as manganese, iron, chrome, gold and uranium, but crucial to this process is the ability to do it at on a high throughout machine that makes economic sense in the mining industry.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

X-ray fluorescence (XRF) systems are used on mine sites for laboratories assay, on core loggers and in the form of handheld XRF analysers. They are used to provide information on the elemental composition of samples and ore bodies that can then be used for a multitude of purposes including mine planning and process control. 

Incorporating XRF systems into ore sorters that can remove individual particles below a set grade has obvious benefits for downstream processing, transport and overall cost savings. These real time ore sorters have been developed for the mining industry over the last two decades<sup>(1)</sup> and more recently improved by Tomra Sorting Solutions. 

The difficulty with the XRF sensors is that they have not kept pace with the increase in speed and precision of the modern sorting platforms. The Tomra Sorting platforms are capable of particle speeds up to 6m/s, handling and individually separating up to 10 000 particles per second. This requires sensors that can measure the physical properties of the ore particle in less than 10ms. 

Although current XRF sensors can collect some data in the <10ms time frame, the continuous drop in head grades for particularly copper and nickel ore bodies, means that the sensitivity and size of these detectors is not sufficient to determine grades accurately in the <1% copper/nickel range. 

Tomra Sorting has teamed up with several international research partners over the last 5 years to develop a XRF sensor with higher sensitivity and speed to match the modern ore sorting platforms available today. These sorters are currently being used in the recycling industry and are now being optimised for mining with particular emphasis on the base metals. 



**Figure 1: Tomra XRF Ore Sorter Current being used in Recycling Industry** 

###### **ORE SORTERS** 

Ores sorters use a variety of sensors to measure physical properties of ore particles. This information is processed through high speed parallel processing electronics which compares the sensor information to predefined cut points that determine if each particle is part of the ore or waste stream. Air ejectors are then used to separate the waste and ore particl

es into different streams. ###### **Mechanical Handling** Presenting the particles to the sensing system and ejectors at high speed in a stable well distributed manner is critical in maximising sorter accuracy. Unstable or touching/overlapping particles increase errors in the sort. Two main configurations of sorters exist. These are belt and chute systems as in Figure 2Figure 3 below. These systems spread the particles stream across the entire width of the sorter and can handle particle sizes from 3mm up to 300mm. The throughput is dependent on the size range sorted but can be as high as 300t/h. Before the arrival of the belt and chute systems channelized sorters where used(5) . These used vibrating channelized feeders to present each ore particle to a sensor and ejector set. ALTA 2013 78 **Figure 4: Channelized Feed Sorting System (Wait K. 1987)****(5)** Although they can produce very good sorting results they are limited to only a few particles per second per channel thus the number of feed channels required for any significant throughput becomes uneconomical. ###### **Ejection/Separation** High speed stable particles require high speed, high flow air ejectors for accurate particle ejection. Modern belt and chute sorters use ejectors with cycle times as low as 2ms and air flow rates of over 1500l/min. This would produce a 12mm ejector resolution for a particle travelling at 6m/s. With many of the base metal ores the compromise between sorter throughput and mineral liberation means that the optimal size range for sorting is quite often in the 10-80mm range and higher throughputs mean minimising the gap between each of these particles, so the fast ejector cycle time and smaller high flow ejectors become a crucial part of the sorter design. These are often coupled with higher resolution sensors like laser scanners, with these higher resolution sensors being used to map the position of the particles as they move through the sorter. This image is then overlaid on the data gathered by the low resolution sensor. With a resolution of 20-75mm XRF systems definitely fall into this category. 

###### **X-RAY FLUORESCENCE IN SORTERS** 

The XRF system uses an x-ray tube to radiate the particles as they move through the sorter. Some of this radiation is absorbed by the material through a process known as the photoelectric affect where the x-ray photon ejects an electron from its atomic orbital. This vacancy produces an atom in an unstable state. To return to its original stable state an electron from an outer shell will occupy the vacancy and in so doing release a secondary or fluorescence photon with an energy characteristic of that element. 

A solid state detector is used to count the number of photons in each characteristic energy band and in so doing determine the elemental composition of the material. 



**Figure 7: X-Ray Fluorescence Schematic** 

ALTA 2013 

80 



**Figure 8: Atomic Level Schematic (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2007**<sup>**(4)**</sup> **)** 

In normal atmospheric conditions and due to limitations of the detectors elements with an atomic number lower than calcium (20) are not reliably detected. Most sorting applications target elements with atomic numbers starting around chromium (23) with particular emphasis on the base metals. This means that the detectors need to be particularly sensitive to x-rays in the 5-9keV range. 

Most XRF systems record data at a rate of up to 100 readings per second which translates to an integration time of at least 10ms. With higher grade particles where the level of fluorescent flux is high this may be sufficient. Getting accurate and reliable readings on ore in the <1% ranges of copper and nickel requires a system that is significantly faster and more sensitive. 

Increasing the speed and sensitivity of the XRF system is done in five ways: 

1. Increasing the flux/power of the primary x-ray sources. This enables higher x-ray absorption and thus more secondary x-ray emission. Although care needs to be taken to ensure that nonfluorescence x-rays do not saturate the detector. 

2. Decreasing the distance between the x-ray tube, ore particle and detector. The x-ray flux, both from the primary source and secondary emissions is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. So if you halve the distance to the detector you increase the flux by a factor of four. Although there are mechanical restrictions on how close the x-ray source, material and detector can be it is important to reduce it as much as possible. 

3. Increasing the physical size of detector to ensure the absorption of more fluorescence photons. Although this is li

mited by the size and spacing between the ore particles to ensure that only one particle is being characterised at a time. 

4. Increasing the speed of the detector to ensure that the increased flux does not saturate the detector high speed counting is required. 

5. Other geometric considerations include the angle between the detector and primary x-ray source, x-ray collimation and solid angle effects of the fan shaped x-ray beam. 

Increases in detector counts rate and x-ray flux can have significant effects on the resolution and background of the x-ray spectrum seen by the detector. The figure below shows an XRF spectrum of pure iron taken using a high spectral resolution detector over 34 seconds. This produces a very clean spectrum with low noise and distinct characteristic peaks.

###### **X-RAY FLUORESCENCE APPLICATIONS** 

The applications for XRF are vast. With high speed elemental analysis of each particle the question may be asked “Why would you need any other sensors?” There are however two major restrictions in XRF. 

One is that it is essentially a surface technique. The energy of the primary x-ray may be increased to get higher penetration into the particle but the secondary fluorescence photos are in the 5-9keV range for the base metals. This means that this photon can only escape through a few millimetres of rock thus restricting it to the outer surface of the ore particle. 

A second is that elements below calcium (20) on the periodic table are not detected in the sorting environment. In the ideal laboratory environment and with the use of pressured gas chambers or vacuums this number can be moved down to the lighter elements but with obvious restrictions for these chambers in sorters most applications focus on the base metals and heavier elements. 

A selection of common applications is described below. Many more ores types can be assessed using XRF and with each ore type and ore body being different the suggested process is to start with collecting data on a few hundred individual ore particles. This data is then compared to laboratory assay results of those particles to gain an understanding of the potential of this and other sensors for that ore body. 

###### **Gold**

Gold is a challenging ore to sort due to its low grade and often very uneven distribution within the ore particles. The nugget affect in gold ores makes sensing the gold directly with a surface technique like XRF unreliable. However gold is very often strongly associated to iron pyrite, arsenopyrite and other metal sulphides. These can be used to track the gold and can be reliably detected resulting in a significant increase in gold grade. 



**Figure 12: Iron and Arsenic Peaks Indicative of Gold** 

###### **Uranium** 

Uranium ore with individual particle grades down to even a few hundred ppm can be sorted using XRF. This system is however affected by the uranium distribution within the particle. Other techniques like using radiometric (RM) scintillation detectors do have advantages over XRF as the RM systems detect natural gamma ray emissions from the particles. The emissions are several hundred keV and so penetrate through from even the centre of the particle producing a system that assesses the entire particle and thus produces a more reliable sort.

###### **Iron Chrome Manganese** 

Iron, chrome and manganese ores with their higher grades are an easy target for XRF sorting. The high count rates in the XRF sensor are further from the noise levels and have lower counting error and thus can be used to accurately grade each ore particle. Other sensing systems like x-ray transmission have the advantage of scanning through the entire particle but cannot differentiate between heavy elements. XRF can distinguish elements like iron from manganese and so can be used to calculated ratios of these elements. This ratio of heavy elements can often be the basis of the sort. 

As can be seen in Figure 14 below there is significant overlap between the iron and manganese peaks. This is common for concurrent elements in the periodic table. ###### **GENERAL INTRODUCTION** 

Poseidon Nickel Limited (“Poseidon”) is developing the Windarra Nickel Project (“Windarra”), located near Laverton, 260km north east of Kalgoorlie, Western Australia. A Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) has been completed for the project, demonstrating robust project economics through low capital and mining costs. 

Windarra is based on two nickel sulphide deposits - Mt Windarra, a brownfields deposit containing 3.95 milli

on tonnes of ore at an average grade of 1.73% Ni and Cerberus, a greenfields deposit which contains 4.55 million tonnes of ore at 1.51% Ni. A nickel sulphide concentrator with a capacity of 900,000 tonnes per annum has been designed to produce 9,600 tonnes of contained nickel in concentrate each year over an initial 10-year life of mine. 

In addition to the nickel sulphide concentrator, a gold tailings treatment plant is also under development. The Mt Windarra deposit was previously mined and processed by WMC over an 18 year period, ending in 1994. During this time, a large amount of nickel and gold tailings were generated by the Windarra plant and other local operations. 

Currently, the gold tailings are stored in the north and south tailings dams. These contain a total of 4.35 million tonnes of material at an average gold grade of 0.72g/t. As part of the Windarra Nickel Project, Poseidon proposes to reprocess the gold tailings using a Carbon-inLeach plant, with the carbon stripping and gold bullion production toll treated by a third party in Kalgoorlie. 

An opportunity to further enhance the project exists in the form of historic nickel tailings and disseminated nickel ore in stockpiled waste dumps that are located within the mining lease. 

Poseidon has developed a hydrometallurgical process that can treat both of these materials simultaneously, as well as low grade nickel sulphide ore that is unsuitable for flotation. The flowsheet is based on a two-stage nitric acid leaching circuit operating at low acid addition rates and at atmospheric pressure. The process was developed in partnership with Direct Nickel Pty Ltd. 

The nitric acid leaching process generates leachate with very low levels of iron in solution under these conditions. Hence there is no need for a further pH adjustment step to remove iron, such as that required in a traditional leach circuit. The filtered leachate solution can be sent directly to a precipitation circuit to produce a high-grade mixed sulphide product. 

The oxide ore/tailings co-treatment product can be sold as a premium product or it can blended with the nickel concentrate from the main Windarra flotation circuit, increasing the nickel grade and reducing impurities. This strategy allows Poseidon to enhance flotation nickel recovery and reduce impurities, thereby maximising operational flexibility and profitability of the overall project. 

###### **FEED RESOURCES** 

The Windarra Nickel Project is based on two main ore bodies – Mt Windarra and Cerberus. 

Mt Windarra is a brownfields deposit, having previously been mined by WMC. Much of the underground infrastructure from this period remains, which will be utilised in the refurbished mine. The Indicated and Inferred Resource of Mt Windarra is 3.95 mt at 1.73% nickel, for a total of 68,300 tonnes of nickel. 

Cerberus was discovered by Poseidon in 2008 and will provide the balance of ore feed to the nickel sulphide concentrator. It has a total Indicated and In

**Figure 1: Process Block Flow Diagram** ###### **OPERATING STRATEGY** The oxide ore/tailings co-treatment project has been designed as a flexible operation, capable of treating different feed sources to produce a nickel sulphide precipitate appropriate for sale or for blending with flotation concentrate. The tailings and oxide dump material does not require any crushing, having been crushed during the historic Windarra operation. A milling circuit is required to grind the oxide material, but this represents less than half of the overall feed rate. The selection of nitric acid as the lixiviant was due to its ability to achieve high leach extraction with both oxides and sulphides under relatively mild conditions. Additionally, testwork conducted by Direct Nickel and SGS has proven that any iron in solution precipitates at relatively low pH levels in the nitrate system, meaning that a separate iron removal stage and neutralising reagents will not be needed. Aluminium also precipitates via the same mechanism. Mixed sulphide precipitation with hydrogen sulphide gas was selected for its high precipitation efficiency, proven operability and broad marketability. Additionally, the mixed sulphide product (as opposed to a mixed hydroxide product) can be easily blended with the concentrate produced by the main Windarra flotation circuit. This allows the flotation circuit to ALTA 2013 92 increase recovery by targeting a lower nickel grade in the flotation concentrate, while also improving the quality of the blended concentrate. ###### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION** ###### **Feed Preparation** The historic Windarra Tailings material requires limited preparation, as it has previously been crushed and milled. Some tramp removal and break up of agglomerates may be necessary. The oxide ore, however, will require both crushing and milling. Both feed materials (Oxide Ore and Windarra Tailings) are repulped using barren liquor from the sulphide precipitation area. Note that the Windarra Tailings may also reclaimed directly from the Central Tailings Dam via hydraulic mining, using infrastructure installed for the gold tailings treatment plant. ###### **Oxide Ore Pre-Leach** The Oxide Ore Pre-Leach uses nitric acid as the lixiviant. The leach is conducted at 90°C and atmospheric pressure in two tanks with an

extended residence time. Nitric acid is dosed at a rate of 600kg/t to the first tank, to facilitate high metal extraction. This also leaves a relatively high concentration of nitric acid in the discharge liquor. 

The general chemistry for the nitric acid leaching process is shown below. This formula can be applied to oxides of aluminium, calcium, cobalt, chromium, copper, iron, magnesium, manganese, nickel and zinc. 

_MO(s) + 2 HNO3(aq) → M[NO3]2(aq) + H2O(l)_ 

###### **Tailings Leach/Hydrolysis** 

The second stage of the process involves the addition of historic nickel sulphide tailings material to the Oxide Ore Pre-Leach discharge. The residual nitric acid present in the feed slurry causes any metal oxides in the tailings to leach via the same mechanism as the Oxide Ore Pre-Leach. 

There are, however, metal sulphides remaining in the tailings that will react simultaneously. These sulphides are expected to be oxidised and form sulphates: 

_3 FeS2(s) + 8 HNO3(aq) →  Fe[NO3]3(aq) + 2 H2SO4(aq) + 2 H2O(l) + 5 NO(g) Ni9S8(s) + 40 HNO3(aq) → 9 Ni[NO3]2(aq) + 8 H2SO4(aq) + 12 H2O(l) + 22 NO(g)_ 

The sulphides display fast reaction kinetics in nitric acid and nitric oxide (NO) gas evolves, as shown in the above equations.  Evaporation of nitric acid (as HNO3 and NO2) can also be observed under the expected operating conditions (95°C, atmospheric temperature.) The offgas reports to a scrubbing circuit, where the NOx species are recovered to form nitric acid for reuse. 

The high proportion of acid-consuming species in the nickel sulphide tailings also causes the pH in the system to rise. This, along with the raised temperature (95°C), promotes the hydrolysis of iron and aluminium to form jarosites and other sulphate-containing species: 

_3 Fe[NO3]3(aq) + 2 Na2SO4(aq) + 6 H2O(l) →_ 

_NaFe3[SO4]2[OH]6(s) + 2 NaNO3(aq) + 6 HNO3(aq)_ 

_3 Fe[NO3]3(aq) + 3 CaSO4(aq) + 3 H2O(l) →_ 

_3 Fe[OH][SO4](s) + 3 Ca[NO3]2(aq) + 3 HNO3(aq)_

The continuous pilot campaign was able to consistently generate leachate with less than 5mg/L iron via this mechanism. 

The flowsheet combining nitric acid leaching with iron removal via hydrolysis was developed in collaboration with Direct Nickel Pty Ltd and proven during on-going laboratory testwork. This has led to the filing of a joint patent for this process. 

###### **Leach Residue Filtration** 

The leach discharge slurry reports to a filtration step, where the filtrate (PLS) advances to Sulphide Precipitation and the residue reports to Tailings Neutralisation. Vendor testwork indicated that pressure filtration was the most effective separation method, as opposed to vacuum filtration and counter-current decantation. 

###### **Mixed Sulphide Precipitation** 

The PLS from Leach Residue Filtration is then used to feed a mixed sulphide precipitation circuit. Two different reductants were trialled in the continuous pilot campaign, with hydrogen sulphide gas (H2S) seen to achieve the best results. Th

e MSP circuit was operated at 80°C and at pressures less than 30kPag. Milled MSP seed was also added to the plant at a rate of 1.5 m2 of seed surface area per litre of PLS. |**Oxide**

This is completed over two main stages, oxidation and absorption. Nitric acid plants are generally standardised and modular in construction, comprising an ammonia oxidation reactor, NOx absorption vessel, heat recovery and compressor units. Poseidon has sourced competitive pricing on nitric acid plants, which is currently at a Prefeasibility level. ###### **WINDARRA FLOTATION CIRCUIT SYNERGY** The combined oxide ore/tailings treatment process is able to provide an important production synergy for the flotation circuit. The MSP product (containing around 50% nickel) can be blended with the flotation concentrate (containing ~10% nickel), thereby increasing its nickel content. This means that this flotation concentrate can potentially be sold at a premium. The same idea of spiking the flotation concentrate with MSP can also be used to improve the overall profitability of the flotation circuit. Laboratory testwork for the Windarra Nickel Project indicated that an inverse relationship exists between flotation product concentrate grade and metal recovery – for example, a target concentrate nickel grade of 10% will lead to around 84% nickel recovery, while a target concentrate grade of 8% nickel means that 90% recovery can be achieved. Higher recovery reduces the amount of nickel reporting to the tailings disposal. The nickel sulphide flotation circuit could target a lower concentrate grade, achieving a higher recovery and reducing the nickel losses to tailings. MSP would then be blended with this ALTA 2013 94 concentrate, increasing the nickel grade to ~10%. This means that the customer specifications would still be met, so there would be no reduction in the sale price. Another synergy between the sulphide flotation plant and the combined oxide ore/tailings plant is the potential to feed low grade sulphide ore to the pre-leach in place of oxide ore. Laboratory testing has shown that >90% leach nickel extraction can be achieved with sulphide ore under similar conditions. Therefore, nickel can potentially be recovered from sulphide ore that would otherwise be rejected, or the resource cut-off grade for the Mt Windarra and Cerberus ore bodie

s can be reduced. 

It may also be possible to further improve overall nickel recovery by feeding the current arisings from the sulphide flotation plant to the combined oxide ore/tailings plant. This may be particularly valuable when there are high feed grades entering the sulphide flotation plant, or to minimise losses during process disruptions of the flotation circuit. 

From another perspective, there is also plant and infrastructure in place for the main Windarra Nickel Project that can be used by the combined oxide ore/tailings plant. Services and utilities, such as water and power, as well as general infrastructure such as roads, accommodation and a laboratory will already be established. This means that the capital investment required for the combined oxide ore/tailings plant is reduced. 

A natural gas pipeline has also been proposed to service the Windarra Nickel Project’s power generation requirements. Natural gas can also be used as a feedstock for producing hydrogen, which is a key building block for the two major reagents required by the combined oxide ore/tailings plant, ammonia and hydrogen sulphide. This would lead to a further reduction in operating costs. 

###### **TESTWORK** 

Both batch and continuous laboratory testwork has been completed for the NATL project, investigating feed blends, operating conditions and other parameters. 

Preliminary batch testwork was completed by Direct Nickel, proving the amenability of tailings, oxide ore and lower grade sulphide ore to nitric acid leaching. 

A pilot plant campaign was completed in early 2012 at SGS Lakefield Oretest. A continuous leach/hydrolysis circuit was operated, trialling the performance of five different blends of Central Tailings Dam material and oxide ores. The impact of changes to the acid addition rate and leach temperature were also investigated, as was the composition of the leach offgas. From this testing, the combined leaching/hydrolysis mechanism was proven, and the leaching kinetics were also observed. 

In addition to the leach testing, continuous sulphide precipitation testing was also completed as part of the pilot campaign. Both hydrogen sulphide gas and dissolved sodium sulphide were able to achieve nickel precipitation efficiencies in excess of 95%. 

Vendor testing was also completed for both thickening and filtration of the leach residue. This showed that pressure filtration was the most effective dewatering technique for leach residue. 

Materials of construction were tested throughout the pilot testing campaign and also using longer term laboratory testing. Polypropylene tanks were used in the pilot campaign without issue, but this material did not withstand longer exposure to the high temperature and nitric acid concentration. A range of metal and plastic materials have also been investigated, with titanium alloys and some lined plastics both holding up in the expected conditions. 

Laboratory batch testwork has been continuing since the pilot camp

aign, in order to further refine operating targets. Particularly, the two-stage leaching process (Oxide Ore Leach followed by Nitric Acid Tailings Leach) has been successfully trialled under a range of conditions. estern Areas has offtake agreements with BHP Billiton for 12,000 tpa nickel in concentrate, and 13,000 tpa with Jinchuan for a total 26,000 tpa nickel in concentrate.

Western Areas acquired BioHeap in 2009, including the technology, intellectual property and key personnel. The BioHeap technology untilizes microbes for leaching of base metal sulphides, including primary copper, nickel and zinc sulphides as well as refractory gold ores. BioHeap has been successful in developing proprietary bacterial cultures that address the needs of the industry through its extensive research and development program for more than the last decade. 

The results of this research program are a wide range of cultures that can leach primary sulphides (including chalcopyrite) over a wide range of temperatures (15°C - 95°C) in fresh, saline and hypersaline water, up to 200 g/L TDS.  Arsenic tolerant variants are also available for treating high arsenic ores and work is continuing on cost reduction and broadening the range of conditions over which the technology is suited. The success of the bacterial development work and practical experiences have resulted in a number of patents that have being filed by BioHeap Ltd. These patents cover areas such as bacterial assisted heap leaching of sulphides minerals including chalcopyrite, to adaptation and improvement of bacteria used in the leaching process.  This paper aims to discuss one of the diagnostic techniques used during BioHeap test work programs. 

###### **DEVELOPMENT OF A HEAP LEACHING PROJECT** 

Typically the development of a heap leaching project, be it bacterial, or otherwise, follows a standard engineering pathway, such as that outlined by (White, 2012); scoping study, pre-feasibility study, feasibility study, engineering and construction. 

The complication for heap leaching projects, is that the leaching process itself tends to be slow, and the testwork programs for each stage of engineering tend to be quite long.  The testwork for heap leaching tends to drive the project development timeline, rather than the studies themselves. Project managers and engineers will invariably be waiting on results from leaching tests before the project can progress to the next stage of the study.

For heap leaching, testwork is likely to be the driver of development, and this is where the focus should be on reducing the development time. ###### **TESTWORK DELIVERABLES TO THE STUDIES** The various testwork stages deliver different types and quality of information. From an engineering perspective, the purpose of the testwork is to deliver data to form the engineering design criteria, a critical document upon which a large proportion of the engineering design, and therefore the cost estimates hinge. Most engineering firms define not only the value of a particular parameter, but also a range, and importantly a measure of quality (or data source). For a scoping study, it may be appropriate to have the majority of your design criteria sourced from estimates, factors or engineering databases, but as the study progresses, the aim is to have as much of the design criteria backed by quality testwork data. (Steemson & Smith, 2006) outlined a number of “critical heap leach” parameters, and while they were discussing nickel laterite heap leaching, these are equally important to sulphide heap leaching. The parameters listed are: 1. An understanding of acid consumption versus metal (including impurity) uptake. 2. An understanding of the impact of agglomeration on heap leach performance and the optimum agglomeration method. 3. Leach kinetics for nickel/cobalt and key impurities 4. Development of the most appropriate heap leach cycle, for example, the extent of recycle needed to increase nickel tenors in the PLS. 5. An understanding of scale-up issues in nickel laterite heap leaching. 6. An understanding of the variability in heap leaching behavior for different parts of the orebody, especially if there are significant variations in mineralogy. Some other parameters that are important, particularly to hard rock, low grade sulphide ores destined for bacterial heap leaching, include: 7. Bacterial performance. 8. Operating pH (and ORP and DO). ALTA 2013 128 9. Crushing Parameters (eg crushing index, abrasion index etc). 10. Mineral Liberation (recovery estimate versus crush size). There are many other parameters that are important to developing a project, including mining/geotech parameters, water sources, balance and management, infrastructure, power, downstream processing, marketing, logistics and financing, but for the purposes of this paper we will limit our discussion to the leach cycle. In order to improve the

outcomes of the engineering study, we want to have solid data for these parameters, as early as we can in the testwork cycle. The earlier we can select a parameter (for example crush size), the less costly the future testwork and studies will be, and the more that the large scale testwork programs will be verification, rather than discovery of leaching performance. ###### **DIAGNOSTIC TESTS** There are a range of diagnostic tests that are routinely used to give information about the ore. These include: mineralogy/QEMSCAN, sequential copper leaching, Cyanidation/LeachWELL™, percolation testing, acid mine drainage assays, all of which can provide specific information for various studies. BioHeap have long used an internal diagnostic technique called Nitric Acid Digest (NAD), to aid in determining the crush size for heap leaching, and we are increasingly relying on it as a predictor for leach recoveries. From the pilot trials that we have conducted to date, we have found that it provides a reasonable estimate of final nickel and copper recovery, that is better than either amenability, or column leaching, for the BioHeap technology. ###### **Nitric Acid Digest Procedure** The procedure for the nitric acid digests has evolved over time. This is expensive and time consuming. Our experience with engineers is that the one piece of data most widely relied on from column trials is the leach recovery, and a better estimate can probably be obtained (at least for BioHeap) from NAD tests in a few weeks. Piloting (or large columns) is best done on site and at large diameters. In our experience, 300mm columns x 8m high are notoriously difficult to get to run reliably, especially for jacketed perspex columns, and the column wall effects may be significant at such small diameters. At these diameters agglomeration or percolation issues may not become evident. Stainless steel or Polyethylene columns do tend to perform better, and the most reliable data is from fully integrating the downstream processing into the process and recycle streams. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** Our experience with using Nitric Acid Digests for crush size estimation has shown that Nitric Acid Digests tend to give a better estimate of copper leach recovery from chalcopyrite ores than either amenability or column leaching, in a much shorter time frame and at reduced cost. There is good agreement between a 2 week NAD test and a pilot trial on the same ore. For nickel, the results are not as compelling as those for copper. NAD testing of nickel tends to give a “worst case” estimate of leach recovery’s using a 1 week test. BioHeap feels that 2 week tests would probably give a better estimate, but it has not been possible to test this to date. The test work results seems to indicate that 2 week NAD tests are preferred to 1 week NAD tests for the purposes of estimating leach recovery’s. For crush size estimation 1 week NAD’s could be used, but again 2 week NAD’s are preferred. Finally, sample selection is critical. If the sample is unreliable, then the testwork techniques are irrelevant. The results will be unreliable. For any level of testwork, it is critically important that the ore origin is well

understood, as well as how the samples relate to the overall reserve and resource. Testing a sample that is not representative of the ore body may give erroneous results the results of which will be magnified as the project develops.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

With a selected organic system consisting of 50% TEHA (tris-2-ethylhexylamine) and 10% Shellsol A150 in octanol, over 80% H2SO4 was extracted from a feed solution containing 200 g/L H2SO4 at an A/O ratio of 1:2 in a single contact. After 3 stages of successive extraction, nearly 99% of acid was extracted with only 2 g/L H2SO4 left in the raffinate. It is found that the extracted acid was stripped readily from the loaded organic solution using water. After acid recovery, the remaining metals such as copper, cobalt, nickel and zinc in the concentrated solution in low acidity could be further recovered, again using SX. When the concentration in mining waste and process solutions is low, membrane distillation (MD) can be used to recover fresh water and concentrate the acid and metals with low cost if waste heat is available in the mine site. A combination of MD and SX is perfect for recovering water, acid and metal values using the proposed flowsheet. 

ALTA 2013

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Solvent extraction (SX) is a well established technology to separate, purify and concentrate metals. It has been also applied for acid recovery from waste solutions and bleed streams of copper, zinc and precious metals (Gottliebsen et al. 2000a and 2000b, Agrawal et al. 2007 and 2008, Agrawal and Sahu 2009). The use of SX to recover various acids has been reviewed by Ritcey (2006) and recently by Kesieme et al. (2012a). 

Extractants including TEHA (tris-2-ethylhexylamine), Alamine 336 (tri-octyl/decy

l amines), TBP (tributyl phosphate) and Cyanex 923 (hexyl/octyl phosphine oxides) have been tested and applied to recover acids using solvent extraction (Rickelton 1993, Alguacil and Lopez 1996, Gottliebsen et al. 2000a and 2000b, Liao et al. 2002, Sarangi et al. 2006 and Agrawal et al. 2007). Agrawal et al. (2008) studied the extraction of sulphuric acid from zinc electrowinning bleed stream containing 174 g/L H2SO4 using TEHA in kerosene. It was found that TEHA had very good acid extraction capacity even in the presence of a large amount of zinc. In a similar study, Haghshenas et al. (2009) investigated the extraction of sulphuric acid from aqueous media in terms of thermodynamics and other conditions. It was reported that the acid extraction increased with increase in the TEHA concentration in the organic solution and reached a maximum depending on the initial acid concentration in the feed solution. Furthermore, a comparison of TEHA and Cyanex 923 for sulphuric acid extraction was studied in terms of thermodynamics (Haghshenas et al. 2009). It was found that stripping of sulphuric acid from TEHA is achieved more readily than from Cyanex 923 while the stripping of acid was easier from Cyanex 923 than from amine extractants (Wolter et al. 2002). Agrawal et al. (2007) studied the extraction of sulphuric acid using Alamine 336 and found that the extraction of sulphuric acid increased with increase in the Alamine 336 concentration. Although, Alamine 336 showed higher extraction ability for sulphuric acid than Cyanex 923, the acid extracted could not be stripped completely using hot water. 

The acid concentration in mining waste solutions is usually low and can be concentrated using membrane distillation (MD) which offers advantages of low energy consumption, high efficiency and operating at low temperatures to recover fresh water and concentrate the acid and metals (Tomaszewska et al., 1995; Tomaszewska, 2000; Kesieme et al., 2012b). After concentrating, solvent extraction can be applied to selectively recover the sulphuric acid and valuable metals. 

In the current paper, the most suitable extractant for sulphuric acid recovery in terms of extraction and stripping will be selected, optimised and characterised. The composition of the extracted species will be investigated using slope analysis and a process flowsheet to recover water, acid and metals proposed. 

###### **SELECTION OF ORGANIC SYSTEM** 

###### **Selection of Organic System in Terms of Extraction** 

Three organic extractants including TEHA, Alamine 336 and Cyanex 923 were used to extract acid in the feed solution containing 200 g/L H2SO4 at an A/O ratio of 1:2 and 22 °C. Preliminary experiments were performed using extractants in the concentration range of 20 - 60% (v/v) TEHA and Alamine 336 and 20 - 100% (v/v) Cyanex 923 (Table 1). Initially, octanol was used as the diluent for all three systems. For the Alamine 336 system, gel was formed with octanol as the diluent. Agrawal et al

. (2007) found the same phase separation problem and used a system containing Alamine 336, kerosene and isodecanol to overcome the problem. Therefore in this study, Shellsol D70 (100% aliphatic) was used as diluent and isodecanol as modifier for the Alamine 336 system. No phase separation problems were observed with the Cyanex 923 system. In fact, the 100% Cyanex 923 system without diluent also performed well in terms of phase separation. For the three systems tested, the acid extraction increased with increase in the extractant concentration (Figure 1). Gottliebsen et al. (2000a and 2000b), Agrawal et al. The acid extraction with the Alamine 336 systems followed the same trend as that with the TEHA system. When the Alamine 336 concentration increased from 20% to 60%, the acid extraction increased from 38% to 91%. The acid extraction was much less with the Cyanex 923 systems. When the Cyanex 923 concentration increased from 20% to 60%, the acid extraction increased from 7.6% to 20%. With the 100% Cyanex 923 system, the acid extraction reached only 50%. **Figure 10: A conceptual flowsheet to recover water, sulphuric acid and metal values from mining waste solutions.** ###### **CONCLUSIONS** Three extractants for the recovery of sulphuric acid from acidic waste solutions were tested including TEHA, Alamine 336 and Cyanex 923. Amongst the three extractants, TEHA performed best in terms of acid extraction and stripping. Therefore, the TEHA system was selected for optimisation. A number of diluents and modifiers were tested with various TEHA concentrations. An optimum organic composition consisting of 50% TEHA, 40% octanol and 10% Shellsol A150 was determined. The acid extraction increased with increasing extractant concentration and decreased from 82% to 72% when the temperature increased from 22 to 60 °C. The change in enthalpy (∆H) was found to be -13.2 kJ mol-1 , indicating that the extraction reaction is exothermic in nature. As a result, increase in temperature results in decrease in acid extraction and increase in acid stripping. The optimised TEHA organic system was further characterised. The acid extraction reached 99% after three successive extractions with fresh organic solution. Only 2 g/l acid was left in the raffinate, indicating almost all acid can be recovered with the optimised TEHA system. The extraction and stripping kinetics of the optimised TEHA system were fast. Within 0.5 min 81.8% acid was extracted and the extraction reached equilibrium and within 2 min, 75% acid was stripped and the stripping reached equilibrium. Extraction distribution isotherm and McCabe Thiele diagram showed that three stages are required at a flowrate O/A ratio of 2 and 22 °C to leave ~5 g/l acid in the raffinate. Stripping distribution isotherm and McCabe Thiele diagram showed that three stages are required at a flowrate A/O ratio of 2 and 60 °C to leave ~2 g/l acid in the stripped organic solution. The optimised TEHA system was used to extracted acid from a synthetic process solution containing a number of metals. It was found that the system only extracted acid with a small amount ALTA 2013 148 of metals entrained. After scrubbing the loaded organic solution in a single stage at an O/A ratio of 10 and 22 °C, 97-100% of entrained metals were removed in a single contact with 4% acid lost in the loaded scrub liquor. A conceptual process flowsheet has been developed to recover fresh water, acid and metals from acidic waste solutions using a combination of MD and SX. ###### **ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS** The authors would like to thank Dr Zhaowu Zhao for reviewing this report and providing valuable comments. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Mass transfer is a key issue in solvent extraction processes and may actually be a bottleneck in some plants. To achieve the necessary stage efficiency an optimum droplet size must be created. Those droplets must be maintained in a turbulent environment to ensure intensive mass transfer. Low intensity mixing does not provide sufficient turbulence or mass transfer. Mixing that is too aggressive will develop fractions that cannot be separated in the settler. Previous studies have shown that the primary reason for separation problems is the extremely non-uniform energy distribution in the mixer which leads to extremely non-uniform distribution of droplet sizes. 

New types of impellers have been developed in recent years which produce a more uniform energy distribution and more uniform droplets which reduce the entrainment of the dispersed phase in the continuous phase; even for high power inputs. 

This study examines the influence of distribution of energy on mass transfer efficiency.

###### **ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN THE MIXING TANK** 

Studies have shown that the volume of the highly turbulent zone around typical hydro-foil impellers is small. Consequently, only a fraction of the extraction takes place in this zone and the majority of the extraction actually takes place in the, less efficient, bulk of the mixer volume. For this reason, an increase in turbulence in the bulk of the mixer has a positive impact on mass transfer efficiency. Studies have also shown that mass transfer is increased the most under conditions of low percentage of extractant. 

Distribution of energy in mixing tanks is normally highly non-uniform. Because of a complete lack of systematic experimental data collection on the energy distribution, the models and experimental correlations related to drop or bubble breaking and mass transfer in disperse systems have been based on average energy dissipation values. The average energy dissipation is also known as the specific power – mixing power per unit of mass (W/kg) in the tank. The specific power has been used for many years as the basic parameter for scaling-up, especially – for the pr

ocesses connected with mass transfer. The use of the average parameter instead of data on real values of turbulent dissipation places strict limits on ones ability to compare and select optimum mixing devices. The knowledge of energy distribution provides a useful tool for development of mixing equipment. A method has been developed(1) that allows definition of not only the location of zones with different intensity of turbulence, but also a quantitative evaluation of the volume and energy dissipation in these zones as a function of tank and impeller geometry. The intent of this paper is to show how application of these methods corresponds to solvent extraction of metals. As mentioned previously, in the typical design of mixers for liquid-liquid metallurgical extraction processes there exists a very small zone of high energy dissipation in the vicinity of the impeller blades and extremely low energy dissipation in the bulk volume of the mixing tank. The special mixers, newly developed for these applications by Turbulent Technologies (TT) and Tenova Bateman, provide much more uniform distribution of energy. With any mixing impeller and tank design, the degree of non uniformity depends not only on the impeller type but also on many other parameters. Figures 1 and 2 illustrate the influence of impeller diameter on the ratio of maximum to average energy dissipation rates and on the relative volume of zone of maximum energy dissipation. The calculations were performed for an industrial scale (80 m3 ) mixing system with a standard hydrofoil impeller and the same system with a special TT impeller. According to these results, the maximum energy dissipation rate (W/kg) decreases while the volume of the zone of maximum dissipation increases with increase of impeller diameter. The width of the baffles is another important parameter that affects turbulence distribution in the tank. Studies by others have shown(2) that the installation of baffles in mixing tanks creates a resistance to the tangential flow and thus dramatically decreases tangential velocity of liquid, transforming tangential flow to axial circulation. As a result, the difference between the velocities of the blade and the liquid increases, thereby increasing the energy dissipation. ALTA 2013 152 260 Hydrofoil

###### **RECOVERY OF NICKEL AND COBALT FROM LEACH SOLUTIONS CONTAINING IRON AND ALUMINIUM USING ION EXCHANGE RESINS** 

By 

Zhaowu Zhu, Yoko Pranolo and Chu Yong Cheng

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Recovery of Ni and Co from solutions generated by heap and atmospheric leaching with high concentrations of Fe and Al is a long-standing problem and a serious challenge. Although nickel can be recovered by ion exchange (IX), the recovery of cobalt in the Ni-depleted raffinate has not been resolved. In this study, the recovery of cobalt from a synthetic Ni-depleted raffinate using resin in pulp (RIP) with Dowex M4195 resin was investigated. To obtain high recovery of cobalt and its good separation from iron, the solution pulping or neutralisation should be conducted in a pH a

round 4 before addition of the resin. Using this method, the recovery of cobalt reached 92% and the iron adsorption was only 3% in a single contact. More than 95% Co was recovered by two successive RIP operations. Impurities including Zn, Fe, Al, Mn, Mg etc. reported to the eluate with cobalt could be removed by solvent extraction (SX) and precipitation to obtain pure cobalt product.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Nickel laterite ores are becoming the main source for nickel supply as its sulphide ores are being depleted gradually (Mudd, 2009; Kyle, 2010). At present, processing nickel laterite ores with high pressure acid leach (HPAL) is preferred, although the capital and operating costs are very high. Therefore, processing nickel laterite ores with atmospheric leaching instead of expensive HPAL is becoming the trend in the nickel industry (McDonald and Whittington, 2008). Heap leaching, one of atmospheric leaching methods, is economical for nickel laterite processing and has been successfully implemented in some cases (Moroney et al., 2009; Steemson et al., 2009). 

Atmospheric leaching of nickel laterite generates pregnant leach solution (PLS) containing a large amount of iron and aluminium because these cannot be hydrolysed under atmospheric pressure. For example, in a heap leach process, the PLS contained 3.1 g/L Ni and 11.0 g/L Fe when 66.1% nickel was extracted from a laterite ore (Duyvesteyn et al., 2001). In some cases, iron content could be as high as 20 g/L (Agatzini-Leonardou et al., 2009). Direct neutralisation to remove iron and aluminium would cause high nickel and cobalt losses due to adsorption. Therefore, the recovery of nickel and cobalt from the PLS containing large amounts of iron and aluminium is a serious challenge. 

The resin in pulp (RIP) technology has been developed to recover nickel and cobalt from nickel laterite ores (Duyvesteyn et al., 2002; Mendes and Berni, 2009; Mendes, 2010). Zainol and Nicol (2009) used Amberlite IRC748<sup>®</sup> and TP207<sup>®</sup> in pulp to recover nickel and cobalt from laterite leach tailing solutions to improve the total recovery of nickel and cobalt. Efficient recovery of nickel and cobalt was achieved for the laterite tailing containing a small amount of nickel and cobalt (Zainol, 2005; Zainol and nickel, 2009). A chelating resin of Dowex M-4195 (former Dowex XFS-4195 containing functional group of bis-(2-picoyl) amine) was used in an RIP process to recover nickel and cobalt (Duyvesteyn et al., 2002). Other types of resin such as Ionac SR-5<sup>®</sup> and Purolite S930<sup>®</sup> were also investigated for this purpose. It has been shown that chelating resin with picoyl amine was more effective in the recovery of nickel and cobalt (Mendes, 2010). 

Using RIP for the recovery of nickel and cobalt from the leaching process, the expensive step of solid and liquid separation can be avoided. However, it is difficult to obtain nickel solutions of sufficient purity to cou

ple with nickel electrowinning or hydrogen reduction processes because many impurities still exist in the solution. A number of purification steps are required to produce nickel product. Additionally, the recovery of a large amount of nickel present in the solution would complicate the operation due to the low metal adsorption capability of the resin. During nickel recovery using ion exchange resin Dowex M4195, Ni can be recovered and separate from the impurities based on the following loading order: Cu >> Ni/Zn >> Co/Fe(III) > Mg/Cr/Mn/Ca/Al. However, the separation of Co from Fe(III) is impossible using ion exchange resin Dowex M4195 unless the Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) due to the following loading order: Co >> Fe(II)/Mg/Cr/Mn/Ca/Al after Cu, Ni and Zn are removed. This process is complicated due to the reduction of Fe(III) to Fe(II) to recover the cobalt. If the cobalt can be recovered during the neutralisation for disposal, the process would be simplified and operating costs saved. The present paper studied cobalt recovery from the raffinate by resin in pulp (RIP). ###### **METAL ADSORPTION ISOTHERMS WITH RESIN IN SOLUTION** Dowex M4195 is a chelating resin and strongly extracts Cu(II) and Ni(II) at pH lower than 2 in the presence of large amount of Fe(III). It has been used to selectively recover nickel from a laterite leach solution to produce ferro-nickel or nickel matte (Liu, et al., 2008). Metal adsorption pH isotherms with Dowex M4195 resin and a synthetic solution containing Fe(III) and Al is shown in Fig. 1. The order of metal adsorption was: Cu > Ni > Zn > Co ~ Fe(III) > Cr(III) ~ Mn ~ Ca ~ Mg. Nickel adsorption was much stronger than that of Fe(III). However, the adsorption of Co was similar to that of Fe(III). Only 48% Co was adsorbed at pH 2.5 where significant precipitation of Fe(III) could occur. The adsorption of other impurities such as Mn, Ca and Mg was much lower than that of cobalt under the same pH. Obviously, Dowex M4195 resin could be used to recover nickel from solutions containing Fe(III), but could not be used to recover and separate cobalt effectively from Fe(III). It can be seen that zinc and cobalt were recovered much more effectively than other metals. With the increase in the resin percentage (w/w), the recovery of cobalt and zinc increased significantly until the resin added reached 4%. The equilibrium pH was about 3.45, slightly lower than 3.5 in the original pulp due to the exchange of H+ with metal ions in the chelating reaction.
