###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The largest single operating loss in many hydro-metallurgical plants is the poor recovery of leached product in the solids sent to tailings. Any reduction, in the

concentration of the valuable species in this solution, will improve the project economics. 

Conventional design, to reduce the soluble loss, is to increase the number of wash stages or the wash water ratio. This approach is limited in effectiveness as it can only reduce the soluble loss to that dictated by the concentration in the returning solution. For copper plants this concentration is set by the recovery in the solvent extraction (SX) plant. When using a single grade of SX feed a single grade of SX raffinate is produced, generally with five to seven percent of the copper still remaining in solution. 

An alternate approach has been developed by BASF<sup>(1)</sup> (previously Cognis Corporation) and implemented on a number of recent projects using engineering input from Miller Metallurgical Services Miller<sup>(2)(,3)</sup> . Other projects were executed as collaboration of the client<sup>(4)</sup> with the design undertaken in-house, or by an engineer as part of the overall project. The SX plant feed is ‘split’ into two different streams: a high grade stream containing up to 75% of the copper and a low grade stream with the remaining copper. The high grade raffinate is recycled 100% to the leach. The low grade raffinate is used as wash water and any excess used for other applications: 

- For flocculant secondary dilution rather than new water 

- Slurry pump gland service. (This requires acid resistant gland water pumps and pump gland systems but the extra costs are quite marginal) 

- For copper-cobalt plants the bleed to the cobalt plant. 

Any further improvement to the soluble loss minimisation and improving the split between high and low grade SX PLS streams needs a fundamental change to the circuit water balance. 

###### **MILLING IN RAFFINATE** 

The biggest issue in the water balance is the moisture brought in with the milled ore. For many DRC and Zambian projects a filtration step after the mill is not viable; due to the extremely low filtration rates with these clayey ores. One method of achieving a negative water balance is to mill in recycled acid raffinate. The practice has been used in the Florida phosphate industry for many years<sup>(5)</sup> . Mills there are typically protected with rubber lining due to the relatively mild corrosion rates experienced. However, the presence of copper in the recycled high grade raffinate stream leads to extreme corrosion rates from the copper-iron cementation reaction. Effective corrosion rates of up to 40 mm per year have been reported in laboratory testing. 

The potential to use milling in raffinate was mooted in 2003<sup>(6)</sup> but not taken up due to the mill suppliers being unable to offer an acceptable method of corrosion protection at that time. The proposed practice needs a stainless steel (or stainless steel lined) mill with ceramic, pebble or corrosion resistant grinding media to be fully effective. The strong process operating cost drivers for the process however resulted

in the first installation at Sepon in 2004<sup>(7)</sup> with optimisation of the plant in 2006<sup>(8)</sup> . The benefits to the water balance are significant as no new water is added to the grinding step, other than the moisture in the ROM ore. 

Despite the success at Sepon some engineering companies were still taking risk averse approaches due to the perceived risk of mill shell failure<sup>(9)</sup> . To some degree this attitude has tended to stifle development of the concept and engineering application of the process. Further work by MMS and SENET engineers, with the active involvement of the MUMI client team, have provided an innovative method of addressing these perceived risks by eliminating them entirely. 

###### **CIRCUIT SELECTION** 

The selection of the overall process circuit was driven by the need to find an alternative to conventional pre-leach dewatering. Filtration rates were extremely slow leading to high capital for a plant to treat the required tonnages. Thickening rates are also around 25% of conventional milled material due to the extreme minus 45 micron clay content. As well as poor thickener unit rates the achievable underflow densities were limited by very high Bingham plastic characteristics with both high initial yield stress and high plastic viscosity. Densities above 50% w/w solids were difficult to

handle as a result. With this level of water input from a conventional milling circuit it became apparent that the SplitCircuit™ would not provide the best achievable results. 

In parallel with the process selection mill vendors were approached for supply of stainless steel lined conventional mills. Three vendors were willing to undertake such units. The overall circuit was selected on the basis of milling in raffinate; with final mill and vendor selection to follow; as part of the basic engineering phase. 

The initial project involving milling in raffinate was phase 2 of the site development. Phase 1 had used conventional water milling with pre-leach thickening. Copper recovery was with a single stage SX and EW. The overall water balance was acceptable as there was a large bleed of SX raffinate to the cobalt recovery plant. This allowed the plant circuit water balance to be acceptable. However there was an accumulation of water in the tails storage facility (TSF) that had longer term implications. 

The phase 2 project was to treble copper production to 60 000 tpa. During the execution of phase 2 the target copper production was further increased to 100 000 tpa (phase 3) by utilising higher grade ore. The basic design included some unusual features due to the characteristics of the ore. 

- A very coarse grind P80 212 microns which was a compromise with the leaching agitation and CCD rake power requirements. A coarser grind is possible without compromising the leach recovery; but the coarse particles will cause blockage and damage issues in the subsequent steps. 

- A limitation on maximum leac

h density of around 20% w/w. The leach solution copper grade is limited to around 25 g/L for effective copper recovery in the high grade SX. The ore is so high grade that the leach density is quite low as a result. This in turn generates issues of fast settling rates in the dilute leach slurry.

In this case modelling of the milling circuit indicated that a single stage SAG mill would be appropriate. This mill was sized to enable the phase 1 mill to be removed from the production circuit and its water input eliminated.

A number of mill ancillary items also needed to be selected to resist the extreme corrosion of the combined copper and acid concentrations. ###### **Civil and Structural** 

###### **Civil** 

The civil design was considered a major part of the corrosion mitigation as this area is generally subject to the most intense and longest exposure to risk from spillage etc. Many basic assumptions were successfully challenged to produce a low risk outcome: 

- Big rafts to eliminate most construction joints. These rafts then carried to mill plinths without introducing further construction joints. 

- Simple geometric shapes to facilitate spillage handling and eliminate pockets of accumulation; especially around mill and column plinths. 

- Steep slopes on all surfaces to shed spillage to the clean-up sumps. 

- Elimination of column plinths inside the bunded area by alternate structural layout. 

- Provision of a drive through clean out bay at the mill feed end to assist in removal of accumulated solids. 

Once these guidelines and layout concepts had been established a number of residual risk issues were addressed: 

- Ball mill scats handling from a bunker with tile lining and stainless steel running surfaces (skid bars) so that FEL buckets did not damage the tile lining. 

- Concrete protection with 

   - Robust acid bricks in high traffic areas and 

   - Acid tiles in hose down area 

   - Epoxy-ceramic trowel on materials for difficult access and small areas. 

###### **_Structural_** 

As with the civil design the fundamental design and layout basis was changed so that the structural corrosion risks were minimised where possible. This challenged the usual mill layout to enable an innovative arrangement to be developed. 

- There were to be no  columns in the bunded area 

   - This was achieved except for a column row at the mill feed end to support the walkway. The columns were supported on corbels constructed from the mill support plinth 

   - The combined mill discharge sump was supported on columns mounted outside the kerb and on the two mill discharge end plinths. 

- The number of columns were minimised by an iterative layout process that gradually reduced the total number. Maximum use was made of the four mill plinths to support steel for platforms, walkways. Pipe supports etc. 

The secondary risk issues were addressed by appropriate selection of materials of construction. Mill building support structures, on the Phase 2 project, are: 316 stainless steel floor members and grating, in the spillage prone areas i.e. feed end and under the cyclones. The remaining structures being mild steel. 

Phase 4 mill building’s entire floor area support structure and grating is manufactured in stainless steel. The suppo

rt columns are mild steel which will be polyurethane coated on site. 

###### **_Mechanical, Piping and Process_** 

The mill feed conveyor head pulley and discharge chute, as well as the scats conveyor tail end are stainless steel. 

Ball addition is conventional with maximum 125 mm balls designed to be added to the SAG mill feed conveyor. The ball mill balls are added via a skip to the feed spout. Currently 90 mm balls are being used in the SAG mill to minimise ball breakage and liner damage with the soft ore being treated at the moment. 

ALTA 2013 

255 

The Phase 2 project is equipped with a fume extraction and scrubbing system with withdrawal points on the mill feed and discharge ends. The Phase 4 project has provision to connect the single SAG mill feed and discharge ends into the existing extraction system, should the acid mist from carbon dioxide release from malachite dissolution prove to be an issue. 

The extracted fume is scrubbed of the SO2 before discharge into the atmosphere. As part of the water balance management, scrubbing is conducted in HG raffinate. This has a number of advantages to the project: 

- Eliminates the use of NaOH as practiced in conventional acid fume scrubbers 

- Recovers the SO2 for use in the process (reduction of cobalt +3 to +2) 

- Eliminates the water associated with NaOH scrubbing from the circuit as it uses HG raffinate that is going to the mill in any case. 

All piping and valves are selected for both internal and external corrosion. HDPE pipes and stainless steel valves are common with the rest of the plant. Despite requiring much greater support, rubber hose was preferred to rubber lined steel pipe for severe slurry handling duties. 

###### **OPERATING EXPERIENCE** 

Unfortunately an unforeseen issue raised its head soon after commissioning. The slipper bearings were failing at short intervals of less than a month. The phosphor bronze pad bearing material was picking up on the LDX2101 sliding ring bearing surface destroying the slipper pads. This was eventually diagnosed as material incompatibility situation rather than a lubrication problem. The LDX2101 stainless steel was ‘galling’ the bronze when they came within micro contact. The slipper pads were changed out with new generation “PEEK” polymer type units which have been running trouble free ever since. 

The mills have only been operating for slightly over one year, and have experienced a number of other operational issues that have been addressed. A long term on site training programme has paid dividends with the mill operators now understanding the key indicators for maximising SAG mill throughput. Early operation suffered from poor mill control by the inexperienced team  As a result SAG mill load run outs and resultant mill liner damage were not uncommon. With steadier mill operation the plant has undergone debottlenecking; and is now operating above design tonnages. The issues addressed in the capability upgrade included: 

- Upgrading

of the CCD units to handle the solid tonnes without rake damage. 

- Improvements to the CCD flocculant make up and delivery systems. 

- Improved CCD feed dilution flow control. 

- Modifications to the leach tanks to minimise spillage and surges from the feed tank pumps. 

- Changes to the grinding media to minimise corrosion rates and ball breakage. 

- Optimisation of mill grate and trommel aperture sizes to account for the adverse slurry rheology. 

- Introduction of a partial recycle of cyclone underflow to the SAG mill to help balance the mill loads. 

- Optimisation of mill ball loads to minimise overgrinding of the already fine feed. 

With the higher tonnage operation a number of subsequent issues needed to be addressed in the supporting operation: 

- Higher pump capacity of the HG raffinate pumps. 

- Increased foaming in the mills (from dissolution of malachite and evolution of CO2). This has in turn adversely affected the mill trommel screening efficiencies. The lack of HG raffinate for trommel sprays has also contributed to the poor screening efficiency. 

- A resultant increase in the tonnes of scats produced from both mills. Scats conveyor now delivers ball mill scats to the SAG mill scats conveyor. The scats are taken to the site heap leach piles and the copper and cobalt recovered in this process. It is unlikely that a scats crusher will be used as the heap leach process is sufficient for metals recovery. 

- Improved CCD feed well design and further optimisation of the feed dilution control. 

ALTA 2013 

256 

- Increase SAG mill feed bin discharge rate. 

- Improved spillage handling and shut down dump of the mill discharge sump and pumps. 

- Increased protection of mill drive components from acid spillage and fumes. 

- Improved chute design and changes to wear resistant materials. 

There have been poor results from the use of low alloy quality balls (low Cr & Ni). Despite vendor claims that the balls were chemically resistant to the solution, ball life was short. The high rate of grinding media corrosion resulted in an increase in the amount of cobalt leached, at a time when SO2 reductant was not being added – this was as a result of reduction of Co3+ to Co2+ by Fe2+ ions. The downside was poor settling and dirty overflows at the post leach thickener and CCD’s. Flocculant consumption was high; and not more than 50% solids could be attained in thickener underflows. A change over to high chrome and high nickel alloy balls (as used at Sepon) has started to pay dividends in terms of better ball life and more ‘normal’ ball size distribution in the mill inventory. However, high ball breakage soon after SAG mill relining has been a problem. Ball breakage has been significantly reduced through controlling mill discharge density at >70% w/w solids, maintaining consistent feed to the SAG mill and operating the SAG mill at low speeds of 6065% of critical immediately after relining. 

Milling in raffinate has resulted in a saving on

fresh water consumption of 0.64m<sup>3</sup> /t of ROM ore treated. Total fresh acid consumption has been around 80kg/t ROM ore (for head grades of 7%Cu and 1.7% Co). The overall water balance constraints have meant that the SplitCircuit™ has only achieved approximately 65% of copper being sent to the high grade circuit rather than the 75% target in the design. 

With the experienced gained in operating the mills it has become apparent that an increased use of stainless steel structure and grating, at the feed end, will be an advantage. As a result the phase 4 mill design has been modified to suit. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The milling in raffinate circuit has shown itself to be a robust process, especially now that large mills can be manufactured from high strength duplex stainless steels. 

The ability to undertake this process has enhanced the SplitCircuit™ process, allowing another quantum step up in the amount of copper than can be sent to a high grade SX plant. 

Milling plant design for corrosion management is a major driving force in the development of the layout of the plant. Changing conventional thinking for concrete and structural design can mitigate the corrosion risk to a large degree.  Follow through to all levels of detailed design is also required to ensure compliance with the primary aims for corrosion mitigation.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Disseminated nickel ore bodies are widely distributed around the world and are found in most of the known nickel sulphide districts.  Teck has developed a novel hydrometallurgical process for treating low-to-high grade nickel concentrates and polymetallic nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide concentrates with high magnesia content without the need for separation at the milling stage.  This paper will focus on the metallurgical components of the CESL hydrometallurgical process and then examine a business case which utilizes data compiled by a third party engineering company.

###### **CESL INTRODUCTION** 

Teck Resources Limited (“Teck”) has developed proprietary hydrometallurgical technology, known collectively as CESL Technology, over the past 20 years. Teck’s focus on use of the technology is in pursuit of growth projects to add to and improve Teck’s core businesses and to develop partnerships with 3<sup>rd</sup> party companies through the provision of technical solutions that apply CESL Technology. Composed of three main areas, the Division’s mandate is three-fold: to advance growth opportunities, including those generated by the application of proprietary CESL hydrometallurgical technology; to transfer technology for operational improvement; and to deliver sustainable solutions to enhance environmental performance and metal use. 

CESL hydrometallurgical technology can be applied to a wide variety of copper and nickel sulphide concentrates, and has the flexibility to treat bulk, low-to-high grade, or impurity-challenged material. In doing so, it recovers a high percentage of all payable metals, including gold, silver and PGM byproducts. The Division is actively seeking opportunities to participate in existing operations and new ventures through the application of the CESL process.  Work at CESL is focused on advancing projects which have the best potential to deliver internal and external growth opportunities for Teck. 

###### **NICKEL SULPHIDE RESOURCES**<sup>**(1)**</sup> 

Nickel resources are typically classified as sulphides or laterites. Approximately 73% of the world’s nickel resources are estimated to be contained in laterites while 27% are classifie

d as sulphide. Currently, some 37% of the world’s nickel supply is derived from sulphide resources and almost all of the sulphide deposits being exploited are of massive sulphide ore, as opposed to disseminated sulphide ore. The balance of nickel supply comes from limonitic and saprolitic laterite deposits which represent an abundant, although often technically challenging, nickel resource.  These statistics are not likely to change unless a significant rise in metal prices and/or the development of new extractive technologies supports the development of resources that were previously considered uneconomic or metallurgically challenged. 

Despite the grade and tonnage disparity between laterite and sulphide resources, global nickel supply from massive sulphide resources will continue to be an integral source of primary nickel supply going forward. This is largely due to laterite ores exhibiting a greater mineralogical and chemical complexity which makes them more challenging to process economically. 

Smelting and refining of massive sulphides begins with the flotation of ore, typically in the range of 0.2-2% nickel, to an acceptable concentrate grade of 10 to 20% nickel. Concentrate smelting produces a high grade nickel matte which is then refined hydrometallurgically. With the majority of the world’s nickel supply coming via pyrometallurgical processes, the technology is well proven and has demonstrated robust economics over the past several decades. Unlike massive sulphide ores, the processing of disseminated sulphide ores has proven to be more challenging even though the ore grades of some of the world’s largest disseminated nickel-copper sulphide deposits are often reasonable (0.6 to 0.9%).The problem has been related to processing; high magnesium bearing nickel-concentrates result from mineral processors pursuing finer primary grind size to liberate and recover economic minerals from low grade ores.  Pursuing maximum metal/mineral recovery in combination with maximizing concentrate grade results in unacceptably high Fe:MgO ratios in the finished concentrate. High magnesium bearing nickel-concentrates result from mineral processors pursuing finer primary grind size to liberate and recover economic minerals from low grade ores. Pursuing maximum metal/mineral recovery in combination with maximizing concentrate grade results in unacceptably high Fe:MgO ratios in the finished concentrate. Nickel smelters typically cannot handle such concentrates without blending, due to inescapable problems with slag metallurgy. As a result, nickel grade and the Fe:MgO ratio in concentrate are key parameters in order to control smelting temperatures and slag viscosity. 

Komatiite-hosted nickel-copper deposits contain some of the world’s most economically significant disseminated ore deposits. These sulphide-poor, magnesium rich deposits are mainly found in Australia, Canada, Brazil, Zimbabwe, Finland and Russia. Various flowsheet considerations and adjustments

to flotation conditions (i.e. particle size, pH and pulp density, etc.) have been developed to manage the well documented problems caused by slime-coating. However, these flowsheets have so far proven to be too complex, costly and difficult to efficiently produce highgrade, low magnesia concentrates for conventional pyrometallurgical treatment. An alternative for

consideration would be the production of a low-grade nickel concentrate for hydrometallurgical treatment. In doing so, significant improvements to overall nickel recovery from lower grade disseminated deposits could be achieved. 

Teck’s CESL Nickel Process is a well-developed hydrometallurgical technology which can unlock the nickel from disseminated sulphides and provide a reliable means of nickel production for future projects. 

###### **NICKEL ECONOMIC STUDY RESULTS** 

###### **Nickel Economic Study Background** 

In 1997, a hydrometallurgical flowsheet processing nickel sulphide concentrates to metal was developed and a pilot plant successfully operated. In 2002; there was renewed interest by Teck in the nickel flowsheet for processing the polymetallic Mesaba concentrate. A successful pilot campaign was operated, producing copper cathode and a nickel intermediate product. Further flowsheet development ensued and in 2008 the Mesaba concentrate was processed to produce a higher grade nickel intermediate. After the successful completion of these campaigns, further flowsheet and bench testing was implemented for the recovery of nickel to metal. Piloting from a nickel intermediate product to metal was again undertaken in 2010 with consistent production of LME grade nickel cathode. 

Examining disseminated nickel projects from in-house capital and operating cost data showed a positive outlook for the technology from an economic perspective, including the increased cash flow of an onsite CESL refinery.  Further verification of these costs using updated third party engineering was needed to support the financials. 

An economic study was commissioned by Teck with the objective of validating the capital and operating costs that would be associated with constructing and operating a fully integrated CESL nickel refinery.  The economic study was completed to a +/- 30% accuracy based on quotes provided for all major pieces of equipment. 

The economic study assessed a conceptual commercial CESL plant to treat nickel concentrate and produce LME grade nickel cathode.  The assessment was based on a concentrate with an average grade of 11% nickel and designed to treat a nominal concentrate throughput of 300,000 t/a. 

It is important to note that CESL has completed extensive metallurgical testwork on concentrates generated from over 20 different nickel deposits, including those similar to the concentrate used in the study.  The conceptual concentrate mineralogy, process flowsheets, operating conditions and expected metallurgical results are well known by CESL and served as the

Disseminated sulphides are widely distributed around the world and are present at most nickel sulphide deposits. Despite their unique metallurgical complexity and mineralogical diversity, their value can be unlocked by Teck’s CESL process which represents a competitive and reliable technology. The paper has discussed this advancement in several key areas: - Metallurgy: The CESL pilot plant has achieved high Ni extraction (>97%) from various concentrates that have been generated from disseminated Ni orebodies. Production of LME grade nickel cathode is achieved. - Economics: An external case study was conducted using a conservative approach to minimize technical risk for the project. The study was conducted on a theoretical 31,700 t/a nickel refinery in central Canada and showed a favourable improvement to project NPV of 424 million US$/annum for onsite refining versus concentrate sales. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Canadian-based Prophecy Platinum Corporation (Prophecy) is considering options for on-site production of copper cathode and a value-added nickel-product at their Lynn Lake operation, located in northern-Manitoba, Canada. An experimental testwork campaign, followed by flowsheet development and economic modelling was undertaken to evaluate the various options open to Prophecy. 

It was established experimentally that 90 percent of both copper and nickel can be recovered to a bulk concentrate of the Prophecy Resources Lynn Lake ore. Various flowsheet options have been considered consisting of either moderately thermophillic or extremely thermophillic bioleaching, combined with copper cathode production followed by nickel recovery either as hydroxide precipitate, sulfide precipitate or cathode. The economically optimal approach would be bioleaching at 70<sup>o</sup> C, followed by production of both copper and nickel in cathode form, yielding an IRR(10y) of 17 percent (rising to 24 percent with a 13 percent rise in metal prices). Various recommendations can be made to achieve further improvements to the economics. 

A graphical method is provided whereby the profitability of other similar projects can qualitatively be determined very simply from knowledge of only (a) the Payable Contained Value and (b) Opex associated with mining plus administration.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

###### **The Business Case** 

Canadian-based Prophecy Platinum Corporation (Prophecy) is considering options for on-site production of copper cathode and a value-added nickel-product at their Lynn Lake operation, located in northern-Manitoba, Canada. 

Current indications are that the production of a low-grade bulk concentrate would maximise the simultaneous recovery of both copper and nickel. However nickel concentrates are not traded for smelting as readily as copper concentrates, and the low grade of the envisaged bulk concentrate would further complicate its marketing, apart from affecting unfavourably the transport and treatment costs per pound of metal. Therefore, the company is investigating means of maximising metal recovery to a concentrate, followed by on-site production of copper cathode and nickel cathode or a saleable nickel-bearing precipitate. 

A technology is therefore required for the on-site hydrometallurgical extraction and recovery of the contained nickel and copper, with Bioleaching being one of the considerations. Furthermore a downstream recovery route needs to be selected, with solvent extraction and electrowinning (SXEW) being an obvious choice for copper recovery, but for nickel recovery multiple options can be considered namely SXEW, as a mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP) and as a sulfide precipitate (SP). Mintek has extensive experience in such studies, some of which has been published<sup>(1,2)</sup> , and was selected to perform the experimental work. 

###### **The Approach** 

###### **_Experimental_** 

Flotation optimisation testwork was undertaken on a Lynn Lake ore sample at Mintek, South Africa, to explore the viability of producing (a) separate nickel and copper concentrates, opposed to (b) a bulk nickel-copper concentrate. It was possible to recover 90 percent of both nickel and copper to a bulk concentrate with a mass pull of 13.5%, which could not be matched by separate nickel and copper concentrate production. The rest of the study was therefore based on bulk concentrate production, and a 100 kg rougher concentrate sample was produced in a continuously operated pilot plant at Mintek for use in the subsequent characterisation and bioleaching testwork described in this paper. 

Continuous mini-plant bioleaching testwork was completed at Mintek using both moderate thermophiles (around 45<sup>o</sup> C) and extreme thermophiles (around 70<sup>o</sup> C), and employing regrinding of the flotation concentrate to 10µm and to 20µm from which the bioleach feed pulp was prepared. The extent of extraction of nickel and copper as well as corresponding reagent consumptions were determined experimentally for each these options of regrinding and bioleaching. 

###### **_Flowsheet Selection and Cost Estimation_** 

For all flowsheet options considered, copper recovery wa

s to be done by SXEW, followed by iron removal prior to nickel recovery. The flowsheet variations considered nickel recovery by either (a) hydroxide precipitation using magnesia, (b) nickel sulfide precipitation using H2S or (c) SXEW to produce nickel cathode. 

The capital and operating cost of the mining, milling and concentration section were provided by Prophecy, based on previously completed studies<sup>(3)</sup> . 

For the leaching and recovery sections the operating cost ascribed to consumables and utilities was derived from mass and energy balances over the flowsheets with the inputs obtained from the experimental bioleaching testwork and known delivered costs to the mine site. For labour and maintenance industry average numbers and factors were used. 

The capital cost estimates for the leaching and recovery sections were derived by the Perth office of Tenova (Perth) by extrapolation from a recent study for a similar project.

###### **_Data Presentation_** 

In the economic analysis for this project, the cost components that were found to simultaneously (a) have the biggest impact on economics and 

(b) be potentially very variable from one project to another depending on the mining method, and even within any given project it can vary over time, (in terms of USD per dry metric tonne of concentrate, [USD/DMT]), 

is the sum of Mining plus Administrative cost. 

This made it possible to represent the areas of profitability in very simple graphs (shown later in this text) that could also be useful to other similar projects, as a function of only Opex of Mining plus Administration [USD/DMT] on the x-axis, and Payable Contained Contained Value [USD/DMT] on the y-axis. The Payable Contained Value equals the nickel and copper contents, multiplied by the extent of extraction of each metal, multiplied by the price to be received for the products produced. 

The economics is less sensitive to capex than to opex which allows the approximation of not having to consider capex as a variable in the graphical representations. Furthermore the various leach/recovery options were found to greatly affect the Payable Contained Value, but the cost structures of the various leach/recovery options were sufficiently similar to also permit their costs to be treated as constants in the graphical representations. 

The operating cost of milling, concentration and tailings disposal should also be less variable between different projects, for the Prophecy project presented here it was about USD 120/DMT of concentrate and these costs are treated as constants in the graphical representations. The data presented here will therefore be of most use to projects anticipating a similar opex in terms of [USD/DMT] associated with milling/concentration/tailings-disposal. 

As a comparison the analysis includes the options of sale of the bulk concentrate. Calculations not shown in this paper indicated that, after treatment and refining charges and transport

As an example of how to use Figure 4 for any other project, the following steps can be followed: 

- a. From the known composition of the concentrate that can be produced, and forecasting the metal prices that will prevail during the project, the contained metal value is calculated as in Table 1 above. 

- b. Select a combination of bioleaching method and downstream nickel recovery. 

- c. Determine either experimentally, or estimate based on the mineralogical composition and experience, the extent to which each metal will be extracted by the bioleaching method selected above. 

- d. Determine or estimate the percentage of the nickel price that will be received for the nickel product to be produced (i.e. MHP, SP or cathode). 

- e. Determine the anticipated Payable Contained Value as defined under the sub-heading “Data Presentation” above, expressed as [USD/DMT]. 

- f. From Figure 4, read off the critical Mining plus Administration Opex, i.e. that which will yield an IRR(10y)=0. A project with a combination of Mining plus Administration lower than this value, and/or higher Payable Contained Value than that determined above, will yield an IRR(10y)>0. 

It can be noted that the method involves only revenue and Mining plus Administration Opex as variables. This does of course constitute a simplification and approximation, nevertheless the economics are much more sensitive to opex than to capex and the simplification is not a gross one for the purpose of order-of-magnitude evaluation. For example by reducing the mining & concentrator capex by a factor of 2.5, the curves in Figure 4 move down by 100 USD/DMT critical Payable Contained Value. 

Of course the economics are dramatically improved by higher metal prices. Nickel and copper prices only 13 percent higher than those shown in Table 1 above would raise the IRR(10y) to 24 percent, i.e. a 41 percent increase in IRR(10y). 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

It has been established experimentally that 90 percent of both copper and nickel can be recovered to a bulk concent

rate of the Prophecy Resources Lynn Lake ore. Various hydrometallurgical options exist for production of copper cathode and marketable nickel products on-site. To date, the optimum economic scenario is the production of nickel in cathode form, i.e. bioleaching at 70<sup>o</sup> C, followed by production of both copper and nickel in cathode form, yielding an IRR(10y) of 17 percent, which rises to 24 percent with a 13 percent rise in metal prices. 

###### **RECOMMENDATIONS** 

With a more liberal time frame the design and cost of the leach/recovery plant could be optimised further to reduce the capex requirement. 

To date no design features towards energy optimisation have been considered to reduce opex costs, for which scope exists. Similarly no consideration has been given for optimisation of general and administrative costs, and these should be pursued. 

Further improvements in metals extraction can be achieved by spreading the leach volume over more reactors in series to obtain a better approach to plug flow. 

The contribution of cobalt to revenue, which has thus far been ignored, should be added, since even without any dedicated cobalt recovery means cobalt is expected to largely follow the nickel and credit for it should be negotiable.

The Kipoi Copper Project contains five known areas of copper and cobalt mineralisation, being Kipoi Central, Kipoi North, Kaminafitwe, Kileba and Judeira; all hosted in deformed rocks of the Mwashya (R4) and Mines (R2) Series sediments of the Roan Group.

The primary mineralisation at Kipoi Central has been oxidised with the copper being remobilised into joints, fractures and voids created during oxidation. The main copper bearing minerals in the oxidised zone are malachite with minor azurite, chalcocite and native copper. Sulphides occur below the base of oxidation. The copper minerals identified to date at Kipoi North are predominately copper oxide minerals (dominant malachite), stratabound and concentrated in the DStrat, RSF, and RSC rock units. ###### **Process Flowsheet Development** 

The original Stage II Project considered a range of options including Leach SX-EW, MillingFlotation, and Leach - Cementation but the latter two were rejected early for an agitated leach circuit described below: 

The initial Leach SX-EW circuit considered consisted of crushing followed by semi-autogenous Milling. The milled product was then introd

uced to an acidic agitated tank leach followed by counter current decantation (CCD) solid liquid separation with pregnant leach solution (PLS) clarification. The clarified PLS was then treated via SX-EW. The acidified tailings was then neutralised and discharged to a tailings facility. This required the full +$400M in capital at the front end of the project. Operating costs were high as full ore had to be milled. In hindsight, Cu recoveries would be lower than expected as there was a greater abundance of slow leaching chrysocolla in the feed than anticipated. 

With the Stage 1 HMS project development there were was a desire to utilise the cash generated from this operation to fund the Stage II development. Additionally there was a desire to be able to commence production from Stage II at the completion of Stage I in mid 2014. The Stage 1 HMS project also generated both high grade reject stockpiles and medium grade ore stockpiles (totalling 4.8Mt @ 2% Cu) and advantage could be taken to use these in the first 3 years to improve the initial project economics and assist in allowing for a phased development reducing upfront capital. 

A conventional Heap Leach SX-EW was considered. This flowsheet had the ability to be able to phase the development from 25,000tpa up to 50,000tpa and hence minimise the initial capital costs and allow for the project to be funded from cash flow. The problem with this flow sheet was that preliminary test work indicated a high proportion of fines in the ore that could create significant problems in heap leach and marginalise the rate and extent of Cu recovery. 

An alternate to the above was the introduction of scrubbing of the ore. Preliminary testing showed positive results with scrubbing capable of removing a significant proportion of the ore fines making the coarse fraction amenable to heap leaching. So a revised flowsheet of crushing followed by scrubbing with the coarse fraction directed Heap Leach SX-EW and fines discarded to tailings. This flowsheet had the disadvantage of ~20% of the contained copper being lost to tailings. 

After considering all of the above flowsheets, the 2011 Scoping study considered the base process flowsheet consisting of crushing and then scrubbing with fines directed to an Agitated Leach with CCDs, neutralisation and then final tailings storage facility (TSF) for the neutralised waste. The clarified PLS was to be directed to a dedicated SX plant and the coarse ore fraction sent to Heap Leach with its own dedicated SX. Solutions from both SX plants are combined prior to a shared EW facility. This project was broken into 3 development phases: Phase 1 was an Initial 25;000tpa Heap Leach SX-EW using high grade rejects from the Stage I HMS operations, then after 1.5 years Phase 2, consisting of an Agitated leach of high grade fines from the Stage I HMS operations. After a further year Phase 3, a crushing facility and expansion of SX and EW up to 50,000tpa. 

The 2012 Feasibility Study invest

igated further opportunities to optimise the flowsheet, maximise Cu recovery and minimise capital and operating costs whilst maintaining the 3 Phase development. The key opportunities were integrating the solution management system for both Heap Leach and Agitation leach. This integration allows for use of acidified tailings, minimising operating costs by removing the need for neutralising agents. Because of the slow leaching chrysocolla this also allows for increased recovery of ~5% from the agitated leach tailings. The solution integration also allowed for the reduction of the number of CCDs from 6 to 3 and removal of PLS clarification without impacting Cu recovery and leading to significant capital cost savings. Finally, the integration allowed for a single train SX plant rather than two separate SX trains dedicated to Agitated Leach and Heap Leach. This again reduced the project capital cost. It is believed this final process flowsheet provides the optimal capital and operating cost outcome with greatest flexibility for future expansion of the project. ###### **Phase 1 – Overview** Under the staged expansion concept, leaching operations and subsequent production of cathode will be achieved at Phase 1 by treating HMS floats material and installing equipment required for the processes of Heap Leach, SX-EW (Figure 7). It is estimated that the HMS floats material will total approximately 1.2 Mt at a head grade of 3.0 %. Equipment installed at the Heap Leach (HL) facility would comprise 2 leach “cells”, along with ILS and PLS ponds and the storage facility for concentrated sulphuric acid. A raw water pond will also be installed at Heap Leach, with raw water being used for inventory make up and “flushing” of heaps as they reach terminal recovery. Solution pumps and piping installed at the ILS and PLS ponds will have a design capacity for the final plant design flowrates of 1000 m3/h. Treatment of the PLS generated in HL would require the installation of an SX-EW plant with the capacity to produce up to 25 ktpa. The SX plant comprises a total of 3 mixer settlers, being two extract units and one strip unit. The civil works required for future expansion of the SX to 5 mixer settlers would be installed during the Phase 1 development. ###### **PLANT LOCATION AND LAYOUT** 

Several potential sites within in the project area were available for the proposed process plant and heap leach pad and tails storage facility. To compare the advantages and disadvantages of each, a “Site Selection Matrix” was developed. The site selection matrix was developed to consider relevant factors including; haul distances, tails facility and heap leach pad constructability, environmental and social issues, impact on existing infrastructure and current and future mining operations. The resultant “score” was used to rank each site to accord with its suitability. 

Six potential sites were considered. Site layouts were produced of each to show existing infrastructure, ore bodies, the proposed process plant, heap leach pads and tails storage facilities and other relevant features. 

Site B-3 was selected on the following advantageous features: 

- Process plant and heap leach pads are upstream of the TSF thus confining runoff to a single valley and simplifying runoff management 

- Short haul distance to ROM pad 

- Short conveyor length to heap leach pad 

- Wholly within project lease area 

As the study progressed, optimisation of the B-3 layout was achieved. With a smaller than anticipated heap leach pad, the process plant has been located between the existing HMS plant and the leach pad. The final Site layout is shown in Figure 10.

The new Leach Pad will be located approximately 600m South East of the existing HMS Plant and will be constructed in a North West to South East direction during the life of the mine. The location was chosen to make best use of the local topography and minimise materials handling during the various stages of the Project. For Phases 1, the agglomerator is to be located North West of the heap pad in close proximity to the existing HMS, to minimise handling and piping distances for the HMS Rejects and Slimes re-treatment. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Ausenco Copper Process has been designed to mitigate changes in the copper grade in ore bodies and provide mines with a way to produce a high copper content concentrate or ‘super con’. Copper ore bodies often show supergene enrichment of the copper minerals, with weathering leading to conversion of chalcopyrite (‘CuFeS2’) to iron-depleted copper minerals such as bornite (‘Cu5FeS4’) and chalcocite (‘Cu2S’). As a mine gets deeper into the deposit the copper content of the copper minerals typically declines and the iron content increases as the mining transitions from the supergene zone to the sulfide zone. A concentrate rich in the supergene minerals typically has a higher copper content than a chalcopyrite concentrate. Additionally, as mines age, the ore grade tends to decline, because operators typically mine the best ores first to pay back the invested capital. To maintain copper output, concentrator throughput is often increased by staged plant expansions. The decline in final grade of the copper concentrate is offset by a higher tonnage output, which also compensates for the decline in copper recovery to the concentrate. 

The throughput of modern copper smelters is frequently constrained by the capacity of the acid plants used to capture the sulfur dioxide they produce. Thus, the copper/sulfur ratio is an important consideration. A smelter so constrained might be interested in purchasing some concentrate with a higher copper/sulfur ratio to blend with lower-grade concentrates to increase total copper output. Availability of super con grade material allows a smelter to increase copper production for a given feed tonnage or have something to blend with lower-grade concentrates to maintain copper production. 

The Ausenco Copper Process<sup>(1)</sup> conceived by Grenvil Dunn and Peter Bartsch, (Australian patent 2008200206) involves a two-stage hydrometallurgical process. It has the twin advantages of producing a higher-grade concentrate for sale while increasing total copper recovery for the miner. Recovery to saleable concentrate is increased by recovering copper from a lower-grade concentrate fraction, in addition to the conventional concentrate. The lower-grade fraction is treated by pressure oxidation (‘POX’) to generate an acid copper sulfate solution. This is then used in a non-oxidizing pressure leach to leach iron out of the high-grade fraction, producing a super con final product. 

The process is also able to reduce the content of some deleterious species, such as uranium

and certain base metals, in the concentrate. In addition, excess acid and ferric oxidant from the POX stage is available for leaching other fractions of the ore. It may also have application to certain copper-gold ores that do not respond well to flotation, provided they are low in pyrite.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper ore bodies close to the surface often have a zone of supergene enrichment, where weathering has converted the copper minerals from chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) to minerals containing less sulfur and iron, such as bornite (Cu5FeS4) and chalcocite (Cu2S). As mining gets deeper, the mineral assemblage transitions to a predominance of chalcopyrite. This results in a decline in the copper/sulfur ratio in the minerals and the resulting copper concentrate. 

Additionally, miners typically extract the high-grade core of a deposit first, as this is frequently the quickest way to pay back the money borrowed to develop the ore body. Thus, as a mine ages, the grades mined tend to decrease. To maintain copper output, mine throughput is often increased by staged plant expansions. The pressure to maximize the copper grade in the concentrate, to minimize smelter treatment and transport costs, can also result in lower copper recovery to the concentrate as the feed grade declines. In terms of tonnes of contained copper, a drop in the final grade of the copper concentrate can be offset by a higher tonnage output, which also compensates for the decline in copper recovery to the concentrate. 

For mines with associated smelters, a decline in the copper grade of the feed concentrate can then limit smelter copper production, unless additional smelter capacity is installed. However, this is may not be as easy to achieve as adding additional comminution and flotation capacity to the concentrator. Modern smelters are typically constrained by the capacities of their associated acid plants to recover sulfur and are therefore not amenable to modular increases in capacity without the addition of extra sulfur capture capacity. Smelters so constrained have an interest in treating copper concentrate containing less sulfur. 

The Ausenco Copper Process was designed to address these issues. It is based on the addition of a two-stage hydrometallurgical process to the concentrator plant. This can probably be sized with more flexibility and modularity than an acid plant expansion. The Ausenco Copper Process was originally developed by Grenvil Dunn and Peter Bartsch, with the rights to develop and market the patented<sup>(1)</sup> process assigned to Ausenco. 

Recovery to saleable concentrate is increased by recovering more of the copper in the ore into the final concentrate. Copper is recovered from a lower-grade concentrate fraction in addition to the copper in the conventional concentrate. The lower-grade scavenger concentrate fraction is treated by pressure oxidation (‘POX’) to generate acidic copper sulfate solution. This is then used in a nonoxid

izing upgrade autoclave to leach iron from the high-grade fraction, producing a ‘super con’ final product. In addition, excess acid and ferric oxidant from the POX stage is also available for onsite leaching other fractions of the ore. This could be the flotation tailings or other low-grade material not amenable to flotation using atmospheric tank leaching or heap leaching. The process is also able to reduce the content of some deleterious species, such as uranium, in the concentrate product sent for smelting. The process may also have application to certain copper-gold ores that do not respond well to flotation, provided they are low in pyrite. ###### **BASIC FEATURES** ###### **Copper Concentrate Upgrade** The desire to maximize the copper grade of the final concentrate can increase pressure on copper recovery, especially for deposits that are less amenable to flotation. This can result in higher losses to the flotation tailings. The Ausenco Copper Process avoids these issues by recovering copper from what would normally be tailings. The flotation plant is modified to produce two concentrates: - a higher-grade concentrate >25% copper content - a lower-grade concentrate, e.g. 15-25% Cu. This allows more of the copper in the ore to be captured without compromising the grade of the final concentrate. The lower-grade concentrate is treated by pressure oxidation. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Neomet has been updating the chloride processing flowsheet for nickel laterite ores and other feeds over the past few years. This paper reviews the more recent developments in the flowsheet, with particular emphasis on the key acid recovery and iron precipitation unit operation. Results of a miniplant campaign leaching composite laterite ores are presented, together with the latest developments and initial results from the pilot scale operation of the acid recovery circuit. The deportment and behavior of impurities, notably aluminium, magnesium and manganese, all major components of laterite ores, are demonstrated, and the implications of these data discussed in the context of the overall flowsheet.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Neomet Technologies Inc. (Neomet) has been actively developing and improving the chloridebased processing flowsheet for nickel laterite ores and various other feedstocks over the past few years<sup>(1,2,3)</sup> . Several robust and economically-viable flowsheets have been defined<sup>(3)</sup> , one of which is now moving into testing at the fully-integrated pilot level of operation. However, despite the fact that the concept of using high-strength chloride solutions for the recovery of nickel and cobalt from all horizons of a nickel laterite profile has been presented and discussed in some detail over the past few years, this approach is still being treated with caution, in particular with respect to the regeneration and recycle of hydrochloric acid. 

The key unit operation in any chloride-based flowsheet is the recycle of the chloride lixiviant, usually hydrochloric acid, coupled with the control and elimination of iron (and other nuisance elements such aluminium, magnesium and calcium) within the process<sup>(4)</sup> . Conventionally, pyrohydrolysis has been, and largely remains, the method of choice, as practiced for example in the steel pickling industry<sup>(5,6,7,8)</sup> , and by QIT in its UGS Process<sup>(9)</sup> . Vale (formerly as Inco) has also chosen this method for producing nickel oxide from its

Goro flowsheet<sup>(10)</sup> . However, pyrohydrolysis is indiscriminate in the recovery of metals and is both energy-intensive and costly to operate<sup>(11,12)</sup> , although recent attempts to use oxygen enrichment have resulted in some improvements<sup>(13)</sup> . 

As a consequence, alternative methods to pyrohydrolysis are now being investigated for the recovery and recycle of hydrochloric acid, such as the addition of sulphuric acid (a nominally cheaper reagent, but highly dependent on the price of sulphur) to spent calcium chloride solutions<sup>(14)</sup> , and the PORI Process which operated briefly during the 1970s<sup>(15,16,17,18)</sup> . More recent variations on the PORI Process have been developed by SMS Siemag<sup>(19,20)</sup> , McGill University<sup>(21)</sup> , and Starfield Resources in collaboration with SGS Lakefield<sup>(22)</sup> , and Queen’s University has proposed a method of recovering HCl via precipitation of magnesium hydroxychloride followed by calcination<sup>(23)</sup> . 

Neomet has also developed a method of hydrochloric acid regeneration which operates at much lower temperatures (180°C) than pyrohydrolysis (650-900°C), and which has some similarities to the PORI and SMS Siemag Processes, although without the fatal flaws inherent in the chemistry of those processes. In this paper, the latest developments in the Neomet Process are presented and discussed, including both miniplant and preliminary pilot plant data. 

###### **THE NEOMET PROCESS** 

The Neomet Process is actually a suite of processes based on chloride leaching and acid recovery/recycle in a closed loop, which can be tailored to a wide variety of feed materials. The chemistry of chloride processing offers many advantages over similar circuits based on the more common use of sulphuric acid. To date, Neomet has processed through its miniplant titaniferous magnetites, gold and silver ores and concentrates, polymetallic massive sulphides, nickel laterite ores and electric arc furnace dust. The hydrochloric acid regeneration/iron hydrolysis unit operation is the cornerstone of the flowsheets for each of these feeds. 

###### **Miniplant Leaching Operation for Nickel Laterite Ore** 

In a previous paper, data were presented on the laboratory leaching performance of a number nickel laterite samples from various orebodies around the world<sup>(2)</sup> . These data showed generally high extractions of Ni, Co, Fe, Mn and Mg, and ~50% extraction of the Al. The rate at which these metals dissolved was dependent on the nature of the laterite, some reacting faster than others. However, in all cases, approximately 50% of the initial mass was lost during leaching, with the resultant leach solids settling and filtering very well. This is in contrast to the very difficult liquid/solid separation experienced with HPAL slurries, and is due to the ability of the high chloride liquor to dehydrate the leach residue.

Temperature-Concentration Curve for Ferric Chloride** The basic thesis of hydrothermal acid regeneration is to heat up ferric chloride solution to a point at which the salt decomposes (hydrolyses), forming hematite and releasing hydrochloric acid. A discussion of the fundamental chemistry involved has been presented in an earlier publication(4) . Briefly, in the PORI and SMS Siemag Process, any ferrous iron is first oxidized in an autoclave, with one third of the iron forming hematite and the balance ferric chloride, with no acid evolution. The resultant ferric chloride is then hydrolysed at 175-180°C in a separate reactor, with the liquid bath at 175-180°C being maintained at 65% ferric chloride (i.e. ~FeCl3•5.5H2O) as described in the SMS Siemag patent application(27) . As can be seen from Table 2, the oxidation reaction for ferrous iron is highly exothermic, whereas the hydrolysis reaction is significantly endothermic. Thus, by carrying out the reactions in separate vessels, the hydrolysis reaction requires a significant input of heat. In fact, the hydrolysis reaction is more or less instantaneous at 175°C, and hence the overall rate of reaction is determined by the rate at which heat can be supplied into the reactor (and solids removed). This, therefore, presents a dilemma when taken in conjunction with the data of Figure 5 If the basic hydrolysis process is operating at 175-180°C, then in a large, commercial plant, the normal use of a heat exchanger would seem to be precluded, because in order to provide the very significant heat input needed, the hot side of the heat exchanger in contact with the ferric chloride liquor would need to be appreciably above the temperature at which ferric chloride goes solid (“dries out”). Thus, it would be expected that the hot side would build up a layer of hematite/ferric chloride scale, ultimately rendering the exchanger inoperative. Sparging of live, superheated steam is also precluded for several reasons. The system comprises a specially-designed reactor and solids removal system It also makes use of an inert solvent matrix, which remains fluid over the temperature range 120-250°C (i.e. autoclave temperatures), but which also remains open to the atmosphere, thereby allowing the formed HCl to be simply and efficiently removed from the system. It also had to be sufficiently ionic at elevated temperatures to allow the chemical reaction to proceed, and to be capable of acting as a solvent for base and other metals. The strength of the acid so-formed is determined entirely by the concentration of the feed ferric chloride solution, e.g. 4M FeCl3 will yield 12 12M HCl. - Formation of crystalline hematite, particle size being determined by the residence time of the formed solids in the reactor, since heterogeneous precipitation takes place the hematite filters extremely rapidly, and since the matrix solution remains fluid, it can be filtered in-situ. It also demonstrates that air can be effectively used. However, whilst the use of air is undoubtedly cheaper than oxygen, there is a downside in that there is a greater strain placed on the subsequent hydrochloric acid condensation system due to the large volumes of nitrogen accompanying the HCl vapours. Further, it should be noted that whilst the nitrogen acts as a carrier gas in removing the HCl from the reactor, it also lowers the partial pressure of water vapour, thus potentially evaporating more water than necessary, and thereby removing additional heat. Standard modeling (and experimental data) shows that the bulk of the acid can be recovered at a superazeotropic concentration (up to 12M HCl), with the tail gas being stripped quite effectively from a gas containing residual air, nitrogen, etc.(30) . To do so requires several theoretical stages of packing and either condensing the right amount of water or adding it to the top of the scrubber to get essentially all the HCl down as about 8-10% HCl in water by cooling the gas to about 50°C, which can be done effectively with cooling water. This latter, of course, is the same problem as faced in pyrohydrolysis, where maximum acid concentrations only of ≤18% HCl are achieved, since there is much more inert gas (from the burners)

. Ultimately, it depends very much on the volumes of HCl being generated, the ability of the condensing system to collect this HCl, and the costs of using air versus oxygen compared to the additional energy required associated with generating more dilute HCl. 

The foregoing discussion points to feeding as concentrated a solution as possible to the oxidation/hydrolysis circuit. The data of Figure 5 indicate that a feed temperature in the range of 130-140°C should be perfectly feasible, and such can be readily achieved when there are significant levels of ferric iron present. In order to test out whether this could actually be achieved, a small laboratory experiment was carried out under conditions where no HCl was liberated (i.e. under conditions of the oxidation reaction shown in Table 2, using oxygen rather than air and in a heavily insulated reactor, but with no heat input and water evaporation kept to a minimum. 

Theoretically, oxidising one mole of ferrous iron in one litre under these conditions should produce a temperature rise of 18.8°C (using the rule of thumb that the mathematical product of specific heat and specific gravity is one), whereas hydrolyzing one mole of ferric iron in one litre should incur a temperature drop of 11.7°C. On the basis that three moles of ferrous iron in one liter are oxidized, of which one hydrolyses to hematite (Table 2), then a temperature rise of 44.7°C would be anticipated. The experiment yielded a result wherein the solution temperature rose from 122°C to 169°C, thus confirming the underlying theory.

###### **Base Metal Chlorides** 

As noted above, the base metals remain dissolved in the matrix solution as the ferric iron and aluminium hydrolyse to form their oxides. Previous testwork has been reported showing that individual solutions of ~10 g/L for each of copper, nickel and cobalt chlorides dissolved in a magnesium chloride matrix can be hydrolysed with water at 180°C<sup>(31)</sup> . It should be noted that magnesium is but one of several matrices that can be used, but because of its tendency to spontaneously hydroslyse at 195-200°C, its use is somewhat limited. However, this factor is made use of in recovering a pure magnesium product in laterite processes. The copper and cobalt precipitates were highly crystalline and filtered extremely well, but the solids formed were not the oxide as observed with iron and aluminium. Chemical analyses and XRD scans indicated that the basic chlorides, with a generic formula of Me(OH)2•Me(OH)Cl•nH2O

, where Me is Ni, Cu or Co, had formed. In the case of zinc, the tetra basic chloride [Zn5(OH)8Cl2•H2O] has been formed. 

However, in reality, there are always mixtures of metals, especially copper, cobalt and nickel. In one test, carried out in the laboratory after iron hydrolysis, the solvent matrix had built up to 30% combined base metals, in the ratio 10:10:1 Cu:Ni:Co. Injection of water at 180°C precipitated a solid phase having the analysis of Cu 50.6%, Ni 0.7% and Co 0.06%, at >90% recovery of the copper. This demonstrates an unexpected benefit of the process, in that copper can be selectively recovered from nickel and cobalt. Further work, however, remains to be carried out on this aspect of the process. 

###### **THE NEOMET PROCESS** 

As noted earlier, the Neomet Process is really a suite of processes, which can be tailored to various different feed materials, with iron hydrolysis/hydrochloric acid regeneration as the key and common unit operation, and is a flexible and basically simple flowsheet. Being chloride-based, high solubilities are possible which reduce the volumetric flowrate, and hence equipment size. Working at high temperatures facilitates rapid reaction times, which leads to short residence times and again to reduced equipment size. A further advantage of the hot, high chloride background is that solids are either crystalline or generally dehydrated, making them amenable to both rapid solid/liquid separation and also to having low liquor retention. This again reduces equipment size, and also has a major beneficial impact on the water, and hence energy, balance, since wash water requirements are minimised. 

The process also allows for the recovery of valuable by-products. It is fair to say that the mining and base metals extraction industry has largely focused on only one or two pay metals in any given feed material. Metals such as iron, aluminium and magnesium generally have been regarded as nuisances rather than opportunities, and other metals such as scandium, gallium, indium, germanium, etc. have only received attention if present in significant concentrations. The Neomet Process is capable of generating pure oxides of all of these, thereby potentially adding considerably to the revenue stream. At the very worst, all are present in an environmentally-benign form that can be safely disposed of.

###### **DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper has presented some more recent data from the Neomet Process, showing that the process conditions are now well-established, that the process is economically attractive, and has been verified by an outside entity. Notably, the development of the unique “atmospheric autoclave” approach to acid regeneration has simplified the flowsheet appreciably, allowing it to handle a variety of different complex ores. 

The highlights can be summarized as follows: 

- The process is capable of treating a variety of different feeds, including any or all horizons of a laterite orebody and complex polymetallic sulphides, and unlike other processes, all valuable components of the ore can be recovered if desired. Iron, aluminium and magnesium, normally regarded as nuisance elements, can each be recovered in a pure form and marketed. At the very worst, they are low-volume, benign solids that can easily be returned to the mine for disposal.

- High recoveries are achieved during leaching, and the resultant leach slurry is amenable to vacuum filtration due to the dehydrated nature of the residual solids. This therefor

e results in a much lower footprint and more concentrated liquors than would be possible by using, for example, the CCD circuit commonly associated with HPAL circuits. 

- Acid regeneration is rapid and efficient, generating a much higher strength HCl than is possible by pyrohydrolysis. Simultaneously, iron and aluminium are precipitated as discrete, pure crystalline solids. If desired, preliminary data indicate that the aluminium can be easily separated from the iron by a simple caustic wash. Being highly crystalline and dehydrated, the solids filter rapidly and have a very low (<10%) liquor retention, even under vacuum filtration, thus requiring very little wash water  This in turn helps both the water and energy balances. 

- After iron removal, base metals can be recovered initially as basic chlorides. It is possible to preferentially recover copper ahead of nickel and cobalt. The basic chlorides dissolve readily in dilute HCl for processing to metal, or can be calcined directly at 200-500°C to give the metal oxide. 

- Magnesium is not an issue in this flowsheet. It can be recovered either as a hydroxy chloride or as magnesia at the end of the flowsheet. 

- Alkali metals, if present, are easily salted out. Potassium, in particular, is marketable as potash if warranted. Calcium is easily controlled by addition of sulphate, or can be sold directly as the chloride. 

The flowsheet is closed loop, in that there are no liquid effluents.  are either environmentally benign, or can be sold directly as additional revenue streams.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Chloride metallurgy is emerging as an alternative process for the production of base metals. Process Research ORTECH Inc. (PRO) has been at the forefront of technological development of chloride metallurgy. PRO’s patented mixed chloride technology has been applied to the recovery of several products including titanium dioxide from ilmenite ores, REE from alumino-silicate ores, base metals and PGM from sulfide ores, gold from refractory ores and base metals from laterite ores. This paper will describe the application of PRO’s mixed chloride technology for the recovery of gold from refractory ores and base metals from lateritic ores. PRO process uses mixed chloride lixiviant (HCl+MgCl2) to bring base metals in solution. The HCl leaching system provides the opportunity to regenerate the acid by pyrohydrolysis, while the presence of MgCl2 in the lixiviant enhances the activity of the hydrogen ion by orders of magnitude, making the lixiviant very aggressive. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Chloride metallurgy is emerging as an alternative process for the production of base metals<sup>(1-10)</sup> . Chloride chemistry is complex and quite different from corresponding sulfate systems. The solubility of metal chlorides is generally higher than their corresponding sulphate salts. The solubility of CuSO4.5H2O is about one fifth that of CuCl2.2H2O, while nickel and ferrous chlorides are also more soluble than their sulphate counterparts. This allows the use of more concentrated solutions<sup>(11)</sup> . Also, the activity of water is <<1 in concentrated magnesium chloride salt solutions, and the activity of the hydrogen ion, H<sup>+</sup> (or H3O<sup>+</sup> ) increases rapidly with chloride concentration as shown in Figure 1<sup>(12)</sup> . in mixed chloride solutions resulting in increased base metals recovery. Process Research ORTECH Inc. The application of PRO’s mixed chloride technology for the recovery of gold from refractory ores and base metals from lateritic ores is described below. ###### **PROCESSING OF GOLD ORES** Gold ores can be divided into non-refractory and refractory ores. Recovery of gold is simpler for non-refractory gold ores compared to that for refractory gold ores. As the grade of non-refractory gold ores is falling across the globe and reserves are depleting, the interest in the treatment of refractory gold ores is increasing(27-30) . ###### **Non-Refractory Gold Ores** Non-refractory gold ores contain free gold particles in a relatively inert matrix. Non-refractory gold ores include placer, free milling and oxidized ores. Nearly 95% of the gold from non-refractory gold ores can be recovered by gravity concentration and/or direct cyanidation. There are mainly two constituents responsible for the refractory behavior of ores: - 1) sulfides, silicates, tellurides, antimonides and selenides - 2) carbonaceous matter Refractory behavior of the first type can be divided further in chemical and physical refractoriness. When gold is combined with other elements in compound form such as tellurides (AuTe2 – calaverite), antimonides (AuSb2 – aurostibnite) and selenides (Ag3AuSe2 – fischesserite), it causes chemical refractoriness. When gold particles are finely disseminated in a matrix such as sulfides or silicates or exist as solid solution, it causes physical refractoriness. The treatment of refractory gold ores is more complex than non-refractory gold ores. The treatment process opt

**Figure 3: Processing of refractory gold ores** The ore is first crushed and ground and may undergo concentration using gravity separation or flotation. Depending upon the type of ore, the crushed/ground ore or concentrate may undergo one of these treatments: 1) roasting, 2) attrition milling, 3) atmospheric oxidative leaching, 4) pressure oxidative leaching or 5) bacterial leaching. Leaching is generally followed by neutralization. This is followed by cyanidation and further processing for gold recovery. ###### **Double Refractory Gold Ores** An ore body is called double refractory, if it contains both sulfides and carbonaceous matter(34) . The carbonaceous matter may be present as organic carbon or elemental carbon. Organic carbon may be in the form of hydrocarbons, humic acids and other organic substances, while the elemental carbon may be graphitic or amorphous. Graphitic carbon is the main source of carbonaceous matter in double refractory gold ores presenting serious challenges in the recovery of gold during leaching. The processing of double refractory gold ores presents a major challenge to gold producers. As with refractory gold ores, double refractory sulfide ores can be oxidized to decompose the sulfide matrix thereby liberating gold and making the disseminated gold amenable to leaching. The oxidizing pre-treatment processes may include the conventional roasting, pressure oxidation, chlorination and bacterial oxidation as described in the previous section. In case of double refractory gold ores, however, one needs to deal also with the preg-robbing behavior of the carbonaceous matter. The carbonaceous matter needs to be either removed or passivated before cyanidation. There are several approaches that are being investigated to deal with the preg-robbing behavior of the carbonaceous matter. These methods include flotation, addition of blanking agents, roasting and competitive loading onto commercial activated carbon. Flotation of carbonaceous matter may be an option, if the amount of gold associated with carbonaceous matter is low. In that case, ALTA 2013 350 carbonaceous matter may be floated and discarded. Further processing can then be done by one of the processes discussed above for refractory gold ores. The treatment of double refractory gold ores is very challenging and there is a need for economical and practical methods to treat these ores. Fundamental understanding of ore mineralogy, solution chemistry along with a deeper knowledge of the limita

tions of various chemical and thermal processing methods are key considerations in development of a robust solution. ###### **Features of PRO Gold Technology** Process flowsheet developed by PRO for treatment of refractory/double refractory gold ores is shown in Figure 4(35) . Typical mineralogical profile of nickel laterite ore bodies is as described below(37-38) : - 1) Overburden: This zone contains low nickel values (< 0.8% Ni) and is discarded). - 2) Limonitic ore zone: This zone contains ~1.2-1.7% Ni, ~ 40 % Fe and ~1-4% MgO. Hydrometallurgical processes are used to extract nickel from limonitic ore zone. High Pressure acid Leach (HPAL) process using sulphuric acid may be used for high iron (> 35 % Fe) limonitic ores. ALTA 2013 351 - 3) Saprolitic ore zone: This zone contains ~1.7 to 2.3 % Ni and low iron (< 15 % Fe). Pyrometallurgical smelting processes are used to produce ferronickel or matte from saprolytic ores. - 4) Base rocks: This zone contains <0.5% Ni and it is not economic to extract nickel from base rocks. In some ore bodies the saprolitic ore profile is either absent, not present or too trace for economical extraction, in which case nickel is extracted from the limonitic ore zone. In ore bodies with rich saprolitic ore zone, the limonitic ores may be stockpiled and stored for later treatment till the higher grade saprolitic ore zone is exhausted. ###### **Commercial Processes for the Treatment of Lateritic Ores** There

are three commercial processes for the extraction of nickel from lateritic ores: Pyrometallurgical process, Caron process and High Pressure acid Leach (HPAL) process. The flowsheet for all three commercial processes is shown in Figure 5(36) . The Pyrometallurgical process is used for saprolitic ores with high nickel values to produce ferronickel and matte with 25 to 75% Ni content. The flowsheet for pyrometallurgical processing of lateritic ores consists of ore drying followed by calcination/reduction in a rotary kiln. The calcine from the rotary kiln is smelted in an electric furnace with carbon as reductant followed by refining or conversion to produce ferro-nickel or matte. The process involves drying, calcining and smelting of entire ore body at successively higher temperatures and therefore is energy intensive. Drying

MgO thus produced can be used for pH control as well as precipitation of Ni and Co compounds from their respective preg strip solutions. These innovative processes use mixed chloride lixiviant (HCl+MgCl2) to bring metals in solution. The presence of MgCl2 in the lixiviant makes the lixiviant very aggressive, which results in high recoveries of metals. Additional advantage of using mixed chloride lixiviant is the opportunity to regenerate the hydrochloric acid by pyrohydrolysis, which can be recycled to leaching stage. For processing of lateritic ores, innovative solvent extraction steps are used to separate base metals successively from the pregnant leach solution (PLS) and generate high purity preg strip solutions of Fe, Ni and Co individually. The process can treat low grade ores as well as rejects from higher grade ores and is also suitable for slags generated from pyrometallurgical operations during the production of Ni, Cu and Co. The PRO process uses atmospheric leaching and therefore is more economical than HPAL process which uses autoclaves to generate high pressure required for leaching.
