###### **ABSTRACT** 

The expected depletion of ore bodies conveniently amendable to orthodox, technologically and energetically relatively effortless refining practices may sooner or later cause serious disturbances in the supply of industrial metals such as – but not limited to – Nickel, Cobalt, Titanium and Vanadium. In parallel the producers of Aluminum and Gold face increasing opposition by environmentalist movements and regulators, who rightfully question the sustainability of production methods that yield undesirable long-term liabilities such as red mud ponds or depend on the use of toxic chemicals in substantial quantities. 

Alternative, seemingly more versatile, cleaner processes for the refining of minerals, which start with a leach in hydrochloric acid, have been proposed and discussed for decades in various academic and industrial circles but consistently failed to win the approval of project sponsors and investors – not unlikely because it has remained a fairly difficult exercise to make an ultimately compelling case for their technical viability and commercial feasibility throughout project related due diligence. 

In the present pape

r, we shall showcase a selected segment of the state of the art in this field, outlining why the subject is of industrial interest and commercial importance, what – to the best of knowledge of the authors – could theoretically be achieved and what may not unlikely remain out of reach for the foreseeable future. 

Advancements, that have been made, and encouraging insight, that has been collected during the development of a certain class of more or less promising flow sheets and techniques, are showcased and discussed. 

Further we elaborate on some perceived major road blocks, highlight some present ideas to improve the status quo and outline a road map for future research and development. 

ALTA 2013 

360 

###### **MOTIVATION** 

Despite an apparent, temporary slow down in global economic growth, which relaxes the supply/demand equilibrium for many commodities, a steadily growing, increasingly urbanized and resource-consuming world population is expected to require expanding quantities of metals for a foreseeable future. 

Naturally, a not insignificant proportion of the easy-to-mine feedstocks amendable to cheap, rather effortless, mostly non-ingenious refining and smelting methods, have already been mined and exhausted by our fathers, leaving future generations not only with the task of dealing with various environmental liabilities that resulted from the utilization of the best available technologies of former times, but also with the challenge to come up with novel processing methods that allow the sustainable production of industrial metals from the left over 2<sup>nd</sup> class ores or waste materials. 

Ecological awareness has finally become a priority on the political agendas of a growing number of developed countries, who introduced legislation which penalizes certain energy-intensive and waste generating operations and renders permitting of new facilities an increasingly complicated, difficult, not entirely predictable exercise. From the increasingly important viewpoint of permitting risk, hydrometallurgical processes are not unlikely to gain an advantage over their pyromet competitors in jurisdictions with high environmental standards; mainly because their liquid effluents appear under most circumstances technically easier to contain, to monitor, to neutralize and to control than gaseous smelter emissions. 

Although it can be debated whether global warming is happening, whether it is at least partially man-made, what exactly its potential consequences would be and whether we should be concerned, it seems relatively safe to assert that one day – which in some geologically underprivileged locations with somewhat distorted foreign relations could be not too far away – mankind will run out of attractively priced fossile fuel. 

Promoting shale gas fracking and ignoring the Kyoto protocol is a truly pragmatic answer to most of the questions posed by the circumstances and developments explained above. It permits the lowcost and profita

ble operation of the energy-intensive industrial processes required to maintain world metal supply – in extreme cases even in locations where skilled industrial labour is generally not available at competitive wages. 

An alternative, less pragmatic but maybe even better answer may be accelerated technological progress. The authors of this paper believe, that the future of metals refining will be in advanced processes and methods, which: 

1. utilize low-grade or less conventional ores and industrial waste materials 

2. comply with stringent environmental legislation by coming as close as possible to ’‘zero waste” 

3. have a low energy consumption and/or use renewable sources of energy 

Within the scope of this essay, the current writers cannot hope to cover all the possible implications of acknowledging the related challenges. The focus of this paper is thus – naturally – on recent advancements and setbacks related to the development of techniques suitable for refining ores economically amendable to a leach in hydrochloric acid. 

###### **Nickel/Cobalt** 

Roughly 60% of world’s estimated Nickel reserves are in lateritic ores. Their refining remains a challenge. Some recent attempts to introduce industrial implementations of novel hydrometallurgical processing methods targeting ever lowering grades did in some cases not exactly yield economic success, turned only marginally profitable or do not appear to be able to sustain future drops in Nickel and Cobalt prices. [Taylor, 2013] 

A number of incumbent processes suffers either from forced sub-optimal resource- utilization as it is tailored towards the treatment of either only the limonite or the saprolite fraction of a deposit or – e.g. in the case of HPAL – from comparatively high energy and maintenance cost. 

###### **_Potential_** 

Over the last years a number of alternative processes based on a leach of nickel laterite ore in

1. simple and efficient agitated tank leach at atmospheric pressure 

2. treat saprolite and limonite equally well 

3. regenerating and recycling of the lixiviant 

4. relatively high nickel and cobalt recoveries 

5. potential for recovery of additional by-products 

No commercial plants have been built and operated so far. However some of the proposed processes have been partially tested and validated on bench and mini plant scale. 

###### **_Economies_** 

Any new Nickel/Cobalt production technology should yield economics that sustain relatively low market prices. In the opinion of the authors a sensible threshold for the gross production cost would be around 8.000 USD per metric ton of Nickel. A naive but for the purposes of this exercise sufficiently accurate back-of-the-napkin estimation of the hypothetical uppe

r limit of acceptable CAPEX (in the presumed absence of any OPEX and ignoring by-product credits) based on that figure, as well as a WACC<sup>1</sup> of 10% and 25 years of plant life yields around 57.000 US-Dollar per annual ton of production capacity. 

Assuming an energy consumption of 510 GJ per metric ton of Nickel<sup>2</sup> as proposed in [Vogl et al., 2012] and an energy cost of 5 US-Dollar per GJ the energy-related OPEX is 2.550 US-Dollar per ton. The authors of the present paper consider it prudent to estimate the non energy-related OPEX of a HCl based flow sheet to be no more than 2.000 US-Dollar per ton. This gives a total of 4.550 US-Dollar per ton. This in turn leaves us with a (back-of-the-napkin) maximum tolerable CAPEX of 24.642 USD for each ton of annual production capacity. For a facility delivering 50.000 tons per annum, this would amount to approx 1.25 Billion US-Dollar, which we currently assume to be within the ball park of what could possibly be the EPC construction cost of such a plant. 



Considering however a higher energy consumption of 840 GJ per metric ton of Nickel<sup>3</sup> , as reported in the more recent publication by [Nowak et al., 2013], economies turn out less favourable, as energy-related OPEX increases to 4.200 US-Dollar per ton, all other things equal resulting in a total OPEX of 6.200 US-Dollar and a maximum tolerable CAPEX of only 12.857 USD per ton of annual production capacity, which would require a refinery for 50.000 annual tons to fit into a budget of roughly 650 Million US-Dollar, which the authors of this paper do not consider a figure that is compatible with current prices of materials, equipment and labour. 

It is probably important to note that the optimization of processing cost and energy consumption is a work in progress and the authors expect the presence of significant room for improvement in this area. Thus the capex constraints estimated in aforementioned exercise are not entirely unlikely to be relaxed as soon as new, updated information becomes available. Furthermore our rough estimate does not take into account any credits for by-products, such as Cobalt and Hematite. Those may or may not make significant positive contributions to project economics.

Most of world Aluminum is produced from Alumina obtained from bauxite using the Bayer process, leaving behind undesirably large quantities of toxid red mud as a long-term environmental liability for which a method of economically acceptable long term remediation has yet to be found. Thus significant charges for the massively fuel consuming long distance transportation of either Bauxite or Alumina are incurred by some of the operators of Aluminum smelters, most of which are located near hydro-electricity sites in the northern hemisphere.

###### **_Potential_** 

For many decades alternative means of producing Alumina – the precursor for Aluminum from raw materials other than bauxite<sup>4</sup> , which may be available closer to the smelter locations, have been subject to intensive study and discussion. Some of the most promising flow sheets start with leaching an aluminous raw material in hydrochloric acid and precipitating the relatively insoluble aluminum chloride by means of hydrogen chloride sparging, followed by calcination and HCl recovery.[Sawyer, 1983] 

So far, no commercial plants implenting this concept have been built and operated. However there have been successful demonstrations at mini- and pilot plant level. 

###### **Iron, Titanium and Vanadium** 

Titanomagnetite ores, which are relatively abundant, have so far attracted only little commercial interest, as they are neither conveniently suitable as an iron source in steel making, nor as a precursor of metallic titanium or titanium dioxide. 

###### **_Potential_** 

However, many Titanomagnetite deposits contain attractive amounts of Vanadium<sup>5</sup> , which have shown to be amendable to upgrading by means of magnetic concentration. At least one flow sheet [TNG Ltd., 2011], based on leaching the resulting concentrate in hydrochloric acid and subsequently extracting low-grade ilmenite, vanadium pentoxide, hematite<sup>6</sup> and a benign mixed metal oxide or sulfide fraction while regenerating all acid has been developed. 

In the presence of favourable economic conditions, logistic circumstances and energy prices, such a process may potentially show significantly improved profitability over conventional salt roasting routes. 

###### **Other Metals** 

Numerous flow sheets for the extraction of other metals from metal chloride brines have been proposed and discussed in the past, most notable for the extraction of Gold [Harris and White, 2011] and Rare Earths [Vogl et al., 2012]. While the elementary processing steps making up those flow sheets have been verified by computer modeling, bench- and mini plant experimentation, no activities towards commercial implementation are known at the time of publishing this paper. 

In the field of gold processing, leaching with hydrochloric acid reportedly can partially or entirely replace the environmentally hazardous but currently prevalent practice of applying cyanide. It also promises the possibility of by-product recovery, notably also for PGMs. 

Rare Earths can be effectively extracted as a valuable by-product from the hydrochloric acid regeneration circuits of facilities which main purpose is the production of other metals or metal precursors such as Alumina. In the light of the current geographical imbalance of supply which is caused by China capturing more than 90% of the market, there is a strong geopolitical incentive not to ove

rlook this possibility. 

###### **TECHNOLOGY** 

Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) is at the time of writing this paper not widely used in hydrometallurgical applications. Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4) is apparently far more common; mainly because it is – in the absence of market anomalities – widely available at reasonably low prices, can be produced in large quantities from raw materials which may be easily obtained at or close to the processing plant site and shows only a neglible volatility. The main metallurgical uses of hydrochloric acid are in the de-scaling of car- bon steel strips after hot rolling operations and in the production of synthetic rutile.

###### **ADVANCEMENTS** 

While Pyrohydrolysis as a means of hydrochloric acid regeneration has been around for more than half of a century and found successful industrial applications in the treatment of iron-, nickel-, cobalt-, magnesium-, aluminum- and rare earth chlorides, it was not until the advent of the PORIprocess [Burtch, 1973], that the selective hydrolysis of particular metal chlorides became available as a potential new, versatile building block for complex metal extraction processes. Since then research work at several independent organizations and companies has verified its theoretical applicability in a variety of fields by means of computer simulations and laboratory test work. In January 2011 SMS Siemag Process Technologies GmbH started commissioning the first large, industrial hydrolytic distillation plant for ferric chloride at ThyssenKrupp Steel in Calvert, Alabama. Initial commissioning results were encouraging. In particular: 

1. data from the plant confirmed the assumptions in the models for mass and heat balancing 

2. energy and utility consumption matched predictions 

3. product qualities matched predictions 

4. the process was easy to control, despite several nested feedback loops 

However severe availability issues with certain 3<sup>rd</sup> party supplied process equipment, for which no short term remedy could be found, as well as several unforeseen complications, which shall be described in the ”Setbacks” section of the present paper, in combination with external economic factors and opportunities led to the prudent decision not to commence commercial operation but to retain the plant, which came at a pre-commissioning cost of 30 Million US-Dollar, as an experimental and development facility.

###### **Development of Advanced Metal Separation Techniques** 

Following the commissioning of the ThyssenKrupp facility, which drew considerable interest from the non-ferrous-metals community, who quickly spotted opportunities for the introduction of novel hydrometallurgical flow sheets that utilized the hydrolytic distillation of HCl as one of their core techniques, a tool box enabling the very selective separation and extraction of certain metal chlorides from a mixed metal chloride brine was developed by SMS Siemag [Vogl et al., 2012]. The newly developed operations have since been tested and verified in laboratory trials and yielded encouraging results [Nowak et al., 2013]. 

###### **SETBACKS** 

While a number of promising results and ideas have been obtained and reported in the literature [Harris et al., 2009, 2012; Vogl et al., 2012], the section of this paper which is dedicated to the presentation and discussion of various road blocks and setbacks is still considerably longer than the preceding one which treated recent advancements. This is a natural result of the not entirely unexpected disillusionment that set in after first attempts to put the bold theories that were spun in our field over the last decade to the practical test encountered some difficulties which flow sheets, models and experimental data only revealed at a second glimpse. 

###### **Water Balance Issues** 

The ongoing development of tailored flow sheets for the hydrochloric acid digestion of particular ores and raw materials and the subsequent selective extraction of compounds from the leachate has shown, that the water balance of those processes is not unlikely to turn

into a serious obstacle in cases, where more external water is introduced than can be driven off without excessive surplus energy consumption. Examples for H2O, unaccounted for in idealized, conceptual flow sheets include ore-bound moisture and crystalline water, materials which are introduced during wet magnetic separation, as well as what is required for various cake washing and product purification steps. The volatile and aceotropic nature of hydrochloric acid renders the de-watering and purification of diluted streams an energetically expensive exercise which requires sophisticated equipment. 

###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

The most sensible solution appears to be to saturate the leachate with iron until no more free HCl is present before undergoing vacuum evaporation. In this case the vapor extracted in the evaporator is virtually free of HCl. It can thus be re-condensed and re-used internally for cake washing purposes before mixing with hydrolyser fumes to form regenerated HCl. Excess water introduced by ore-borne moisture can be discharged from the process as clean water, which requires no or only little further treatment. 

###### **Cooling Water Requirements** 

The process of hydrolytic distillation of HCl from metal chloride solutions consumes not only significant amounts of energy but also requires continuous cooling for vapor condensation. In arid inland locations, where cheap sources of cooling water may not be available or the utilization and 

ALTA 2013 

366 

re-circulation of lake or river water for industrial purposes is environmentally not permissible, this may introduce the need for the installation of large-scale autonomous cooling facilities, which can tie up considerable amounts of capital. 

###### **Difficult Start-Up and Shut-Down procedures** 

The practical experience gathered at world’s first hydrolytic distillation plant for ferric chloride at ThyssenKrupp Steel, Calvert, Alabama [Vogl et al., 2012], shows, that the process takes a considerable time until it reaches chemical and thermal equilibrium. While not in equilibrium it produces hydrochloric acid of diluted strength, which can not immediately be re-utilized but requires blending with a higher-strength source to avoid the need for neutralization. 

Shutting down the plant has shown to be an equally inconvenient exercise, as many of the liquors stored in the plant-internal reaction vessels are prone to crystallization at ambient conditions and contain considerable amounts of solids which pose difficulties to liquor storage and handling. 

###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

Sufficiently large acid storage tanks in the buffer tank farm that decouples leaching from processing, which can hold several times the volume of liquid contained in the processing plant at any given time, could allow a controlled dilution of regenerated acid reserves with weaker strength HCl during plant start-up and an equally controlled strengthening of leachate during shut down. ###### **Tight Coupling** 

Numerical simulations of complex flow sheets for the processing of complex ores by a specific implementation of the proposed technology have shown, that due to the presence of various process-internal feedback loops for both – mass and energy – the process has to be considered a tightly-coupled system, which in order to achieve acceptable availability requires highly reliable equipment in each single processing unit and/or large volume buffers<sup>10</sup> between processing stages to allow short interruptions or irregularities to happen in one processing stage without compromising others. 

###### **Filtration Issues** 

Filtration of metal oxides and insoluble materials from metal chloride brines is technically possible, as the required materials of construction are widely available. Both – pressure and vacuum filtration – have been successfully performed at industrial scale. However the volatile nature of hydrochloric acid tends to impose corrosion-related difficulties on the mechanical construction of the filtration devices and their surroundings, which – in the experience of the authors – leads to high maintenance requirements, shortened life time and resulting high operating cost. Furthermore the filter cakes have in some cases - e.g. during the initial filtration of silicates after leaching – shown to be difficult to form and generally consumed considerable amounts of water for washing and polishing. 

During work performed to support certain scoping studies for projects that consider the utilization of the proposed technology, it was found, that the size and number of the required filter devices is at the very upper end of what’s known to their makers and the required acid proof materials of construction and special technical add-ons to control HCl fumes are not available off-the-shelf. 

###### **Proposed Solution** 

In hindsight it proved to be too ambitious a goal to filter hematite from a molten salt solution in a boiling condition at or above 175°C. Heat expansion, in-situ-hydrolysis and formation of HCl rich, corrosive fumes led to mechanical difficulties, which have so far only be overcome by the introduction of economically not sustainable technical additions. Experiments of cooling the molten salt before filtration yielded ferric chloride crystallization on the surfaces of the applied heat transfer equipment. This was not entirely unexpected. Future filtration concepts are planned to operate at lower temperatures and below boiling point.  One rather promising, thermodynamically neutral

###### **Fouling and Scaling Issues** 

The vast majority of theoretically feasible flow sheets that aim for the regeneration and recovery of hydrochloric acid include one or more steps at which H2O and HCl undergo a phase-transition from liquid to gas. This consumes a considerable amount of heat, which can be introduced by one of two means: direct or indirect heating. When utilizing direct heating – as it is common practice in the pyrohydrolysis of spent pickle liquors in the steel industry – the possibilities of energy recovery become limited, as – to avoid dilution – the water fraction generated during combustion of hydrocarbon fuel cannot be re-condensed but has to be vented off, taking all the latent heat contained therein with  it. 

Indirect heating, as proposed for the hydrothermal acid regeneration process introduced by [Mach, 2009; Vogl et al., 2012] requires the installation and operation of heat exchangers, which could utilize heat-transfer media such as steam or thermo-oil. Practical experiences during the operation of the first hydrothermal acid regeneration plant at ThyssenKrupp Steel, Alabama, have shown that those heat exchangers – Tantalum was selected as material of construction – are not only very expensive but also prone to clogging, fouling and scaling which yielded unacceptably low availabilities and indicates the potential need for the permanent installation of redundant stand-by units to maintain acceptable plant availabilities. 

It seems important to note, however, that heat exchangers are not the only locations at which the formation of adhesive scale has been experienced. The majority of tubes and process vessels at the ThyssenKrupp Steel plant quickly developed a layer of a concrete-like mixture of iron oxides and chlorides, which was not easily removed by mechanical means. In situations where vibrations and heat expansion effects triggered some larger elements of that scale layer to break loose this yielded blocked filters, clogged heat exchangers and stuck control valves. ###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

The optimization of heat transfer is subject to ongoing research and development. The effects of decreased roughness of transfer surfaces, which could be obtained by electropolishing and may yield lower adhesion are studied in laboratory

trials. Alternative heat-up and cool-down curves as well as increased pressures at the point of heat transfer, avoiding the exceedance of the boiling point and hydrolysis inside the heat exchangers are experimentally verified in parallel and have so far shown very encouraging results. 

###### **Abrasion Issues** 

At least some of the process liquors present in the flow sheets as suggested by [Mach, 2009; Harris et al., 2012; Vogl et al., 2012] contain streams that carry notable quantities of abrasive solids which are supposed to exert severe abrasive forces and reduce the useful service life time of most commercially available industrial plastics – which are mechanically softened/weakened at the present operating temperatures that are in a number of locations close to the permissible maxima – below what is tolerable from a maintenance and availability point of view. At the ThyssenKrupp Steel plant rapid abrasion has been observed at PTFE pump casings and impellers, inside control valves and at locations inside plastic tubing, where turbulent or high velocity flow would be expected under certain operating conditions. 

###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

The conclusion of this experience is that plastic materials are preferably avoided in all locations where solid bearing brines are transported at elevated temperatures. To achieve acceptable service life times and availabilities and to prevent premature equipment failure as well as to ensure the safety of operating staff, future plants will have to be equipped with pipes, valves and pumps made of materials that show a higher tolerance to abrasive wear such as glass lined steel, Tantalum or ceramics. 

###### **Energy Consumption** 

As a consequence of the fact, that at least a major fraction of the hydrochloric acid involved in processing is usually regenerated and re-used, considerable amounts of energy are consumed to drive the evaporation of water and hydrogen chloride during hydrolysis or pyrohydrolysis. This is not a significant nuisance in relatively small applications such as those prevalent in the steel industry, where hourly quantities of regenerated liquor do typically not exceed 10m<sup>3</sup> , as the required amount of heat, which would be expected to be in a range between 1.5 and 4 GJ _/_ m<sup>3</sup> depending on the type of regeneration process applied and the hydrochloric acid loop concentration. 

Looking at the considerably larger volumes of HCl that have to be regenerated when applying HCl based techniques for metal extraction applications – which would range between 200 and 2000 m<sup>3</sup> _/_ h to support an operation of common commercial scale – hourly thermal energy consumption would quickly reach dimensions (300 to 8000<sup>GJ</sup> _/_ h which equals 83 to 2200 MW) that require the combustion of large quantities of fuel as well as infrastructure for heat provision such as steam boilers or thermo oil stations. In remote locations with inefficient fuel supply infrastru

cture, high energy prices and no existing infrastructure for energy distribution and conversion the portion of the CAPEX required for the energy supply as well as the energy related OPEX may compromise project economics. 

###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

In general increasing the acid loop concentration, while potentially complicating operations because of the high vapor pressure of over-azeotropic HCl, appers to be the most effective measure to further reduce energy consumption. In some cases, mechanical ore benefication may also greatly contribute to reduced consumptions and improved economics. 

###### **Production of Pure HCl** 

Several of the recently proposed flow sheets extract trace and target metals from concentrated

metal chloride brines by means of crystallization from saturated solutions, whereby the saturation is achieved by sparging the brine with dry hydrogen chloride. While this method has proven to be highly efficient at bench scale it has yet to be demonstrated that the required amounts of dry hydrogen chloride can be produced in industrial size implementations of the processes at feasible capital and operational expenditure. 

While not all conceivable flow sheets require large scale implementations of acid purification, those who do might at the time of writing the present paper not be viable. 

###### **Scale Up / Non-Availability of Commercial Equipment** 

Viable commercial equipment, such as valves, pumps, filters, glass lined reactors and heat exchangers has been found to be available to support plants that can handle acid loop volumina of up to approximately 50 m<sup>3</sup> _/_ h. This does not meet the demands of feasible sized operations for the production of Nickel, Ti/V or Alumina, which would have to be built in multiple parallel trains, which yields no economies of scale and increases the number of staff required for operation and maintenance. 

###### **_Proposed Solution_** 

The constraints imposed on scalability are not process borne but introduced by the limitations in the size of commercially available equipment. It appears to be required to involve equipment makers into the development of the next-generation components and apparatus that are necessary for the construction of the proposed type of metals refinery. 

###### **PROPOSED FUTURE DIRECTION OF RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT** 

Although there has reportedly [Vogl et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2012; Taylor, 2013] been increased activity in the field of hydrochloric acid leach based metal extraction technology over the last couple of years and despite the impression, that this approach promises a number of attractive advantages and benefits, these technologies do not yet appear to have reached a state of maturity that would designate them as ideal candidates for immediate large scale industrial application. Although we see reasonably good prospects for overcoming elementary shortcomings and achieving technical viability within short tim

e, commercial feasibility will depend on further optimization of capital and operating cost. 

Further development is not unlikely to be cost intensive and must involve collaboration among all layers of the supply chain to have a realistic chance of yielding success. Cohesive long term funding of further development efforts will have to be secured, which poses a hard challenge in times of slowing economic growth and temporarily bleakening outlooks for technology suppliers. The authors of the present paper do not expect hydrochloric acid based processes to claim significant industrial market share in the next couple of years, mainly because of present mechanical and apparatus constraints which have unexpectedly grown into a major concern since the publishing of [Vogl et al., 2012] and call for further investigations, tests and development work at equipment manufacturer level. In the long run however – given the emerging scarcity of resources amendable to traditional processing, the need to re-utilize waste materials as well as secondary heat sources and to avoid further irreversible destruction of environments and ecosystems – their utilization for certain applications may – in the view of said authors – become almost inevitable. 

In the meantime and in parallel, hybrid technologies as exemplified by [TNG Ltd., 2011], which combine trivial chloride based operations with well proven technologies such as SX, may position themselves as solutions with a considerably lower risk profile, that would under selected circumstances and projected payoffs indicate the feasibility of fast-tracking their commercial implementations. 

###### **_First Mover Advantage/Disadvantage_** 

A competitive advantage for those who first decide to put that supposedly advantageous technology to industrial use is not entirely unlikely – if the size of such a first move is chosen sensibly small. It appears to be a key prerequisite for success to allow the manufacturers of the required process equipment – who are to deliver a series of mechanical break throughs and innovations to deal with the requirements of the new processes and/or significant price optimizations – to push borders in small steps and learn in manageable, evolutionary increments.

###### **_Aluminum from Coal Fly Ash - An integrated Idea_** 

Fly ash is a by-product of coal inceneration, which is generated in large quantities by coal fired power plants. Typical subbituminous fly ash would consist of 40 - 60% SiO2, 20 - 30% Al2O3, 4 - 10% Fe2O3 and 5 - 30% CaO [Wikipedia]. It potentially contains significant quantities of Alumina. One area of ongoing research which due to geopolitical considerations could soon attract significant funding from concerned Chinese and/or Iranian entities is the extraction of that Alumina from fly ash by means of hydrochloric acid leach and subsequent metal chloride separation. The thermal energy required for driving the required chloride hydromet process as well

as the electrical energy required for the connected downstream Aluminum smelters are delivered by the coal fired power plant, which also produces the fly ash feed for the refinery. While the authors of the present paper recognize that the emissions created by the combustion of brown coal may introduce undesired environmental and ecological side effects, they happen to believe, that in the course of developing a truly integrated concept, more environmentally friendly combustion technologies will be developed. 

The advanced technologies and components, that need to be developed towards industrial maturity to enable the production of Alumina from fly ash, may – if ultimately successful – form a robust foundation for related applications in other fields. In the opinion of the authors of this paper, the further testwork and prototyping which is required to drive the present transformational innovation further may be too complex, too expensive and too risky to justify funding by a single entity focusing on an isolated project. However the expected payoff in case of success is large, as a vast array of possibilities to produce metals from previously untapped raw and waste materials are unlocked in a way that does not compromise high environmental standards and besides commercial feasibility may yield effects that render certain regions and countries less dependent on foreign resources. 

The probability of the alumina-to-fly-ash idea moving ahead cannot easily be estimated by the authors of the present paper. It is even uncertain, whether the method of choice would be a hydrochloric acid based extraction process. We are however confident, that a similar or remotely related set of motives will be the driving force behind the next wave of significant developments in our field.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

For the extraction of nickel from laterite ores, the following flow sheet is proposed: Leaching with hydrochloric acid, preconcentration of the brine, oxidation of ferrous (if present) to ferric chloride, hydrolysis of ferric chloride leading to the precipitation of hematite and evaporation of hydrochloric acid, and crystallization of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides by means of sparging hydrogen chloride into the solution. Hydrogen chloride required in the latter step is produced internally by super-azeotropic distillation of regenerate. The process has a closed water balance, as water driven off in the preconcentration step is used for tailings and hematite rinsing or is released if brought in by the ore into the process. Nickel can be finally recovered from a solid chloride mixture containing only minor amounts of ferric chloride. 

Based on experiments regarding the leaching, the hydrolysis, and the crystallization section of the flow sheet, a rough mass and heat balance is calculated as a part of ongoing work. 

During hydrolysis of artificial oxidized leachate, a rather pure hematite with approx. 0.5 wt% Al, 0.3 wt% Cr, and 0.5 wt% Cl and minor amounts (i.e. < 100 ppm) of other nonferrous metals can be separated in hydrolysis. Hydrochloric acid with 20-40 wt% HCl can be evaporated at 180°C. In the crystallization experiment, a filter cake containing all of the nonferrous metals and 0.4 wt% FeCl3 is collected. 

According to the mass and heat balance, the thermal energy consumption for the flow sheet is estimated to be in the order of 12 GJ/t of the laterite ore used for this study. This value has to be considered as preliminary result of ongoing work and is expected to go down by refining experimental conditions.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

According to the US Geological Survey, Nickel reserves are 75 Mt; in 2012, of which 2.1

Mt are mined<sup>(1)</sup> . The world resources (min 1% Ni) are approx. 130 Mt, of which 60% are lateritic and 40% sulfidic<sup>(1)</sup> . In 2003, 40% of the nickel mined arose from laterite ores<sup>(2)</sup> , which those require more complex processing<sup>(3)</sup> . 

Nickel laterite leaching is usually performed by capital-intensive pressure sulfuric acid leaching<sup>(4, 5)</sup> although hydrochloric acid is more effective<sup>(6)</sup> . As hydrochloric acid can be recycled, operating costs of hydrochloric acid based flow sheets are estimated to be lower as for sulfuric acid flow sheets<sup>(7)</sup> . However, hydrochloric acid based flow sheets for treating nickel laterites are not proven on industrial scale yet<sup>(8)</sup> . 

For selective leaching, there are several possibilities: Wang et al.<sup>(9)</sup> found that the leaching sequence of an Indonesian ore was siderite > chrysotile > magnetite > maghemite > goethite > hematite > chromite ~ ringwoodite<sup>(9)</sup> . Pre-roasting the ore affects both the phase composition and the physical properties of the ore and thus affects the leaching kinetics<sup>(10, 11)</sup> . Also the leaching of iron can be suppressed by this means<sup>(11)</sup> . Another possibility is the usage of other salts affecting the leaching process such as magnesium chloride<sup>(12)</sup> . 

Recovery of hydrochloric acid can be performed by pyrohydrolysis, i.e. spray roasting or fluidized bed acid regeneration<sup>(13)</sup> , by direct hydrolysis of ferric chloride, e.g. the PORI process<sup>(14, 15)</sup> , or by precipitation of with lime and conversion with sulfuric acid<sup>(16, 17)</sup> . The latter of these processes is economically not viable if high amounts of hydrochloric acid have to be added to ore<sup>(18)</sup> or if a lowgrade ore has to be processed<sup>(19)</sup> . 

The energy consumption of pyrohydrolysis is mainly driven by the evaporation of water. In the steel industry for the regeneration of hydrochloric acid from used pickling liquor, typically 2.7 GJ/m³ and 3.6 GJ/m³ thermal energy are required by spray roasting and fluidized bed roasting, respectively<sup>(13)</sup> . These processes principally do not recover the acid selectively but convert more or less all metal chlorides into the corresponding oxides. Alkali chlorides, such as sodium or potassium chloride, will end up in the oxide as they are. Ferric chloride cannot be roasted with standard roasters as its high vapor pressure causes evaporation and re-condensation; it requires either special roaster technologies or prior reduction to ferrous chloride. In the droplets sprayed into a spray roaster or on fluidized bed particles, water is evaporated, ferrous chloride is oxidized to ferric and hydrolysis of ferric chloride occurs. In the PORI process and similar processes these steps are separated to occur in different reactors. Anyway, for the PORI process<sup>(15)</sup> , the energy demand seems to be similar to the one fo

r spray roasting because the condensation enthalpy of the hydrolysis vapor cannot be recovered as direct heat is used. In the SMS Siemag Hydrothermal Acid Regeneration process, indirect heat is used for driving the hydrolysis process. This allows the condensation of the hydrolysis vapors and the recovery of the condensation enthalpy. For pickling liquor, the energy consumption is calculated to be 1.7 GJ/m³. One major advantage of this technology is the selectivity of acid regeneration: Generally, only ferric chloride hydrolyses and precipitates as pure hematite. Non-hydrolysable elements such as e.g. Fe(II), Na, Ca, Pb, Zn<sup>(20)</sup> , or Co and Ni<sup>(21)</sup> concentrate in the hydrolyser. This property requires on the one hand side additional process steps; on the other hand side it makes this technology interesting for the separation of iron in the non-ferrous metals industry. 

For the separation of non-hydrolysable elements, a crystallization process has been proposed<sup>(21)</sup> . In this process step, hydrogen chloride gas is sparged into the solution, which decreases the solubility of metal chlorides<sup>(22, 23)</sup> , whereas ferric chloride is significantly more soluble than nonhydrolysable metal chlorides. Furthermore, the chloride ions associated with iron apparently increase the activity of chloride in the solution<sup>(21)</sup> , which leads to lower required concentrations of HCl than if iron is absent<sup>(24)</sup> . 

In this paper, a flow sheet for the treatment of iron rich nickel laterites is presented. This flow sheet consists of the steps leaching, oxidation, ferric chloride separation and acid regeneration by means of hydrolysis, and crystallization of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides by means of sparging hydrogen chloride into the solution, Figure 1. Based on experiments performed, a rough mass and heat balance is calculated as a part of ongoing work.

###### **THE HYDROTHERMAL TECHNOLOGY FOR THE RECOVERY OF VALUABLE METALS FROM ORES** 

In many hydrochloric acid flow sheets, valuable metals are recovered from leachate by different means and the residue is then sent to the acid regeneration. This is necessary if a non-selective acid regeneration process such as pyrohydrolysis is used. As ferric chloride hydrolyses selectively in the hydrothermal process<sup>(20, 21)</sup> , it is proposed to recover the major amount of hydrochloric acid as early as possible, Figure 1. Thus the core of the flow sheet is the hydrolysis of ferric iron [step 6 below]. Non-hydrolysable metal chlorides are removed in a crystallization process [step 10 below], where hydrogen chloride gas is sparged into the solution. One major issue in this flow sheet is the water balance, as this is considered as very important for chloride processes<sup>(6)</sup> .<sup>The</s

up> proposed flow sheet consists in detail of the following steps, Figure 2: 

1. Crushing and grinding. In this process step, the grain size of the run-of-mine is adjusted for leaching. 

2. Leaching. The ground ore is leached with hydrochloric acid. It is assumed that at least a two-stage leaching process is used, where the concentration of free HCl in the liquor is lowered with fresh ore, so that the liquor after leaching contains no free hydrochloric acid. Tailings are washed with water (4) in order to reduce chloride losses there. The wash water ends up in the leaching liquor (6). 

3. Preconcentrator. In the preconcentrator, the liquor from leaching (6) is concentrated by means of vacuum evaporation. It is operated at approx. 60°C and thus allows the utilization of the condensation enthalpy (7) from the hydrolysis vapor for driving the process. The vapor (8) consists of water and is further used in the process. 

4. Condenser preconcentration. The preconcentration vapor (8) is condensed in an indirectly cooled heat exchanger. It is operated under the same vacuum conditions as the preconcentrator. The condensation of the vapor ensures that the vacuum pumps do not have to deal with large volume flows. 

5. Oxidizer. In the oxidizer, ferrous chloride (if present in the liquor) is oxidized to ferric chloride by means of autoclave oxidation according to (Eqn 1) 4 FeCl2 + 4 HCl + O2 → 4 FeCl3 + 2 H2O (Eqn 2) 12 FeCl2 + 3 O2 → 8 FeCl3 + 2 Fe2O3

(Eqn 1) occurs if free hydrogen chloride is present in the solution. If no free HCl is present, ferrous chloride is oxidized according to the overall reaction in (Eqn 2) which is the sum of the reactions (Eqn 1) and (Eqn 3). For the oxidation, pure oxygen gas (11) is used; typically the reactor is operated at 150°C and 3-7 bar(g). 

6. Hydrolyser. In this process step, the selective hydrolysis of ferric chloride occurs: (Eqn 3) 2 FeCl3 + 3 H2O → Fe2O3 + 6 HCl 

Hematite, Fe2O3, precipitates and hydrogen chloride evaporates together with water. The specific equilibrium vapor hydrogen chloride concentration is a function of temperature, pressure, and the concentrations of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides. In order to maintain the hydrolysis equilibrium, water (14) is added to the hydrolyser and hydrolyser solution is continuously removed (16). The hydrolyser is operated at atmospheric pressure and 160-190°C. 

7. Recuperator. The recuperator is a heat exchanger, which heats the preconcentrator by condensation of the hydrolysis vapor (15). 

8. Cooler hydrolysis solution. This heat exchanger is used for lowering the temperature of the suspension (16). 

9. Hematite filtration. Typically, a vacuum belt filter is used for this purpose; therefore fumes (21) will be sucked off by vacuum pumps. Distillate from the preconcentrator (19) is used

for the rinsing of the oxide in order to lower the chloride

concentration and losses of valuable metal chlorides in the hematite (20). 

10. Crystallization. The filtrate from hematite filtration is sent to the crystallization of nonhydrolysable metal chlorides. In this process step, almost pure hydrogen chloride gas (19) is sparged into the solution in order to lower the solubility of those metal chlorides. 

11. Filtration of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides. Crystallized metal chlorides (25) are removed from the suspension. The filtrate, rich in FeCl3 and HCl, can be either sent directly back to the hydrolyser or to another evaporation process for the recovery of concentrated HCl gas (which, in turns, can be used again for crystallization). 

12. Flash evaporation. The filtrate from crystallization (26) is heated and highly concentrated hydrogen chloride (27) is driven off. 

13. Acid purification. For the production of hydrogen chloride gas (23) which is required for the crystallization process, the condensed hydrolysis vapor (17), the gaseous flash product (27), and fresh make-up acid (28) are distillated in a single stage superazeotropic rectification column. 

14. Water balancing. The proposed flow sheet has a closed water balance. Water required in the process, e.g. for filter cake rinsing, is taken from the preconcentrator distillate. Water brought by ore moisture or from elsewhere in the process, is released as excess water (29). 

The extraction of the valuable metals from the metal chloride mix (25) is not part of this paper, although options similar to existing hydromet laterite processes<sup>(25)</sup> are proposed here: 

- Re-dissolution of the salts, oxide precipitation with magnesium oxide, common oxide processing and acid recovery from the magnesium chloride brine (e.g. by pyrohydrolysis or evaporation and roasting). 

- Re-dissolution of the salts, and solvent extraction which has been tested for various feeds<sup>(26-29)</sup> followed by HCl recovery from MgCl2.

###### **Leaching** 

In a stirred reactor with a heat jacket for temperature control, 400 g of milled laterite ore is placed. At the start of the experiment, 1570 g of temperature adjusted 20 wt% hydrochloric acid is added resulting in an acid-to-ore ratio of 1.25. This acid-to-ore ratio has been found effective for leaching<sup>(9)</sup> . 20 wt% hydrochloric acid is used as this order of magnitude is typical for industrial applications (e.g. carbon steel pickling: 18 wt%). 

###### **Hydrolysis** 

For the selective hydrolysis of ferric chloride, a similar setup as in a previous study<sup>(21)</sup

> is used; see Figure 3. At the start of the experiment, a 75 wt% FeCl3 solution is placed in the reactor and heated to the desired set-point temperature. Then, de-ionized water is fed into the reactor. The distillate is sampled; when the distillate concentration is constant, the feed is switched to a solution containing 30 wt% FeCl3, 60 wt% H2O and 10 wt% non-hydrolysable metal chlorides. The chosen ratio of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides under themselves is the same as present in the ore; see Table 1. Samples from both the distillate and the reactor solution are taken every 15-30 min. They are analyzed by ICP-OES and titration. At the end of the experiment, the reactor’s content is filtrated. h is based on some experiments performed, although the experimental conditions do not fit exactly the conditions assumed as this is a part of ongoing work. In order to avoid trial and error<sup>(18)</sup> , the favored procedure of developing such a flow sheet is step-wise: A heat and mass balance is calculated based on several assumptions; in an iterative procedure these assumptions are experimentally evaluated leading to a refinement of the balances. This iterative process is necessary due to the cycle Hydrolyser [6] to Crystallization [10], where the reflux affects both hydrolysis equilibrium and crystallization curves. The status of this work is the first set of experiments, which are more or less based on a feed forward process (which is however not aimed): 

- A one-stage leaching experiment is conducted; however, for the heat- and mass balance, a more sophisticated system is assumed. Anyway, for hydrochloric acid processes leaching can be considered as not difficult compared to the rest of the flow sheet<sup>(30)</sup> . 

- For the hydrolysis experiments, the ratio of non-hydrolysable elements is chosen similarly to the contents of aqua regia digestion. Including the reflux as calculated in the mass balance, will shift the hydrolysis equilibrium. Especially the hydrolysis equilibrium has a significant impact on the total energy consumption: Higher HCl vapor concentrations avoid the evaporation of high amounts of water and reduces the energy consumption during acid purification. Higher concentrations of non-hydrolysable metal chlorides in the hydrolyser will reduce the amount bled and therefore the amount of HCl gas required and the energy required for cooling and re-heating. 

- For the crystallization experiment, generic solubility limits were targeted. This goal has hardly been met, as only the last data points show a significant decrease in concentration. Also, the concentration of ferric chloride has not been met in the experiments (44 wt% desired, 35 wt% achieved). This decreases the chloride activity in the solution and thus a higher concentration of hydrogen chloride gas is required. In turn, this increases the cooling demand in the crystallization process and also the energy consumption in the 

ALTA 2013 

386 

acid purification process. The – potentially higher – concentration of non-hydrolysables in the reflux leads to lower concentration ratios in the hydrolyser. 

- For this first shot, trace elements are neglected. Due to the reflux nature of the cycle Hydrolyser [6] to Crystallization [10], any trace elements/ions can be concentrated in the cycle, as long as they do not hydrolyze, as long as they are not removed as moisture with one of the filter cakes, and as long as they do not evaporate. For the full study of the ore it is therefore also necessary to run the experiments continuously (e.g. in a laboratory mini plant) with the original leachate. This will lead also to refinements in the heat and mass balance. 

- Some pro

cesses are not investigated experimentally at this stage. This is due to their small impact on the process performance and the dependency on project settings (e.g. Preconcentration [3]). Others are not studied because they are well known from available thermo-chemical data<sup>(32)</sup> (e.g. Acid purification [13]) or from the experience with the SMS Siemag industrial-scale proto type in Calvert, Alabama, U.S. (e.g. Oxidation [5]). Again others will be part of future studies (e.g. Flash distillation [12]). 

Regarding the process flow sheet and the principal performance of the process especially in terms of hematite analysis (Table 5), iron can be rather selectively separated from chloride solutions. For this specific ore it can be even considered to omit the oxidation process as the concentration of ferrous chloride is rather low. If this was done, FeCl2 would end up with the nonhydrolysable metal chlorides. If required by down-stream processes, subsequent reduction of ferric or oxidization of ferrous chloride in the chloride mix can be due to the comparable small mass flow considered as easy. 

Due to the facts mentioned above, it is expected that the energy consumption goes down with a better agreement of mass balance and experimental conditions. Anyway, a major disadvantage of atmospheric leaching and therefore of hydrochloric acid processes is the non-selective leaching behavior<sup>(25)</sup> . For the described process, the steady-state energy demand is determined by the leachate iron concentration and the iron-to-other metals-ratio. The more iron contained, the more hydrochloric acid has to be boiled off increasing the energy consumption. If significant amounts of non-valuable metals are contained in the ore (such as Mg), the acid consumption increases, which furthermore increases the make-up acid consumption and the need for the acid regeneration from magnesium chloride brine. Selective leaching is therefore anticipated, which will be part of a future study. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

In this work, a hydrochloric acid flow sheet for treating nickel laterites is proposed. This flow sheet consists of leaching ore with hydrochloric acid, brine oxidation, hydrolysis of ferric chloride recovering hydrochloric acid, and crystallization of other metal chlorides by means of sparging hydrogen chloride into the solution. Experiments regarding leaching, hydrolysis, and crystallization were presented and a simplified mass and heat balance was calculated. 

The thermal energy consumption for driving the iron separation and hydrochloric acid regeneration process was calculated to be 12 GJ/t of laterite ore. However, as mass balance and experimental conditions did not fit exactly, this value has to be considered as preliminary result of ongoing work. It is expected to go down by refining conditions leading to a better agreement. Anyway, it could be demonstrated that a rather pure hematite and a filter cake containing only traces of FeCl3 can be separ

ated in hydrolysis and crystallization, respectively. 

Generally, the leaching strategy used in this work, i.e. non-selective dissolution of leachable compounds, does not seem to be promising as it consumes significant amounts of acid. Although hydrochloric acid can be recovered from chloride brines this is a matter of energy consumption.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Cost effective planning and consideration is required when outsourcing specialized titanium welding contractors to perform both planned and emergency on-site maintenance, repairs and modifications on titanium pressure equipment and piping. There are many facets to consider to organizing specialized weld repair teams ready to commence work upon arrival on a work site. Plant maintenance managers who outsource titanium repair scopes should consider the following: Leaching plants using titanium and other high-end corrosion service materials should develop a core relationship with the group of specialized, experienced contracted service to develop a seamless work flow during critical path activities; This includes early involvement of the specialized welding contractor to define the effective scope of work and confirm repair outcomes; knowing there are often multiple disciplines (contractors) involved in most tasks and how crucial to identify and harness any experience within the nominated contractors during the remedial assessment. Longer term relationships can benefit by involving contractors in the plants’ routine inspections and more importantly during any failure assessment. A contractor must become familiar with each plant’s staff, the process circuit, operations systems and facilities to become an integral part of the plants’ reliability team. The plant managers should tap into the valuable information an experienced titanium repair team can offer when defining and forecasting effective maintenance strategies.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Specialized maintenance is often a costly operation due to limited understanding of the complexities associated with sourcing, resourcing, handling, preparing, qualifying, facilitating, and conformance prior to titanium weld repair teams and allied services arriving on site. 

The assessment of significant titanium repairs should consider the following list of activities before the repairs are started: 

- Mi

nimum lead times to procure materials and define resources for routine maintenance. 

- The value of involvement from experience contractor when performing failure investigation. 

- The benefits of compiling structured engineered repair plans, both short and long term. 

- Roles and responsibilities when conforming to statutory requirements. 

- The value of compiling a detail and accurate repair schedule. 

- Defining the minimum labor levels and skill-set required amongst the repair teams. 

- Timely and practical compilation of the inspection test plan and work instructions. 

- Performing the materials /weld take-off and compiling the equipment and tool list. 

- Compiling the repair budget up front. 

- Define and confirmation of the repair crews, with timely coordination and mobilization. 

- Allowing for all site prerequisites are accessible to minimize obstruction to repair front. 

Prompt, effective weld repair happens on site when a relationship with professional and experienced repair teams exists between the plant Managers, Engineers, Planners and Supervisors. 

The integral relation and utilization of available experience with each repair is often the key to efficient repairs. 

###### **ASSESSMENT** 

Plant and equipment can be compromised due to any number of performance issues ranging from: 

- Under design. (Mechanical, materials, process) 

- Original equipment manufacturer and/or maintenance workmanship. 

- Process deterioration (Erosion, corrosion). 

- Process excursions. 

- Introduced contamination. 

- Secondary damage from internal activities. 

- Etc. 

The main remedial objective is to reinstate the equipment integrity to meet process parameters as per original design criteria, unless engineering design has been identified as part of root cause. 

Determining the actual mode and root-cause of failure of the plant and equipment is paramount. This may require the enlistment of both experienced and qualified plant (internal/external) experts to perform root cause analysis (RCA). 

A thorough RCA is often not contusive to plant production schedules and the need to perform a timely localized failure assessments utilizing the experience of those involved in the repair is typical. 

Strategically recording and removal of an affected material samples, making particular note of the various attributes within the affected area, can be key to determining the root-cause and initial failure assessment.

Experienced repair teams will be involved in the removal of meaningful samples to assist the Metallurgist's examinations. Some compromises may need to be considered to use certain insitu examination techniques, ie microscope, replications, portable hardness and other NDE process. 

Metallurgist, Vessel Design, Process and Welding Engineers will determine the root-cause and define the repair objectives within safe equipment operating parameters, which meet statutory requirements. 

Each plant will adopt an in-servi

ce inspection standard, which specifies minimum investigation criteria. Examples of standards include: API 510; AS 3788 

Once a failure assessment and the repair method have been compiled with participation from stake holders, experts and supplementary contribution from repair contractors when requested, a repair statement is compiled by the Asset Owner (and/or plant Engineers) and issued to the Repair Coordinator who issues the documents to the assigned planners, supervisors, inspectors, NDE, heat treaters, etc to devise their respective work instructions, inspection and test plans and other quality assurance documents.

###### **STATUTORY** 

The majority of process plants operating around the world are required to meet the local government operations laws. These laws are legal obligations and are known as statutory regulations. 

The United States, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and other international communities have all adopted a code of conduct, which specifies the minimum legal obligations a process plant owners shall follow to assure safe operation for its workers and the surrounding communities. 

If a plant’s pressure equipment, piping or other integral components become damaged  during operations or maintenance or subject to unacceptable rate of deterioration, this  damage may be determined as non compliant with statutory requirements, becoming categorized as a “notifiable” repair and shall be reported to local authorities. The local authorities will require details of how the damage has occurred and the engineered method of repair to recognized standards and regulatory laws. An engineered repair statement will need to be compiled and presented to the local authorities for review and comment. Once the minimum statutory requirements have been adequately considered and satisfied, the repair statement is then approved for the process plant to commence repairs. 

Each stage of the approved repairs must provide traceability to demonstrate that the minimum repair criteria has been met and properly recorded with the minimum required information for archiving in the plant’s technical library. 

###### **REPAIR STATEMENT** 

The repair statement (or repair plan) is the crucial remedial document, which drives the main repair objectives and demonstrates that the minimum statutory requirements have been met (as abovementioned). The statement covers key engineering, safety, statutory, quality, and reliability aspects. It should be known that failure investigations can also implicate other problems elsewhere in the circuit or in another train of same design, manufacture and process conditions. 

When a plant completes the investigation and determines extent of the remedial works to improve design and equipment performance, Mechanical, Production and Process Engineers may need to consider temporary or incremental strategies to be implemented due to

plant production constraints. This does not remove the process plant’s obligation to assure safe operating condition of the equipment after partial or staged repairs. Engineers shall compile a draft repair statement, which meets the satisfaction of the statutory authorities and the company board. 

The repair teams will compile a series of documents demonstrating their understanding and ability to meet quality requirements. There are many document forms, which are used to present and record quality aspects of a critical repair.

The typical forms common to virtually all repairs are noted here as: Job Hazard Analysis (JHA); Inspection & Test Plan (ITP); Work Instruction (WI); Materials and consumables traceability record sheet; Drawings; Production Schedule; Weld Procedure Specifications (WPS); Welder Performance Qualifications (WPQ); Equipment calibration certificates; NDE test requests; Heat treatment charts; Coating conformance; Etc. 

The documents mentioned are all collated as a Repair-Traceability-Dossier (RTD) which may go by another name. This compilation of the RTD should regularly maintained and be available for audit by the process plant quality department and statutory authorities during repairs. 

###### **HUMAN RESOURCING** 

The issuing of approved the repair statement allows Repair Coordinators and Planners to work with Supervisors to determine the manning and skill levels required to do the work. Pressure equipment repairs can employ a number of skilled disciplines to isolate, secure, clean and prepare repair areas for remedial activities. 

Skilled resources include: Isolation Officers; Safety Representatives; Mechanical Fitters; Equipment Cleaners; Crane Operators and Riggers; Scaffolders; Inspectors; Supervisors; Qualified Welders; NDE Technicians; Heat treatment; Grit Blasters; Coaters; Insulators; Others. 

This does not include the Managers, Engineers, Planners, Repair-Coordinators and Administrators integral to repair activities. 

Background support personnel may also include: immigration; travel; accommodation and support amenities. 

This extent of resources required can be significantly increased when: Day and night shift coverage; Restricted labor hours per week (local industrial labor laws); Availability of specific experienced skilled labor at given time; Length of time a resource may commit; The length of time the resource will be required and R&R arrangements. 

Human resources will often have a high cost impact on specialized maintenance work if planning, sourcing, provision and coordination are not determined and managed prior to the start of the job. 

###### **_Establishing a contusive team at every level is essential when striving to maximize maintenance efficiencies and to minimize down time during scheduled maintenance and emergency breakdowns!_** 

###### **SPECIALIZED TITANIUM REPAIR TEAMS** 

Gathering a group of titanium welders is arguably not the most difficult task on most major co

ntinents around the world. However gathering an experienced, qualified, certified, site-savvy titanium repair team is not the same!  There are only a limited number of reputable specialized (weld) maintenance companies available.  In some regions there may not be any. 

An experienced site-savvy manager, supervisor and welding supervisor must understand: 

- There can be limited access to specialized equipment, consumables, materials, accessories, tooling and jigging components in remote locations. 

- Possibility of having to contend with a range of process affected materials. Or dealing poor workmanship and discovering imperfections and defects. 

- Requirement of difficult in-situ repairs as opposed to more controlled remove and repair environment in workshop conditions. 

- Quantities of inert shielding gas with the qualified purity may not be readily available - including special considerations for different regulator to cylinder fittings when working in new country. 

- Workspace specifically set-up with equipment, tooling and peripherals dedicated to titanium weld contamination control and segregation.

###### **REMEDIAL SCOPE REQUIREMENTS** 

A detailed and approved repair method statement and scope of work is essential for any assigned specialized weld repair contractor, as they must understand what is actually available and accessible in the required time frame and what will need to be procured, issued or supplied. 

This extends to various onsite items and includes: 

- Grade / specifications of titanium materials, ie grade, product form, (sheet, plate, pipe, forging, castings, etc.). 

- Materials and weld takeoff to determine the grade, type and amount of welding consumables, i.e. shielding gas, filler metal and any preparation equipment. 

- The labor skill set of repair team required by the plant may include fitters, trade assistant to work with experience/ qualified titanium welders. 

- Readily available procurement of any required facilities, equipment, materials or consumables, that which can be sourced locally and that must be transported ahead of repair team. 

- The amount of lead-time needed to get tooling, equipment and coordination of facilitation to the site. This may also include more stringent focus when items are being sent to another country with customs and duty requirements. 

- Additional time allocated for site inductions, orientation, and array of approved training requirements recognized by the plant. This includes: confined space; working at heights; hot works; breathing apparatus. 

- Possible requirement of specific non-standard NDE methods and equipment. This should be covered in the repair method statement.

###### **NANOSTRUCTURED AND CONVENTIONAL CR2O3, TIO2 AND TIO2-CR2O3 THERMAL SPRAYED COATINGS FOR METAL SEATED BALL VALVE APPLICATIONS IN HYDROMETALLURGY** 

By 

1Luc Vernhes, Craig Bekins, Nicolas Lourdel, 2Dominique Poirier, Rogerio S. Lima, 

3Duanjie Li, Jolanta E. Klemberg-Sapieha 

1Velan, Canada 

2National Research Council of Canada, Canada 

3Polytechnique Montreal, Canada 

Presenter and Corresponding Author 

**Luc Vernhes** luc.vernhes@velan.com 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Thermal sprayed ceramic coatings are successfully employed to enhance the load carrying capacity and the tribological performance of the base material in order to extend the in-service life of equipment, including metal-seated ball valves (MSBV’s) in Hydrometallurgy service. Ceramic coatings are vital to protect machines in the harsh abrasive conditions encountered in corrosive processes such as Pressure Oxidation (POx) and High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL). 

Velan, a leading designer and manufacturer of industrial valves, has 20 years of experience in the engineering of severe service MSBV’s for critical isolatio

n applications around the autoclave. The National Research Council of Canada (NRC) in Boucherville and Polytechnique Montreal have world recognized know-how on coating engineering and characterization, in particular for wear. 

A detailed characterization project was undertaken by Velan in collaboration with the NRC and Polytechnique Montreal to perform mechanical and tribological resistance evaluation of the most promising ceramic coatings potentially suitable for this service, including a novel blend of n-TiO2Cr2O3. Hardness and shear strength were evaluated using micro-hardness indentation testers and universal tensile testing equipment. Wear resistance of the coatings under different conditions such as sliding wear, abrasion and galling were measured by standard pin-on-disc tests, abrasion tests and custom-design galling tests. 

It was found that TiO2-Cr2O3 offers superior tribological performances compared to n-TiO2, mainly due to the presence of Cr2O3. Optimized balance between the hard and brittle Cr2O3 phases and the soft and ductile TiO2 phases yields to higher abrasion, sliding and galling resistance. In parallel, the novel mix of n-TiO2 and Cr2O3 is considered as a promising evolution of the current TiO2-Cr2O3 blend. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Over the last two decades, metal-seated ball valves (MSBV’s) have become the industry standard for Hydrometallurgy application, providing tight, reliable shut-off in this critical service which facilitates maintenance and contributes to a safe working environment. Typical MSBV’s design for this application consists of a floating ball in contact with a fixed seat. Ball and seats are manufactured with either titanium or duplex stainless steels substrates and protected with a ceramic coating. The primary function of the ceramic coating is to enhance the load carrying capacity and the tribological performance of the base material in order to extend the in-service life of the equipment, especially during ball motion phases. 

Conventional Cr2O3 applied by Air Plasma Spray (APS) was the coating selected 20 years ago to protect MSBV’s against the extreme abrasion, pressure and elevated temperature inherent to the Pressure Oxidation (POx) recovery process used for gold where the ore is mixed with oxygen and sulfuric acid into an autoclave. Over the years, based on field experiences, silicon dioxide and titanium dioxide have been gradually added to the originally pure Cr2O3 blend in order to improve its ductility and toughness. Velan’s Cr2O3 blend has proved itself in gold extraction technologies such as Nerco's Con Gold mine - Canada, Barrick Goldstrike, and Lone Tree mines - USA. Lihir and Porgera Gold Mines in Papua - New Guinea’s have also reported good experience with Velan Cr2O3 blend material applied to MSBV’s<sup>(1)</sup> . 

Similar to POx, High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) is a recovery process for nickel where the laterite ore is leached in a sulfuric acid environment into an autoclave at 4.1

bar (600 psi) and temperatures above 240ºC (464ºF). Unlike POx, HPAL process operates at high pressure that, combined with a higher chloride content, leads to a more corrosive environment (i.e. Titanium is susceptible to crevice corrosion in HPAL). Based on Velan’s experience with different coating blends at Falconbridge mines - Canada, Cr2O3 blend optimized for POx corrodes prematurely when used in HPAL. Being relatively inert in such an environment, TiO2 seems an instinctive choice for HPAL<sup>(2)</sup> . However, conventional TiO2 mechanical and tribological performances are significantly lower than those of Cr2O3 leading to higher wear rates, as experienced by Velan at Cawse and Murin-Murin nickel mines - Australia. 

The industry has been working to optimize coating solutions for HPAL<sup>(3)</sup> . Several options have been considered and unsuccessfully tested by different companies to mitigate corrosion. This includes the use of intermediate bond coats, such as gold and tantalum, in between the base material and the Cr2O3 top coat. One engineering firm has utilized a nanostructured TiO2 coating, which has worked reasonably well at Ravensthorpe – Australia  and Ramu – Papua New Guinea<sup>(4,5)</sup> . At the same time, Velan has developed a proprietary ceramic blend containing TiO2 and Cr2O3 in order to get the corrosion resistance of a pure TiO2 and the tribological performances of Cr2O3. This coating has demonstrated superior performance on several HPAL projects, including Coral Bay - Philippines and performs satisfactorily on most recent installations such as Goro - New Caledonia and Ambatovy – Madagascar (1). All critical isolation valves installed on the recent Taganito - Philippines project have also been supplied with this optimized TiO2-Cr2O3 blend. 

In collaboration with the NRC and Polytechnique Montreal, a detailed characterization project was undertaken by Velan to perform mechanical and tribological resistance evaluations of the most promising ceramic coatings potentially suitable for Hydrometallurgy application, including a novel nano-structured blend of n-TiO2-Cr2O3. All test results have been compiled to help Velan selecting the appropriate coating to optimize the MSBV’s performance in POx and HPAL applications. 

Section 2 describes experimental procedures, including materials and characterization techniques. Section 3 presents research findings and their analysis. Section 4 concludes.
