###### **Characterization Techniques** 

###### **_Microstructure_** 

Microstructures of the coatings were obtained with a JSM-6100 SEM from JEOL or the FE-SEM Hitachi S4700, under back-scattered electron (BSE) mode. EDS analyses were performed using JEOL JSM-840 SEM. Coatings were sectioned with a coolant-assisted diamond wheel and then cold vacuum mounted in an epoxy resin.  Grinding and polishing were done using standard metallographic preparation procedures 

###### **_Mechanical Property Characterization_** 

Micro-Hardness and shear strength were evaluated using respectively micro-hardness indentation testers and universal tensile testing equipment. 

Microhardness measurements were performed on coating polished cross-sections with a Buehler Micromet II Tester (Vickers Tip) under a 300 gf load. For each specimen, a minimum of 12 indentations was performed (straight line pattern, at the center of the coating cross section), and the highest and lowest values removed from the dataset. 

Coating adhesion on Ti substrate was assessed through shear tests (ASTM F1044 respectively). An Instron 5582 universal testing machine was used to determine the maximum shear loads required to obtain sample separation. 

###### **_Tribological Behavior Evaluation_** 

Wear resistance of the coatings under different conditions such as sliding wear and abrasion were measured by standard pin-on-disc tests and abrasion tests. Galling resistance was measured using a custom-designed and automated galling tester. 

###### _Sliding Wear Resistance_ 

A custom-made pin-on-disc tribometer was employed to evaluate the sliding wear behavior of the coatings. A normal load of 25 N was applied to a tungsten carbide ball (4.75 mm diameter) used as a counterpart material. A new ball was used for each test. The diameter of the wear track ring, d, was 7 mm and the rotation speed was 546 revolutions per minute (rpm). This results in a linear 

speed of 20 cm/s. (7.9 in/s.). The coefficient of friction, COF, was recorded every second during the test. The wear rate, K, was evaluated using the formula K=V/(FЧs), where V is the worn volume, F is the normal load, and is the sliding distance. Pin-on-disc wear track profiles were evaluated by the Sloan Dektak II profilometer, and the wear track morphology was examined by optical microscopy (Nikon Epiphot 200). 

###### _Dry Sand Abrasion Resistance_ 

Coating dry abrasion resistance was tested through dry sand/rubber wheel abrasion test (ASTM G65 / procedure D-modified, 45 N, 2000 wheel revolutions, Durometer A-60 wheel).  Two samples were tested for each coating type. Prior testing, the sample surfaces were ground with diamond wheel to produce a surface finish of about 0.2-0.3 µm. Evaluation of the sample volume loss due to the test was performed with an optical profilometer. 

###### _Wet Sand Abrasion Resistance_ 

Coating wet abrasion r

esistance by means of wet sand / rubber wheel was measured following ASTM G105-02 modified procedure guidelines using a Falex® sand abrasion test machine and controlled slurry. For each coating type, one rectangular shape specimen (1’’ x 3’’ x 0.5’’) has been submitted to a 5,000 cycles run with 22 N normal load using a 7’’ diameter and Durometer A-60 neoprene rubber wheel at a nominal speed of 245 rpm. The slurry mixture was composed of rounded quartz grain sand AFS 50/70 and deionized water with respect to the ratio of 0.940 kg water / 1.500 kg sand. Prior testing, the sample surfaces were ground with diamond wheel to produce a surface finish of about 0.2-0.3 µm. Test allowed for ranking coating that resists penetration to its substrate while wet abrasion rate has been reported as mass loss (accuracy +/0.1 mg) of the specimen. ###### _Variable Temperature Galling Resistance_ Galling resistance was measured using a custom-designed and automated galling tester developed by Engineered Valve International Inc. in collaboration with Velan (see _Figure 2_ ). The tester consists in quarter-turn rotating an annular coated specimen (dia. 1.25’’ x 1.5’’ thickness, 1 in2 coated surface) against a second annular coated and fixed specimen under controlled contact pressure, stroke motion and temperature conditions. Contact load and stroke motions are respectively applied with a pneumatic thrust actuator (Samson 3277) and a quarter-turn actuator (Metso B1CU6/20L) while the temperature is adjusted with a radiation-type furnace (Lindberg Blue M Tube Furnace) coupled with a K-Type thermocouple probe tack-welded on one specimen. All test parameters are controlled from a centralized panel. Coated surface of each specimen is successively prepared and inspected before being tested. The coated surface preparation consists in manually polishing with several grades of polishing clothes (from P320 to P1200 grit) using a thin buffer of commercial machinery oil. The specimen inspection allows for selecting specimens presenting a surface roughness Ra below 10 µin with a flatness below 0.005 inch in addition to measuring the specimen mass (+/- 0.5 mg). For each coating type, one set of two self-mated specimens has been tested according to the procedure detailed in _Table 2_ . The test procedure is stopped as soon as one coated specimen displays significant wear pattern (ex.: micro-welding, scoring). ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

In this study, the load carrying capacity and the tribological resistances of 4 ceramic coatings potentially suitable for HPAL have been evaluated. 

Pure Cr2O3 blend has shown the highest hardness and best sliding wear resistance and COF while the n-TiO2 has demonstrated the lowest hardness, the poorest wear rate and the highest COF. As 

predicted by the intuition, Cr2O3-TiO2 and n-TiO2-Cr2O3 blends have offered hardness and sliding measurements in between the measurements of each pure ceramics in its composition. 

When looking at abrasion, our study shows positive and counter intuitive results. n-TiO2-Cr2O3 blends has obtained superior resistance for both dry and wet abrasion test compare to other pure ceramics. According to a study published by Velan, the high performance of the TiO2-Cr2O3 has been attributed to the optimized balance between the hard and brittle Cr2O3 phases and the soft and ductile TiO2 phases. The current paper shows how the synergy between those two materials yields to abrasion performances exceeding the one of each individual. 

When looking at galling, n-TiO2-Cr2O3 ranks 1<sup>st</sup> by achieving the highest number of steps prior significant wear patterns observation and by exhibiting low mass loss. Cr2O3 , TiO2-Cr2O3 and n-TiO2 are respectively ranked 2<sup>nd</sup> , 3<sup>rd</sup> and 4<sup>th</sup> . 

Promisingly, the novel mix of n-TiO2 and Cr2O3 has systematically offered better tribological performance than Velan proprietary TiO2-Cr2O3 blend. Consequently this novel blend appears as a promising evolution of the current TiO2-Cr2O3 blend. Further optimization is needed to commercialize use. 

Works is still needed to optimize surface preparation, spraying procedure and post-treatment for the novel mix of Cr2O3 and n-TiO2 in order to achieve equivalent or better results than current TiO2Cr2O3 blend, especially regarding bond and shear strength. Indeed, current TiO2-Cr2O3 has displayed the highest bond and shear strength compare to all other materials, including the nanocoatings. Developing an HVOF process capable of spraying TiO2-Cr2O3 could be an interesting process to achieve these results.  The challenge for such development is to ensure melting of the Cr2O3 particles in order to avoid the rebound of those particles when impacting the substrate as well as the erosion of the deposited TiO2 layer by the same

particles. 

Works is also needed to secure supply chain and develop quality standard for this novel material in order to avoid production delays and / or quality issues. Furthermore corrosion tests will be required to fully assess material corrosion performance with different types of sealant. 

In the meantime, in view of those recent results, TiO2-Cr2O3 offers the best overall tribological performance compare to other tested ceramics, namely Cr2O3 and n-TiO2.

By

The University of Queensland, Australia

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Worldwide there is a large research effort into technologies for the sequestration of CO2 due to the overwhelming concern of what might happen if there is a runaway greenhouse effect. One potential technology being pursued examines whether the enormous re

serves of magnesium silicates in the earth could be converted to magnesium carbonate which is considered to be a safer option than the storage of supercritical CO2 deep underground. But a viable technology has not been found because the use of acid and base, in the traditional processing sense, is prohibitive due to the scale and need for both low energy and low cost. One idea that might circumvent this problem is to use a regenerable buffer to enable both low pH for Mg dissolution and high pH for MgCO3 carbonation. 

Given that the magnesium silicate reserves of interest also contain significant levels of Ni, it could be worthwhile to combine the CO2 sequestration pursuit with the pursuit of Ni extraction, whereby a symbiotic relationship exists and the two operations can assist each other to achieve technical, environmental and economic process goals. 

This paper presents our work to date on the use of a tertiary amine as a regenerable buffer, including a process concept. We have found that both tripropylamine and triethylamine are capable of raising the pH of an acidic solution to over 8 and therefore able to precipitate MgCO3 when added to the extract solution from the treatment of serpentinite with HCl while low pressures of CO2 are also sparged into the solution. Precipitation of the carbonate was found to occur within minutes. It has been found that the amine can be regenerated through heating to over 80ºC. Preliminary work has shown that the pH can be decreased to 3.4. The precise mechanism for regeneration is still being established, however, it appears that when heated, the miscibility of triethylamine in water decreases dramatically and that phase separation of it might be the driving force for the dissociation of protons from the amine. 

Future work is focused on: Potential for amines to be regenerated such that the corresponding acid concentration is capable of dissolving both Mg and Ni from serpentinites in a reasonable timeframe; evaluation of technical feasibility of each unit operation needed for the overall process; determination of potential for selective precipitation of Mg and Ni carbonates; identification of optimum amine and acid counter ion. If the process is successful with a sulphate counter ion there is also the potential to treat Mg sulphate tailings to regenerate sulphuric acid.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

There is currently a significant research effort into the development of a process to convert Mg in serpentine minerals into magnesium carbonate (MgCO3) as a means to sequester CO2 from power stations<sup>(1-11)</sup> . The stumbling block has been a viable means to dissolve magnesium from the serpentine and then raise the pH to precipitate MgCO3 on a large scale, ie. without the need to purchase either acid or base. The University of Queensland has been investigating a novel concept, which is to use a tertiary amine as a regenerable buffer<sup>(12,13)</sup> . Tertiary amines complex protons stro

ngly at low temperatures, however, the strength of the bond decreases with increasing temperature and so they release protons at higher temperature. The concept therefore involves treating serpentine with acid loaded amine at a moderate temperature of approximately 90ºC whereupon protons are released and react with the serpentine to release Mg into solution, as shown by the stepwise reactions 1a and 1b. The unreacted silica is gravity separated and the solution is cooled to ambient temperature and sparged with CO2. At the low temperature protons in solution are attracted to the amine and the pH rises causing MgCO3 to precipitate, as shown by the stepwise reactions 2a and 2b. In order for this scheme to work, the pH generated by reaction 1a must be low enough for reaction 1b to occur within a reasonable time. Serpentine dissolution work has shown that for a temperature of 90°C the pH needs to be < 2 in order for the reaction to proceed in a few hours. As the pH exceeds 2 reaction times become excessive. While the kinetics of dissolution are strongly dependant on both pH and temperature it is possible that with higher temperatures above 100°C (and higher pressures) decent extractions could be achieved for pH > 2. The scheme also requires that the pH generated by reaction 2b is high enough for MgCO3 to precipitate. ###### **Precipitation of Carbonate** 

Samples of 0.5 g of serpentinite were treated with 10 ml aqueous solutions of 2.5 M HCl for 3 hours at ~100°C. Analysis of the solid using the ICP method described above showed that 85% of the Mg had dissolved into solution. This extract solution was then sparged with food grade CO2 regulated at 1.4 bar and with a flow set at approximately 1 L/min. During sparging triethylamine (TEA) or tripropylamine (TPA) was added dropwise via a burette while simultaneously measuring pH via a pH electrode. The solution was observed for the onset of precipitation. If a precipitate formed, it was filtered through Whatman no. 1 filter paper, dried and weighed. Precipitated solids were analysed by XRD and ICP-AES for compound and elemental determinations, as described above.

###### **RESULTS** 

###### **Precipitation of Carbonate** 

As triproplyamine (TPA) was added dropwise to the extract solution the pH increased to approximately 5 at which point a light brown precipitate formed which was found from elemental analysis to contain around 20.1 wt% Fe, 10.8 wt% Si, 5.5 wt% Al, 0.2 wt% Mg and no Ni. This product comes from the hydrolysis of Fe, Si and Al which dissolved during serpentine dissolution. After removing this precipitate by filtration further additions of TPA raised the pH to approximately 8.2 at which point a white precipitate formed. This precipitate began forming within a few minutes. After bubbling CO2 for 45 mins, the precipitate was recovered by filtration, dried and analysed. The weight was 0.20 g. XRD analysis indicated the formation of nesquehonite (MgCO3.3H2O). Elemental analysis showed that the purity was high with a composition of 18.8 wt% Mg, 0.2 wt%

Ni content in the carbonate product also shows that Ni precipitates as NiCO3 as the basicity increases. Ni carbonate has a significantly lower solubility than Mg carbonate and should be possible to selectively separate. Further work is necessary to study the feasibility of selective precipitation. When triethylamine (TEA) was added instead of TPA the pH increased to 10.2 and simultaneously the solution became milky with precipitation, ie. the precipitation occurred very quickly. This is due to TEA being a stronger base and it follows that the kinetics of precipitation are strongly dependant on the basicity of the amine. ###### **Regeneration of Amine** When the solution made with a 1:1 molar solution of TEA and HCl was heated to approximately 84°C, the pH of the solution decreased from the initial level of 6.8 down to 3.4 after 120 minutes, as shown in Figure 3. The trend suggests that further heating would cause the pH to decrease further. This result is in line with the TEA-HCl bond strength decreasing with temperature. However, the pH level of 3.4 was maintained as the solution was cooled, suggesting that the pH change is not due to temperature swing regeneration. Given that the solution volume decreased from the initial level of 25 ml to approximately 10 ml, it is apparent that water and amine are evaporating from the system. However, the pH change cannot be solely explained as a concentration of HCl in solution on account of water evaporating as this would decrease the pH only mildly to 6. **Figure 3: pH of aqueous solution of TEA-HCl upon heating to 84°C.** The reason for the drop in pH can be explained by considering Figure 4 which shows the lower consolate temperature for amine-water mixtures. The lower consolate temperature is the temperature above which the amine and water are immiscible. TEA is shown by the open circles. The concentration of TEA-HCl in this system is only 1 wt% and so at low temperatures the small amount of TEA in equilibrium with TEA-HCl is miscible in water. As the temperature increases the miscibility of TEA reduces dramatically and phase separation of TEA is thought to occur and ALTA 2013 428 thought to be the driving force for dissociation of TEA-HCl, allowing the concentration of HCl in solution to increase and hence the pH to decrease. The reason why pH is maintained as the solution is cooled may be due to the concentration of amine increasing. Figure 4 shows that as the concentration of amine increases the lower consolute temperature decreases, therefore as the concentration of TEA increases the TEA is more immiscible, even at low temperatures of 20°C, suggesting that the amine remains immiscible as the temperature drops and does not re-enter the aqueous phase and rebond with the acid. 90

cal Society.** The boiling point of pure TEA is 89°C which means that the phase separated TEA could be selectively separated. In the simple single stage experiment conducted here the amine and water both boiled off to a substantial extent. This is not thought to be necessary and certainly evaporation of any component is undesirable due to the goal of minimising energy needs for the process. The latent heat of vapourisation for TEA is, however, only 15% of that for water. Further work is necessary to investigate the phase separation behaviour of TEA with temperature to examine the pH changes without evaporation, particularly evaporation of water. The effect of phase separation as the means to regenerate the buffer was not initially intended in this research, however, it could be an effective way to use TEA. For stage 1, the solution would be heated to cause TEA to phase separate and consequently enable the pH to drop to a sufficient level for acid to dissolve Mg and Ni out of the Mg silicate structure. The solution is then cooled which causes TEA to re-enter the aqueous phase and act as a buffer when CO2 is sparged into the solution in stage 2. ###### **DISCUSSION** This study has found that low concentrations of TEA in water have a strong tendency to phase separate with increasing temperature and that this may be an effective way to use TEA as a ALTA 2013 429 regenerable buffer in a process that simultaneously converts Mg in silicate ores to MgCO3 and extracts and concentrates Ni. Figure 5 shows a simplified schematic of how the process could work. In stage 1 the acid loaded amine from stage 4 would be heated to regenerate TEA. The liberated acid would dissolve Mg and Ni out of the laterite ore. The temperature would then be cooled to cause the TEA to re-enter the aqueous phase and bind with protons, thus causing the pH to rise. This cooling would be staged so as to enable stages 2, 3 and 4 to occur at progressively higher pH values. It might be necessary to selectively separate some TEA via evaporation in stage 1 through evaporation and then re-introduce it into stages 2, 3 and 4 to enable the pH increases to occur. In stage 2 the pH increases to 5 at which point any Al and Fe in the solution hydrolyse as a solid and can therefore be separated. In stage 3 the pH is raised to 7 and CO2 is sparged into the solution. Because NiCO3 has a substantially lower solubility product than MgCO3 it would precipitate first. Once separated it would be further processed into the desired Ni product. Following this the pH is raised further to approximately 8.5 to precipitate MgCO3 which is also separated and sent for storage. The solution, containing acid loaded amine returns to stage 1. After treating a serpentinite sample with HCl to extract Mg and Ni, it was found that the addition of either triethylamine or tripropylamine was capable of raising the pH above 8 and therefore capable of precipitating carbonates within minutes when CO2 was sparged into the solution at a low pressure of 1.4 bar. Regeneration of the triethylamine was found to be possible through heating. The precise mechanism of regeneration is still being sought, however, it appears that as the temperature increases TEA becomes immiscible in water and this provides a driving force for the dissociation of acid bound TEA. Further work is focused on examining the mechanism(s) by which acid loaded tertiary amines regenerate upon heating and from this establish their potential as regenerable buffers. By 

1J. Vaughan, 1W. Hawker, 2T. Keating, 3J. Cox 

1The University of Queensland, Australia 2UniQuest Pty Ltd, Australia 3Ausenco, Australia 

Presenters and Corresponding Authors 

###### **James Vaughan and Tony Keating** 

james.vaughan@uq.edu.au t.keating@uniquest.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The precipitation of mixed hydroxide is increasingly being considered as an intermediate step in the hydrometallurgical processing of nickel and cobalt. Producers currently receive roughly 75% of the value of the contained nickel and zero value for contained cobalt. In this paper, a new selective leach process for refining the mixed hydroxide is described that allows for recovery of the majority of the nickel as final metal product and realizes value for the cobalt. The features of the new process are compared with two other alternative routes (1) acid leaching followed by solvent extraction of the cobalt and (2) ammonia leaching followed by solvent extraction of the nickel. The outcomes of a process simulation for the selective acid leaching process are presented along with capital and operating cost estimates. The operating and capital costs of the process are estimated to ±50%. For the processing of 50,000 t-Ni/y in the form of MHP, the operating cost is estimated to be $93 million AUD ($0.87 per lb of Ni contained in MHP) and the capital cost as defined for this study is estimated to be $287 million AUD. A new 20 year plant processing MHP would have a payback period of less than 2 years, an IRR of over 60% and an NPV of greater than $1.5 billion AUD. Over 94% of the total value (nickel and cobalt) contained in the MHP is extracted by the new process.

###### **INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND** 

###### **Processing of Nickel** 

Nickel reserves are largely in the form of laterite ore bodies. While laterite ore is easy to mine relative to sulfide deposits found deeper underground, efficient processing has proven to be a challenge. One of the problems is that for most nickel laterite ore bodies, the extent to which the nickel can be concentrated by physical means is limited, thus the majority of the ore must be chemically processed. 

There are three main routes for chemical processing of nickel laterite ore, ferronickel smelting, reduction roast followed by ammonia leaching (the Caron process) and acid leaching (Figure 1). Ferronickel smelting is a high temperature process whereby the ore is melted and the dense ironnickel rich component is separated from the slag b

y gravity. Dueto the high energy requirement for heating, ferronickel smelting is limited to feed with nickel grades greater than 1.5%. Cobalt is not recovered in ferronickel smelting and the amount of cobalt in the feed that can be processed is restricted to a Ni:Co ratio of greater than 30 (Oxley and Barcza, 2012). In the Caron process, nickel and cobalt are liberated from the host mineral by a reduction roast making them available for selective leaching in an ammonia / ammonium carbonate liquor (Caron 1924). While some Caron operations continue, no Caron plants have been built in recent times. In the past 20 years, acid leaching processes have been selected for treating the low grade nickel laterite ore. High temperature and pressure acid leaching is particularly suitable for the iron rich fraction of the laterite ore as the dissolved iron tends to precipitate as hematite in the autoclave making the leaching process somewhat selective for nickel and cobalt (Carlson 1961). Developments have been made in ambient pressure acid leaching (Panagiotopoulos and Kontopoulos 1988) using continuous stirred tank (Liu et al 2004) or heap leach configurations (Readett and Fox 2009). Processes that make use of acids that can be recycled such as hydrochloric acid (Harris et al 2006) and nitric acid (McCarthy and Brock 2011) are also currently being considered for the treatment of nickel laterites ores. For the acid leaching processes, the solubilised nickel and cobalt can be concentrated and separated using solvent extraction as was practiced at Bulong in Western Australia and at Goro in New Caledonia. It is however more common to recover the nickel and cobalt from the leach solution together in a concentrated solid form by precipitation as a mixed sulphide or a mixed hydroxide. ||Ferronickel Smelting|| |---|---|---| |Nickel Laterite Ore|Caron Process|Solvent Extraction| ||Acid Leaching Process|Mixed Sulphide

The efficient separation is achieved by stabilising cobalt and manganese in the solid phase by oxidation. ###### **Ion Exchange** 

Pregnant leach solution passes through polishing filtration and the pH is adjusted to 3.0 prior to the ion exchange process. In ion exchange, zinc is removed from the pregnant leach solution using DEHPA (Di-2-ethyl hexyl phosphoric acid) impregnated cation exchange resin which is highly selective for zinc over nickel. Laboratory test work indicates that the zinc concentration in the catholyte can be maintained below 5 mg/L in the presence of 100 g/L nickel. The process configuration is two columns in series with a third column on standby or being regenerated. The nickel catholyte passes through a carbon filter prior to electrowinning to remove residual/minor amounts of organics (DEHPA) dissolved from the ion exchange resin.

###### **Nickel Electrowinning** 

The nickel electrowinning circuit is conventional with the only difference from current industrial practice being the elevated magnesium concentration in the electrolyte. It has been demonstrated that bright, smooth, coherent nickel electrodeposits can be produced with a catholyte feed of 60 g-Ni/L, 15 g-Mg/L at 60ºC, pH

2.5 and current density of 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> (Tripathy 2001). These results were confirmed with an electrowinning study at the University of Queensland using a catholyte containing 85 g-Ni/L, 20 g-Mg/L, 20 g-Na/L at the same operating conditions. In the current flowsheet, evaporative cooling is employed to control the catholyte feed solution to 50ºC. 

###### <u>Key reaction</u> 

###### NiSO4 (aq) + 2H2O  Ni (s) + 0.5 O2 (g) + H2SO4 

###### **Reductive Acid Selective Cobalt Leach (RASCL)** 

The remaining nickel along with the cobalt and manganese are extracted from the solid residue in the reductive leaching process. The process is carried out in two stages. In the first stage the pH is controlled to 2.5 to maximise the nickel and cobalt extraction. In the second stage the pH is adjusted to the range of 4-6 to precipitate dissolved impurity metals. The residue from this process could be recycled back to the start of the primary neutralisation stage (prior to MHP precipitation) to recover some of the small amount of nickel and cobalt in the residue. If the residue contains significant copper, a copper recovery process could also be considered.

###### **SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS** 

A new process for refining mixed hydroxide precipitate is described based on selectively leaching nickel at mildly acidic and strongly oxidising conditions. The new process is streamlined as the leaching of nickel and separation of nickel from cobalt, manganese and copper occurs in the same stage unlike alternative processes which require leaching followed by solvent extraction to achieve this outcome. Two scenarios were evaluated based on a feed of 50,000 t/y nickel in the form of mixed hydroxide, both of which are favourable, even at low nickel price. The impact of a smaller refinery and the location of the plant need to be carefully considered. The next stage in the process development is for a continuous integrated pilot plant campaign.
